detail.abstract: This paper reconstructs the FERZ doctrine as a unified analytical argument. Beginning with the distinction between observation and pre-execution authorization, it states the additional definitions and integrity requirements from which the runtime authorization boundary, authorization artifact, Authorization Boundary Integrity Model, and Five Tests Standard follow. The argument is conceptual and classificatory. It does not report empirical validation or claim that these constructs follow from a single premise alone. The derivation proceeds from the governance problem through the separation of authority, delegation, policy, authorization, and enforcement; positions the resulting structure relative to the reference-monitor, access-control, and runtimeverification traditions, to proof-carrying authorization and related evidence models, and to the provenance tradition; and culminates in the Authorization Non-Substitution Principle [1], for which the corpus's substitution analyses provide representative applications. An appended source map identifies the controlling publication for each doctrinal position, and a claim-status appendix states, for each principal construct, what kind of claim it is, how it can be independently examined, and what it does not establish.

title:
Artificial Intelligence in the Financial Sector:

Tools, Opportunities, Risks, And A Strategic Roadmap for the Next Decade
affiliations: and Unaffiliated Authors

detail.title:
Artificial Intelligence in the Financial Sector:

Tools, Opportunities, Risks, And A Strategic Roadmap for the Next Decade

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest

detail.abstract: Not long ago, artificial intelligence sat at the margins of financial-sector strategy a tool for shaving costs off back-office processes. It no longer does. AI now sits at the center of how banks, asset managers, and fintech firms think about competitive advantage, and this article tries to make sense of that shift. Drawing together research from Harvard Business School, Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI), and MIT Sloan Management Review, alongside a close technical case study of AI-driven venture-capital decision-making, it builds a working account of how artificial intelligence- large language models (LLMs) in particular- is remaking banking, asset management, and financial technology. Along the way it draws a sharper line than most practitioner writing does between the pattern-recognition logic of conventional machine learning and the generative, language-native reasoning that LLMs perform, then traces where each pays off across the buy side and sell side of the industry. The failures get equal billing with the successes: Knight Capital's algorithmic collapse, Zillow's home-pricing losses, and a run of recent agentic-AI incidents all feature, because the limits and ethical hazards of automated financial decision-making are as instructive as its gains. The article closes with a phased roadmap for responsible adoption, a ten-year outlook, and a look at how venture-capital financing patterns and professional networks are reshaping the fintech pipeline itself.

title: Survival Analysis and Burstiness of Order Cancellations as a Retention-Marketing Signal

detail.title: Survival Analysis and Burstiness of Order Cancellations as a Retention-Marketing Signal
detail.abstract: Retail order cancellations are almost universally treated in practice, and in the academic literature on this specific dataset, as noise to be filtered out before analysis. We treat cancellations instead as a genuine behavioral signal-a real-world, completed-and-reversed analogue of cart abandonment-using the publicly available UCI Online Retail transaction dataset (541,909 line items, a UK-based online gift retailer, Dec 2010-Dec 2011). First, using Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and Cox proportional-hazards regression on 7,846 cancellation events, we ask whether and when customers go on to repurchase a product they cancelled: 38.1% eventually do, with cumulative reconversion reaching 21% by 30 days and 44% by 180 days. Customers with a longer history of prior cancellations repurchase markedly faster after any given cancellation (hazard ratio 1.29 per logunit of prior cancellation count, p<0.001), while cancelling a larger quantity is associated with slower repurchase (hazard ratio 0.94, p=0.022). Second, using the Goh-Barabási burstiness parameter and a Monte Carlo null model preserving each customer's event count and active window, repeat cancellations are dramatically more clustered in time than chance predicts (observed mean B=0.192 versus a null mean of-0.173; Kolmogorov-Smirnov p<10⁻²⁵⁰): cancellation behavior comes in bursts, not as isolated events. Together these results suggest cancellations mark a recurring, predictable, time-bounded reconsideration process rather than simple lost sales, with direct implications for the timing of win-back and retention messaging.

title: Human Oversight or Automation Bias? Closing a Gap in Canada's Directive on Automated Decision-Making

detail.title: Human Oversight or Automation Bias? Closing a Gap in Canada's Directive on Automated Decision-Making
detail.abstract: Canada's federal government relies on the Directive on Automated Decision-Making and its companion Algorithmic Impact Assessment to govern automated systems used in decisions about immigration, benefits, and other matters affecting people's rights. The Directive treats human oversight as a safeguard against algorithmic error, requiring that a person be able to review and override an automated output. Decades of research on automation bias show that this safeguard is weaker than it looks. People working alongside automated systems tend to accept their outputs even when those outputs are wrong, particularly under time pressure or when a system reports high confidence. This paper reviews that research, traces the specific gap in the Directive's current text and supporting guidance, and proposes changes federal institutions could adopt now. The stakes are higher than they might otherwise be, since Canada has no federal AI-specific statute to fall back on after the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act died on the order paper in early 2025.

title: Do Learned Temporal Aggregations Improve Advertising Attribution? Target Drift and Inference Diagnostics for Attention-Based Lag Models
affiliations: and

detail.title: Do Learned Temporal Aggregations Improve Advertising Attribution? Target Drift and Inference Diagnostics for Attention-Based Lag Models
detail.abstract: Digital advertising platforms compress high-dimensional customer-journey exposure histories with flexible machine-learning components before estimating channel effects, and the learned attention weights are often read as evidence about which lags matter. We study the statistical consequences of this practice. A sequence learner estimates channel-specific temporal aggregation rules and the resulting indices enter a low-dimensional projection model. We distinguish learner-conditional, fixed-population, and realized fold-mixture projection targets, and derive an exact generated-regressor expansion showing why sample separation alone does not generally eliminate first-order drift relative to a fixed-population target. Monte Carlo experiments show that learned aggregation reduces estimation error relative to saturated distributed-lag regression and that cross-fitting lowers false-positive rates, but that in the most difficult designs fixed-target coverage deteriorates because active-channel bias increases rather than because standard errors are understated. An application to the Criteo attribution data finds weak temporal differentiation, low fold stability, and no predictive advantage over simpler aggregation rules, indicating that the learned lag weights do not identify economically meaningful temporal structure. We provide a four-step reporting protocol that lets analysts separate genuine temporal structure from artifacts of representation learning.

title: Institutional Requirements for Sovereign Local Agent Runtimes
affiliations: University of St. Thomas - School of Law (Minnesota)

detail.title: Institutional Requirements for Sovereign Local Agent Runtimes
detail.abstract: A new class of system has arrived. Models, agents, tools, and data resources now compose on the user's own machine, hold state locally, and settle payment for outward work machine-to-machine. This Article calls that class the sovereign local agent runtime and argues that its central achievement is narrower than its advocates claim. Sovereignty is a custody property. Accountability is an institutional property. The first does not produce the second. Relocating execution to the user's device answers the question of who holds the data. It does not answer who acted, under what authority, over which data, toward what outcome, and with what recourse when the outcome is wrong. Those are institutional questions, and architecture alone does not answer them. The Article specifies six institutional requirements that any adequate coordination layer for such runtimes must satisfy, derives each from two decades of research on decentralized governance, reputation, and dynamic regulation, and applies them to the shipping public implementation of Mosaic, read from source, as a worked example. That reading produces eight findings, of which the most consequential is that cross-component provenance is not merely incomplete but structurally impossible in the Chronicle: records are per-tool and carry no workflow, causal, or principal identifier, so a workflow spanning three tools produces three logs that cannot be joined, while the built-in, protocol-server, and payment execution paths produce no records at all. The Article closes with six minimal-delta engineering contributions, each expressed against the existing design and none requiring a new subsystem. The first two convert cross-component correlation from impossible to feasible and make local alteration detectable. Full satisfaction of the provenance requirement additionally demands coverage of every execution path and evidence a third party can verify.

title: A Structural Theory of Cooperative Games with Nonlinear Returns

detail.title: A Structural Theory of Cooperative Games with Nonlinear Returns

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and principal of Wisdom Agent Inc., which funded this research. No other personal or financial relationships that could have influenced the study exist.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is purely theoretical and involves no human participants, patient data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by Wisdom Agent Inc.

detail.abstract: Classical cooperative game theory takes the characteristic function v : 2^N → R as an unstructured primitive: it can allocate a surplus but cannot derive one. Coalition Intelligence Theory is a structural theory of heterogeneous interacting agents that equips v with decomposable causal factors: the companion paper constructs v(F) = D(F) • R(F)-rank diversity times an aggregate resource function-and proves a Spectral Invariance Theorem separating a structural layer from an interchangeable domain layer. This paper develops the domain layer through five nonlinear specializations, each entering a major field of economics and inheriting the structural theory without re-derivation. Increasing returns to variety nests Ricardo, Heckscher-Ohlin, Krugman, and Dixit-Stiglitz in one gains decomposition whose dominant margin is determined by rank alone, yields unconditional superadditivity, and reveals that the scarcity rent dissipating as 1/n under linear returns converges to a permanent share under power-law returns. Convexity fails universally for every variety premium; full linear independence restores it and places the Shapley value in the core. Network-enhanced returns derive winner-take-all from the convexity of total network value and yield a scale-free curation rule. Coordination-dependent returns produce a three-factor value function whose ceiling-and-floor architecture separates organized firms from decentralized markets, proves superadditivity under capacity non-degradation with a merger-value converse, and provides microfoundations for the theory of the firm without behavioral assumptions. Concave returns produce a sharp diversity threshold for positive gains, and sector-heterogeneous returns extend the decomposition with heterogeneous elasticities. The decomposition transforms cooperative game theory from a theory of division into a theory of design.

title: Attention as a Scarce Resource: Exploring the Determinants of Attention Consumption among Gen-Z
affiliations: and Cotton University

detail.title: Attention as a Scarce Resource: Exploring the Determinants of Attention Consumption among Gen-Z
detail.abstract: In today's digital economy, attention has emerged as a scarce resource, with online platforms competing continuously to capture and retain users' cognitive engagement. Against this backdrop, employing a multivariate regression model, our study examines how various determinants, such as attention fragmentation, fear of missing out, and attention awareness, influence the attention consumption of Gen-Z. To achieve the objective, primary data is collected from 150 respondents in Assam. Findings show that attention fragmentation has a positive and significant effect on attention consumption, whereas fear of missing out and attention awareness do not exhibit such significance. By viewing attention through the lens of microeconomic scarcity, these findings suggest that addressing attention fragmentation should be prioritised over awareness-based interventions and support emerging global efforts, such as the European Union's Digital Services Act, that advocate greater transparency in AI-driven recommender systems and more human-centred digital platform design.

title:
From Business Rules to Decision Flow in ERP Systems

How SAP BRFplus and Decision Flow Govern Coordinated Rule Change When Conditions Shift

detail.title:
From Business Rules to Decision Flow in ERP Systems

How SAP BRFplus and Decision Flow Govern Coordinated Rule Change When Conditions Shift
detail.abstract:
Enterprise rule engines such as SAP BRFplus define, manage, and execute business rules with speed, consistency, versioning, simulation, and auditability. This paper argues that enterprises also need a distinct governance layer — Decision Flow — that determines when the governing rules themselves should change, coordinates that change across dependent decisions, and records the premises and conditions behind each rule state. The two layers are complementary rather than competing. BRFplus executes and manages declared rule states; Decision Flow governs the enterprise-level transition from one rule state to another when a material condition changes.

The argument is developed through a constructed worked scenario: an urgent multi-product, multi-country export operation (European Union, United States, and Gulf Cooperation Council) in which one event — a customs clearance delay — should trigger a coordinated review and, where warranted, change of decision rules across sixteen affected decision areas spanning the Plan-to-Produce and Procure-to-Pay business cycles. At each stage the paper identifies the normal rule (the BRFplus default), the changed rule the condition requires, and the consequence of leaving the rule unchanged. The scenario shows that organisations frequently communicate events (information flow) without explicitly representing the premise changes those events require (condition flow), so that each function interprets new information through unchanged local rules — producing decisions that are locally correct yet globally incoherent.

The paper presents one architecture with several components: a formal Event → Condition → Rule → Decision vocabulary; a Critical Path Alert that identifies which decisions become questionable, and in what dependency order, when a condition changes; a three-level taxonomy of conflicting conditions (same-process competing priorities, same-resource competing demands, same-task contradictory conditions); a decision-authority model in which BRFplus switches a validated rule set, a Decision Flow Owner adapts a recorded scenario, or a human governance cascade handles a novel case, with an AI-assisted mode available within any of these; and a mapping of BRFplus's own capabilities — simulation, active-versus-inactive version comparison, time-dependent rules, tracing, versioning, rule sets, and APIs — as instruments through which Decision Flow governs and optimises the use of the rule engine.

Implementation begins not with new technology but with the enterprise's existing ERP process maps. By adding three questions at each process step — what rules govern this step, what changes would require them to be reviewed, and which other steps are affected — the enterprise assembles the decision dependency graph from documentation it already possesses. The recommended sequence is practice, then instruments, then system. The paper positions Decision Flow relative to adjacent approaches (BRMS, DMN, adaptive case management, event-driven architecture, policy engines, decision intelligence) and locates it within the author's broader Symbiotic Intelligence Programme.

title: The Pedagogical Dial: Negotiated Friction and Sycophancy as a Relational Parameter
affiliations: and Vassar College

detail.title: The Pedagogical Dial: Negotiated Friction and Sycophancy as a Relational Parameter
detail.abstract: Researchers attempt to mitigate sycophancy in language models through internal mechanisms-such as calibrated abstention and steerable reward models-treating the phenomenon as a defect of the model. This paper argues that sycophancy is instead a relational parameter, representing the frictionless extreme of a user-model interaction. The training pipeline optimizes for comfort, removing the friction required to produce correct outcomes. Because this dynamic is relational, it cannot be fixed solely from within the closed room of model training. Alignment requires relocating control into the hands of the user. We introduce negotiated friction-a pedagogical instrument, implemented as a user-adjustable dial, that governs the level of pushback and elaboration without altering factual honesty. By allowing users to feel the difference between a comfortable exchange and an effortful, correct one, the dial shifts the alignment burden from uninspectable preference modeling to tangible user experience. The dial treats the user as a learner, teaching the value of resistance and transforming an otherwise hidden structural failure into a negotiated choice.

title: Deep Collaboration Methodology 2.0: A Working Paper

detail.title: Deep Collaboration Methodology 2.0: A Working Paper

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved non-invasive, anonymous street-intercept interviews with adult participants in public spaces. In accordance with standard research ethics, all participants provided informed oral consent prior to engagement. No identifiable personal data or sensitive information was collected, and all data were strictly de-identified to ensure privacy. As an independent empirical study posing minimal risk, formal institutional IRB approval was not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. It was entirely self-funded by the author as an independent study.

detail.abstract:
This study proposes and executes the Deep Collaboration Methodology 2.0 (DCM 2.0), taking responsibility attribution perception in contexts of AI use as its research object. Street-intercept interviews were conducted at Da'an Forest Park in Taipei and at several university campuses, producing 328 valid interviews spanning 33 nationalities (including Taiwan, with 32 foreign nationalities). Field execution ran from December 22, 2025 to April 15, 2026.

The study employs a Convergent Mixed-Methods Design, using two fixed core questions as quantitative anchors: Q1 asks "when AI output is erroneous, to whom does responsibility belong?" (the level of moral attribution), and Q2 asks "when a loss results from acting on an AI-generated answer, who bears the loss responsibility?" (the level of practical allocation). Ten rotating question sets (Q3/Q4) were used to explore respondent reaction patterns across different AI social issue contexts.

The principal findings are organized across three levels. First, the user internalization of loss responsibility in Q2 exhibits overwhelming cross-group robustness (79% overall), remaining stable across stratifications by gender, age, nationality, and tool choice for most background characteristics — indicating that "when a loss results from acting on an AI-generated answer, the user should bear responsibility" constitutes a cross-group ethical intuition about tool use. Second, the Q1 responsibility framework is systematically moderated by usage experience, forming a continuous gradient from non-AI users (AI attribution 52%) to short-term users (33%) to long-term users (24%), with the core mechanism being the accumulation of error-encounter experience. Third, a structural epistemic gap exists between Q1 and Q2: Q1's tripartite dispersion (user attribution 25%, shared responsibility 37%, AI attribution 31%) collapses abruptly upon entering Q2's loss responsibility framework — even among respondents who attributed Q1 responsibility to AI, 71% still pointed to the user in Q2 — reflecting the systematic fusion that occurs when two distinct ethical questions ("who caused the error" versus "who should bear the consequences") are presented in sequential order.

At the methodological level, DCM 2.0 fills structural gaps in existing AI cognition research across three dimensions — ecological validity, cross-cultural coverage, and sample diversity — providing a traceable, replicable, and institutionally unaffiliated street-intercept mixed-methods protocol. The construction of DCM as an independent methodological framework is presented as a core academic contribution alongside the substantive findings of this study.

Working Paper & Archive Notes

This document is a condensed working-paper version. Full methodological detail, field logs, complete respondent background data, and the instrument design notes for all rotating question sets are permanently archived and accessible at:

  • Full Version (Zenodo): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20280700
  • Supplementary Field & Technical Notes (Zenodo): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20281517

title: Finding the Familiar in the Age of AI
affiliations: University of Cambridge - Murray Edwards College

detail.title: Finding the Familiar in the Age of AI
detail.abstract: Why do we automatically respond to new technologies by wanting to create more? The Mexican writer Juan Villoro observes that our relationship with technology has evolved into one of dependence in which failure is defined by “the fear of missing out”. This is the fear that pushes us towards production fed by our tendency towards addition and complexity, a phenomenon well documented. When solving problems, we tend to add rather than subtract. Faced with the challenge that generative AI presents to learning and research in higher education, the same instinct has shaped our response.

title: Understanding Customer Behavior by Mapping Complaints to Personality Based on Social Media Textual Data
affiliations: Telkom University, Telkom University and School of Economics & Business, Telkom University, Jl Telekomunikasi, 40257, Indonesia

detail.title: Understanding Customer Behavior by Mapping Complaints to Personality Based on Social Media Textual Data

publicationDetails.detailsText: Data Technologies and Applications, volume 59, issue 1, 2024[10.1108/DTA-02-2024-0162]

detail.abstract: Purpose: Technology serves as a key catalyst in shaping society and the economy, significantly altering customer dynamics. Through a deep understanding of these evolving behaviors, a service can be tailored to address each customer's unique needs and personality. We introduce a strategy to integrate customer complaints with their personality traits, enabling responses that resonate with the customer's unique personality. Design/Methodology/Approach: We propose a strategy to incorporate customer complaints with their personality traits, enabling responses that reflect the customer's unique personality. Our approach is twofold: firstly, we employ the Customer Complaints Ontology (CCOntology) framework enforced with multi-class classification based on a machine learning algorithm, to classify complaints. Secondly, we leverage the Personality Measurement Platform (PMP), powered by the Big Five Personality model to predict customer's personalities. We develop the framework for the Indonesian language by extracting tweets containing customer complaints directed towards Indonesia's three biggest e-commerce services. Findings: By mapping customer complaints and their personality type, we can identify specific personality traits associated with customer dissatisfaction. Thus, personalizing how we offer the solution based on specific characteristics. Originality/Value: The research enriches the state-of-the-art personalizing service research based on captured customer behavior. Thus, our research fills the research gap in considering customer personalities. We provide comprehensive insights by aligning customer feedback with corresponding personality traits, extracted from social media data. The result is a highly customized response mechanism, attuned to individual customer preferences and requirements.

title: Beyond "Check the Source": Information Literacy for Health Decisions in the Age of AI
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh

detail.title: Beyond "Check the Source": Information Literacy for Health Decisions in the Age of AI
detail.abstract: For decades, the golden rule of information literacy was simple: check the source. Who wrote the article? When was it published? Does the URL end in .gov or .edu? Those questions still matter, but in today’s digital ecosystem, they are no longer enough. Modern users don’t just read static webpages; they navigate a chaotic blend of search engine snippets, algorithmic social feeds, influencer testimonials, and AI-generated summaries. In high-stakes arenas like personal health, evaluating a single “source” is no longer the primary task. The real challenge is making sense of an entire information environment.

title: Information Literacy in a Time of Polycrisis
affiliations: University of Sheffield

detail.title: Information Literacy in a Time of Polycrisis
detail.abstract: You know that polycrisis isn't just an academic obsession when the accountants start saying it’s a thing. In a document that mentions polycrisis 84 times, the Chartered Institute of Management Accountants (CIMA) identifies that understanding “the interconnectedness of external factors such as climate change, nature, or inequality, and seeing the patterns of change and the feedback loops between the factors” is essential for developing a sustainable business model.

title: Unlocking Legal Data: A Knowledge Graph Framework for New Zealand

detail.title: Unlocking Legal Data: A Knowledge Graph Framework for New Zealand

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This paper is an independent research work. All views expressed are those of the author and do not represent any organisation or employer.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Open data sources are used for experimentation purposes. No ethical approval required.

detail.abstract:
This white paper presents a framework for building ontology-based legal knowledge graphs using New Zealand open government legal data. The aim is to improve the accessibility, integration, and analytical value of legal information for legal professionals, researchers, and the public.
Legal data, including court decisions, statutes, and legal concepts, is currently distributed across multiple platforms and formats. This fragmentation makes it difficult to search across sources, connect related information, and reuse data for analysis or smart legal applications.
The proposed framework transforms heterogeneous legal datasets into linked open data using RDF triples and a domain-specific ontology that models key legal entities and their relationships. The resulting knowledge graph can be queried through SPARQL endpoints to retrieve structured, explainable results that support advanced search and analytics.
A prototype implementation demonstrates semantic enrichment using open datasets from New Zealand legislation, court judgments and legal glossaries. The approach supports transparency, legal research, and the development of AI-enabled legal tools built on structured, machine-readable legal data.

title: Incorporated Labor, Expelled Labor:Algorithmic Automation, the Incorporation of Knowledge, and the Technological Dividend
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Incorporated Labor, Expelled Labor:Algorithmic Automation, the Incorporation of Knowledge, and the Technological Dividend

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or no financial interessa rilevante to this research
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: This research no external funding

detail.abstract: This paper develops a social theory of algorithmic automation centered on a sequence usually obscured by the language of technological substitution: labor is first incorporated as knowledge and only later may be expelled as cost. Artificial intelligence does not enter organizations as an external force that simply replaces pre-existing tasks. It is built through accumulated practices, organizational memory, procedures, classifications, data, language, corrections, judgments, and forms of social cooperation that are progressively formalized and translated into technical capacity. Once this capacity appears as an autonomous property of the system, the human subjects who contributed to its formation may be reclassified as redundant while their knowledge remains active inside the technical infrastructure. The paper names this asymmetry the movement from incorporated labor to expelled labor and interprets artificial intelligence as a revealing incident in a broader transformation of contemporary capitalism. Drawing on Marxian political economy, labor-process theory, platform capitalism, surveillance capitalism, and the literature on hidden digital labor, it reconstructs the genealogy of algorithmic productivity and examines the roles of annotators, moderators, data labelers, platform workers, users, and organizational knowledge. Case histories including InvestCloud Italy, Nielsen Media Italy, Meta, Microsoft, Kenyan and Indian AI workers, Amazon Mechanical Turk, and the Hangzhou labor case are used as indicators of distinct trajectories rather than as linear causal proof. The argument then moves from diagnosis to law and institutional design. It proposes a labor law of automation that does not intervene only at the final moment of dismissal, but along the entire trajectory through which work is observed, formalized, incorporated, and potentially rendered dispensable. The paper develops the concepts of organizational derivability, strengthened justification, dynamic redeployment, paid retraining, protected transition, supply-chain responsibility, and a technological dividend. The latter is not conceived as compensation after displacement, but as a principle of productive justice: when automation generates productivity from socially accumulated labor and knowledge, part of that productivity should return in the form of time, income, training, participation, security, and institutional capacity. The concluding section opens, without fully developing, the broader categories of social generativity and Global Social Capital as a theoretical threshold beyond the employment relationship.

title: Powering Rural Prosperity: The Local Economic Impact of Utility-Scale Wind and Solar Developments
affiliations: University of Missouri, University of Missouri and

detail.title: Powering Rural Prosperity: The Local Economic Impact of Utility-Scale Wind and Solar Developments
detail.abstract: A growing literature documents a relationship between renewable energy development and local economic outcomes. Yet, important gaps remain in understanding how these effects manifest in rural economies, across technologies, and within specific sectors. Using county-level data on U.S. energy installations between 2001-2023, we examine how renewable energy adoption shapes sector-specific economic activity, focusing on GDP, employment, and wages in rural counties. We extend prior work in three ways. First, we focus explicitly on rural outcomes, where utility-scale renewable development is concentrated but where economic structures may limit local benefits. Second, we incorporate solar adoption alongside wind, enabling a comparison of technology-specific impacts. Third, we move beyond aggregate measures to conduct a sectoral analysis, identifying how effects vary across industries. Wind development is associated with significant GDP gains concentrated in the utilities sector, while solar development is associated with modest wage and employment gains driven largely by utilities and construction. For very large utility-scale solar (e.g. 5MW or 20MW) agriculture, construction, and utility GDP increase with solar adoption. Neither technology is associated with detectable declines in agricultural GDP, employment, or wages, providing little evidence of substantial disruption to agricultural production or related labor markets. These findings provide a more nuanced understanding of the local economic consequences of the energy transition and highlight the importance of technology type and sectoral composition in shaping rural development outcomes.

title: Forecasting Oil-Price Tail Risk with Newspaper Attention

detail.title: Forecasting Oil-Price Tail Risk with Newspaper Attention
detail.abstract: Does newspaper coverage contain information about future crude-oil volatility beyond standard realized- and option-implied-volatility benchmarks? Using oil-related articles published in major U.S. newspapers from 1988 to 2024, we construct monthly measures of oil-market attention, risk-related attention, uncertainty, and price-pressure tone. We evaluate their ability to forecast one-month-ahead realized volatility, downside realized volatility, and Value-at-Risk for WTI and Brent crude oil. Adding oil-news attention to autoregressive and HAR benchmarks significantly improves out-of-sample forecasts of downside realized volatility for both WTI and Brent, with larger gains for downside volatility than for total volatility. These improvements survive controls for contemporaneously observed oil returns and persist when the benchmark includes the VIX and the oil-specific OVX, indicating that newspaper attention contains predictive information beyond option-implied volatility. Oil-news attention also improves out-of-sample Value-at-Risk forecasts in the lower tail of the return distribution. The predictive content comes primarily from the volume of coverage rather than its tone: directional sentiment does not improve forecasts, and risk-language weighting adds little once overall attention is controlled for. Newspaper attention therefore provides a useful real-time signal of future crude-oil volatility and tail risk.

title: The Impact of Carbon Tax on Ecological Footprint
affiliations: , University of Insubria and University of Insubria - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Impact of Carbon Tax on Ecological Footprint
detail.abstract: This study estimates the causal impact of carbon tax implementation on ecological footprint across 183 countries from 1961 to 2022. Using a quasi-experimental framework and a staggered difference-in-differences estimator approach, we find that carbon taxation leads to a significant and persistent reduction in ecological footprint. Specifically, implementation lowers the production-based ecological footprint by about 19.58% and the consumption-based footprint by 1.19% in treated countries relative to controls. Because ecological footprint incorporates both domestic environmental pressures and those embodied in international trade, our estimates capture the overall effect of carbon taxation on ecological footprint rather than isolating domestic abatement alone; the substantially larger production-side response indicates that these effects concentrate more heavily on domestic activity than on trade-embedded consumption. These environmental gains remain statistically significant and robust for at least two decades after adoption, as confirmed across a series of robustness checks. Nonetheless, when we examine the underlying transmission channels, we find that renewable energy adoption is the primary driver of these gains, and that they are amplified in countries with higher productivity, lower income inequality, and stronger egalitarian democratic institutions. The main findings of the study suggest that carbon tax policies should be paired with complementary measures that target consumption behaviour directly, so as to strengthen the consumption-side environmental gains of adopting countries.

title: Carbon Pricing and Technology-Driven Transition in Net-Zero Steel: A CGE Analysis of Korea
affiliations: Seoul National University and Seoul National University

detail.title: Carbon Pricing and Technology-Driven Transition in Net-Zero Steel: A CGE Analysis of Korea
detail.abstract: Decarbonizing steel requires both reducing national emissions and replacing coal based production, but policies that achieve one objective need not achieve the other. This paper examines this distinction in a recursive dynamic CGE model of Korea that represents BF–BOF, EAF, and hydrogen direct reduction as competing steelmaking routes, treats blast-furnace reductants as a fixed process requirement, and embeds the announced hydrogen steelmaking deployment plan, about 4% of output by 2035, as a policy-driven path common to all scenarios. A carbon tax rising to KRW 200,000 per ton of CO₂ by 2050 reduces national emissions by 47.7% at a cumulative GDP cost of 0.43%. It shifts production from BF–BOF toward EAF, but lifts the H₂-DRI share only from the planned 4% to 6%, and to below 3% without the plan. By contrast, an exogenous improvement in H₂-DRI production efficiency raises the share to 43%, and to 8–78% across the examined range. It roughly halves the modeled GDP cost, gross of the cost of achieving the productivity gains, and reduces emissions by a further 8 Mt beyond the carbon tax. Improvements in hydrogen supply have little effect while H₂-DRI remains small, but become more effective after production expands. Without carbon pricing, however, production efficiency transforms the steel mix while delivering essentially no national abatement. Carbon pricing and route productivity improvement therefore perform different but complementary roles: the former delivers nearly all aggregate abatement, while the latter, if technology policy achieves it, enables the production transition and adds a modest further reduction.

title: Energy-to-Food Price Transmission across Regions and Economic Structures: A Multi-Benchmark CGE Analysis
affiliations: Meiji Gakuin University

detail.title: Energy-to-Food Price Transmission across Regions and Economic Structures: A Multi-Benchmark CGE Analysis
detail.abstract: This study examines how crude oil, natural gas, and coal price changes are transmitted to food-sector prices across regions and economic structures. We develop a multiregional, multisectoral computable general equilibrium model covering 13 regions, 16 sectors, and seven GTAP benchmark years from 2004 to 2023, each treated as a separate comparative-static economy. Region-specific ARIMA models fitted to annual energy production data are used to calibrate stochastic energy-sector production shocks, and 500 Monte Carlo simulations are conducted for each region–benchmark–energy combination. Energy-to-food price elasticities are related to Leontief-inverse measures of direct and indirect energy requirements and to pathway-specific exposure indicators for transportation, fertilizer and chemicals, and electricity. Crude oil produces the largest and most widespread food-price response, whereas natural gas and coal generate smaller and more heterogeneous effects. Structural energy dependence is strongly associated with pass-through, with pooled correlations of 0.821 for crude oil, 0.765 for natural gas, and 0.652 for coal. After controlling for region and benchmark fixed effects and applying wild-cluster-bootstrap inference, oil–transport and gas–electricity exposure remain positively associated with pass-through, while gas–fertilizer exposure is not statistically significant and the coal–electricity result is sensitive to the bootstrap specification. When fertilizer and electricity exposures are included jointly for natural gas, only gas–electricity exposure retains a clear independent association. These findings highlight the importance of production-network energy dependence, power-sector resilience, and region-specific policy design.

title: How does voluntary environmental regulation affect corporate investment? Evidence from the green factory identification in China
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: How does voluntary environmental regulation affect corporate investment? Evidence from the green factory identification in China
detail.abstract: As awareness of low-carbon development grows across society, voluntary environmental regulation has become an option for enterprises to proactively manage their environmental performance; however, its impact on corporate investment remains unclear. This study constructs a Stackelberg game model to theoretically analyze the potential impact of Green Factory Certification (GFC)—a voluntary environmental regulation—on corporate investment. Then, employing China's Green Factory Certification program, implemented in phases starting in 2017, as a quasi-natural experiment, the study empirically examines the impact of the GFC program on corporate investment using data from Chinese listed companies from 2008 to 2024. The findings indicate that when firms voluntarily apply for and are selected to participate in the GFC program, their investment levels are suppressed. This conclusion is not only consistent with the theoretical analysis but is also supported by a series of robustness tests. Furthermore, mechanism tests suggest that this negative impact is transmitted through increased precautionary savings and cost adjustments (rising in operating costs and declining in institutional transaction costs). Further analysis indicates that the GFC program’s dampening effect on corporate investment is more pronounced among non-state-owned enterprises, firms with weaker environmental competitiveness, or smaller-scale enterprises; furthermore, the GFC program exhibits a peer effect, namely investment also declines significantly among firms in the same industry that do not participate in this program. These findings clarify the impact of the GFC program on corporate investment, providing empirical evidence and policy insights to enhance voluntary environmental regulations and optimize corporate investment in emerging economies.

detail.abstract: The Indian labour market has seen significant changes over the past decade or so, and the gig economy has certainly been no small contributor to that. The proliferation of digital platforms, coupled with the penetration of cheaper internet and smartphones into semi-urban areas, has ensured that a broad cross-section of the workforce has been able to leverage app-based jobs as a means of livelihood. The likes of Uber, Ola, Swiggy, and Zomato are merely the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the gig economy. However, it is also a part of a larger movement than merely food delivery or taxi services. The objective of this paper is to explore how the advent of gig-based jobs has impacted workers across various educational and skill levels. The research is based on secondary research, which includes academic research, government labour reports, and industry data. The findings indicate a mixed bag. For workers without formal educational qualifications, there has been an opening into the economy that was previously unimaginable. For workers with educational qualifications, there has been a take-up of gig jobs for various reasons. For skilled workers, there has been a leveraging of freelance platforms to reach a much larger clientele. That said, the gig economy has not been straightforwardly beneficial. Income volatility, the absence of social protection, and the structural insecurity of contractor-based work are recurring concerns in the literature. This paper argues that policy frameworks in India have not kept pace with the speed of this transformation, and that without deliberate intervention, the growth of gig work risks deepening existing inequalities rather than resolving them.

title: The persistent effects of prepayment on residential electricity use in Bangladesh
affiliations: University of New South Wales

detail.title: The persistent effects of prepayment on residential electricity use in Bangladesh
detail.abstract: Prepaid metering in public utility services have gained popularity in developing countries, where service providers often face challenges in revenue recovery. Yet, improved revenue collection may come at the cost of reduced consumption have distributional consequences. Using the staggered, large-scale implementation of prepaid monitors in Dhaka, Bangladesh, from January 2014 to November 2019, we identify the causal impact of prepaid electricity metering on household monthly electricity use. Employing a difference-in-difference design with 54.6 million observations, we find a significant and persistent reduction in residential electricity consumption; households reduce their monthly residential electricity use by 15.8 percent (~37 kWh) on average, and the effect persists over 4 years into the switch to prepaid metering. Moreover, the study highlights that the impact of prepaid metering is more pronounced among households belonging to the lower electricity tariff line group compared to those in the upper tariff line samples.

title: Architectural Restructuring of Korla Fragrant Pear Canopies: Spatial Dynamics of Photosynthetic Photon Flux Density and Resultant Fruit Quality Metamorphosis
affiliations: Harbin Industry University

detail.title: Architectural Restructuring of Korla Fragrant Pear Canopies: Spatial Dynamics of Photosynthetic Photon Flux Density and Resultant Fruit Quality Metamorphosis
detail.abstract: Osteoarthritis represents a conceptual parallel in mammalian biology to the structural degradation seen in poorly managed botanical systems, where both require precise, targeted interventions to preserve function. Within the realm of pomology, the architectural geometry of fruit-bearing trees fundamentally dictates the biological efficiency of the entire orchard ecosystem. We investigated the specific biophysical mechanisms governing how structural tree training modalities dictate fruit quality evolution in Korla fragrant pear (Pyrus sinkiangensis). Our primary objective centered on precisely quantifying the intersections between orchestrated canopy architectures and the internal spatial distribution of photosynthetically active radiation to establish a predictive framework for microclimate-driven orchard management. Four divergent architectural training frameworks were instituted within a high-density commercial orchard environment. An advanced three-dimensional spatial coordinate system was subsequently deployed to synchronously map macroscopic structural variables, highly localized photosynthetic photon flux densities across diverse spatial coordinates, and the exact physical and biochemical traits of the fruit harvested from those matched positions. Empirical observations indicated that implementing restrictive structural pruning successfully preserved highly dense, compact canopies (measuring approximately 3.12 cubic meters). Conversely, intensive spatial thinning interventions catalyzed an aggressive, rapid volumetric canopy expansion. The absolute vertical tree height was identified as the paramount structural determinant dictating the spatial infiltration of sunlight through the foliage. Modifying the canopy via apical lowering successfully elevated the average light interception metrics within the superior and medial foliage strata, whereas whole-tree spatial thinning drastically improved photon penetration deep into the inferior and central canopy zones. It is definitively concluded that architectural training modalities regulate pear development via two completely distinct biophysical conduits. The physical geometry of the canopy exerts primary control over epidermal lightness and cellular tissue firmness, while the localized penetration and distribution of photosynthetic photons dictate epidermal anthocyanin expression and carbohydrate accumulation. A stark agronomic trade-off was identified: constrained canopies guarantee uniform biochemical profiles across the harvest, whereas expansive, thinned canopies maximize gross biomass production at the expense of severe spatial quality heterogeneity. Executing aggressive tree thinning within dense plantations successfully elevates both light infiltration and total yield, though this approach mandates aggressive secondary fruit thinning to prevent profound quality degradation.

detail.abstract: The global waste management problems interacting with increased percentages of urbanization and industrialization are discussed within this research. Improved recycling systems are critically studied with deep learning techniques. In total, five models, such as 2-layer CNN, 3-layer CNN, VGG16-Mobile, MobileNet, and MobileNetV2 with self-attention, have been tested on waste images to be classified as organic or recyclable waste. Normalization and augmentation in data preprocessing gained high levels of accuracy on classification, especially with transfer learning models like VGG16 and MobileNet. Importantly, the addition of self-attention layers in MobileNetV2 improves the accuracy above 93% while focusing on significant parts of an image. Therefore, deep learning results in significant outcomes in waste management and minimization of environmental effects.

title: Behavioral Money Velocity (V**): A Multi-Source Empirical Test of the ‘Anatomy of Inflation’ Framewor
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Behavioral Money Velocity (V**): A Multi-Source Empirical Test of the ‘Anatomy of Inflation’ Framewor
detail.abstract: This study empirically tests the behavioral money-velocity (V**) framework proposed in the book Anatomy of Inflation (Enflasyonun Anatomisi), using three independent data sources covering Turkey over 2014-2026: monthly series from the Central Bank of Turkey's Electronic Data Delivery System (EVDS), weekly banking-sector bulletins from the same institution, and the CPI (2003=100) index. Of the four behavioral channels the book proposes-foreign-currency flight, short-term deposit shifts, new credit flow, and credit-card spending-credit-volume expansion is found to lead realized monthly inflation by approximately one month, with statistical significance, while parity-adjusted foreign-currency deposit flow is significantly and negatively associated with inflation. Both relationships hold consistently-in sign, significance, and relative weight-across the two independent data sources. The findings are interpreted strictly within the book's own framework: V** is not a pointforecasting tool for inflation, but a diagnostic indicator for the early detection of behavioral regime shifts.

title: From species to setting: understanding harmful algal bloom risk across Indonesian coastal waters
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Technology Sydney

detail.title: From species to setting: understanding harmful algal bloom risk across Indonesian coastal waters
detail.abstract: HABs have posed a risk to Indonesia’s fisheries production and public health since the 1930s. With over two decades since national HAB monitoring (1991-1999) ceased and significant recent environmental changes, we conducted a structured literature review of publications from 1976 and 2021 to compile information on HABs in Indonesia. Our study documented 105 HAB events from 1976 to 2018, involving 27 species across 18 locations. The most frequently observed species, Noctiluca scintillans, Pyrodinium bahamense, and Trichodesmium erythraeum, along with Gambierdiscus toxicus and Margalefidinium polykrikoides, were linked to blooms posing high to very high risks in areas with medium to dense coastal populations. Our analysis revealed a discernible rise in species diversity and frequency of HABs, particularly in densely populated areas such as Ambon, Jakarta, and Lampung Bay. The high number of publications focusing on these locations may reflect increased awareness of HABs and more extensive sampling efforts in these significant economic areas. Partitioning the dataset into regions, we determined that HAB blooms causing environmental impacts occur primarily in western Indonesia, while those with human health impacts occur across the archipelago. Describing the consequences of HABs according to their environmental and social settings, as well as their impact and recurrence, indicates that it is not just the HAB species that defines the risk, but the setting of the bloom. Amid resource constraints, prioritizing high-risk blooms becomes paramount for effective management. This study provides a baseline reference of patterns of HAB risk in Indonesia and guides future monitoring, mitigation and policy development.

detail.abstract: US public defined benefit (DB) plans have undergone a significant transformation in investment policy, funding discipline, and governance over the past several decades. Dominated by fixed income investments, public pension portfolios have shifted toward diversified allocations that include public equities and alternative assets. At the same time, demographic shifts have increased liability duration and contributed to negative net cash flows for many plans. Public DB plans must now navigate a landscape characterized by lower expected returns, evolving macroeconomic risks, and heightened fiduciary scrutiny, emphasizing disciplined governance, liquidity management, and transparency to support long-term plan sustainability.

title: Before or After the Outbreak? Comparing the Economics of ASF Prevention and Response in European Pig Production
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Scotland’s Rural College (SRUC), affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Copenhagen, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Ghent University

detail.title: Before or After the Outbreak? Comparing the Economics of ASF Prevention and Response in European Pig Production
detail.abstract: African swine fever (ASF) poses a serious economic threat to European pig production, with no vaccines or treatments available. This study consolidates the scattered economic evidence on ASF costs and biosecurity expenditure and applies a benefit-cost framework to assess whether prevention-focused investment is a sound economic strategy relative to outbreak response. A structured literature search across PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, CAB Abstracts and EconLit (January 1990–December 2025) screened 1,247 records, of which 34 were retained to parameterise an illustrative expected-value benefit-cost analysis, with all costs converted to 2025 EUR. For a 122-sow reference farm, preventive biosecurity was estimated at €125,750 infrastructure plus €22,051 annual operating costs (€12.37 per pig), whereas an outbreak imposed farm-level losses of approximately €838,000, exceeding 830% of annual profits (€101,000). European simulations for larger industrialised herds suggested per-herd direct costs of €0.9–1.2 million, while government-funded control reached €28.4 million even for a geographically limited wild boar outbreak with no domestic pig infections, alongside export losses from trade bans. At base-case assumptions (10% outbreak probability, 50% prevention effectiveness), the farm-level benefit-cost ratio was 1.21:1, rising to 2.42:1 at 20% probability; the break-even threshold was 41.3% prevention effectiveness. Because farm-level analysis captures only part of total costs—indirect trade losses may reach 29 times direct control costs—the sector-wide case for prevention is substantially stronger. Despite considerable uncertainty, the evidence consistently favours prevention over reactive approaches, suggesting policy should prioritise biosecurity investment, particularly for vulnerable small-scale producers facing the highest per-unit costs and greatest outbreak risk.

title: Economic Burden of Brucellosis in South Africa (1990–2025): A Longitudinal Economic Burden Analysis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Economic Burden of Brucellosis in South Africa (1990–2025): A Longitudinal Economic Burden Analysis
detail.abstract: Brucellosis remains a persistent zoonotic disease with significant economic implications for livestock systems and a public health threat, particularly in developing countries. In South Africa, however, limited longitudinal evidence exists on its long-term economic impact. This study addresses this gap by estimating the economic burden of brucellosis over a 35-year period (1990–2025) using secondary surveillance and economic data. Descriptive statistics, mean comparison tests, and logistic regression were employed to examine temporal trends, spatial patterns, and the drivers of high-impact events. The analysis indicates a cumulative economic loss of approximately R906.4 million, with an average annual loss of R25.9 million. Productivity losses constitute the largest share of total costs, exceeding direct animal losses, showing that disease control is not only a veterinary concern but also a sustainability issue affecting production efficiency, household income and food security. The burden is highly concentrated spatially, with North West and Mpumalanga provinces accounting for more than half of total losses. Although annual economic impacts have declined over time, the probability of high-impact events remains significant and is primarily driven by case intensity, spatial factors and temporal dynamics rather than seasonality alone. The findings support risk-based disease control strategies that combine targeted interventions in high-burden areas, stronger surveillance in vulnerable regions, early-warning systems and farmer-centered biosecurity. The study provides policy-relevant evidence for more sustainable brucellosis control in South Africa and comparable livestock-dependent economies.

title: Analytical Dynamics of Epidemiological Models (Sir) In Credit Portfolios

detail.title: Analytical Dynamics of Epidemiological Models (Sir) In Credit Portfolios
detail.abstract: This note adapts deterministic epidemic dynamics to credit deterioration and derives an analytically tractable cure-default decomposition. The framework provides threshold, final-size, and stress-path formulas for stylized credit portfolios, with a Colombian supervisory interpretation.

title: Heterogeneous Job Loss Risk and Precautionary Savings with Financial Frictions

detail.title: Heterogeneous Job Loss Risk and Precautionary Savings with Financial Frictions
detail.abstract: This paper studies how heterogeneity in job loss risk across industries and regions affects households' saving behavior and welfare in an economy with incomplete markets. Using U.S. micro-level data, I show that manufacturing and construction industries exhibit significantly higher separation rates, and their uneven spatial concentration correlates with regional disparities in savings incentives. Motivated by these facts, I develop a heterogeneous-agent model in which unemployment risk depends jointly on workers' industries of employment and regions of residence, and the risk-free rate is endogenously determined. With parameters estimated using U.S. data, the model shows that the variations in risk exposure are large enough to result in significantly more savings in risky states and industries, as well as varying welfare consequences across subgroups. In a counterfactual policy experiment that tightens credit limits, the endogenous decline in the risk-free rate partially offsets welfare losses for the constrained households while widening welfare differences across regions.

title: UIP holds conditional on monetary policy shocks
affiliations: Reserve Bank of New Zealand and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: UIP holds conditional on monetary policy shocks
detail.abstract: We estimate SVAR models for six advanced small open economies to evaluate the extent of deviations from uncovered interest parity following SOE and US monetary policy shocks. Since UIP implies that currency movements are driven by the expected path of the spread between the domestic and foreign short term interest rates, our econometric strategy disciplines the dynamic response of the SOE-US policy rate differential to monetary disturbances. Specifically, our approach jointly identifies the systematic component of SOE and US monetary policy by combining block exogeneity and sign restrictions on policy parameters. We find that UIP broadly holds conditional on SOE and US monetary policy shocks irrespective of the observed exchange rate overshooting patterns.

detail.abstract:
On January 20, 2025, which is the first day of the second term of President Trump, the United States formally initiated the U.S. withdrawal from the World Health Organization’s (WHO) membership through a Presidential Executive Order. Ironically, the U.S had founded the WHO in 1948 in the aftermath of World War II, and established it as a specialized agency of the United Nations to promote global health and coordinate responses to health emergencies. When the termination process completed after the required 12-month notification period in 2026, it left the rest of the world to grapple with “what does a WHO divorced by the US mean for the rest of the world to enable access to healthcare?.”

The paper indulges in the question and underscores that capacity building through appropriate policies comporting with new realities is critical to achieving healthcare access. The paper presents policy options within a regional framework to promote transfer of technology and innovation with the goal of inducing more efficiency into regional and local pharmaceutical industry. Next, the paper will discuss components of innovation policy at a sub-regional/national level focusing on intellectual property policies that affect pharmaceutical research and access such as patents, licensing, know-how and transfer of technology. The study concludes by emphasizing the need for formal regional health centric instruments to promote regional cooperation in critical areas such as prosecution and regulatory approvals.

title: Who Bears the Cycle? Time-Consistent Fiscal Policy and the Financing Assignment in Emerging Markets

detail.title: Who Bears the Cycle? Time-Consistent Fiscal Policy and the Financing Assignment in Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: Fiscal rules are often recommended to limit procyclical spending in emerging and developing economies. This paper looks at these rules using a calibrated small open-economy model. In the model, the government cannot commit in advance, so it chooses public spending each period and faces shocks to productivity, world interest rates, and household preferences. Results show that, despite the absence of political or default risks, procyclical spending remains the Markov-perfect best response. With public debt held constant, cyclical rules only shift the adjustment between spending and taxes rather than remove it. In this model, the main cost of discretion is the overall level of public purchases, not how it changes during the cycle. Sustained restraint would improve welfare, but a government making decisions year by year will not maintain it. Cyclical rules mostly shift which periods bear the cost. Rules focused on spending cause losses during times of tight fiscal limits, while rules focused on financing shift losses to high-productivity periods. In all the cases we study, the effect on the overall level is greater than the effect of shifting costs between periods.

title: Governing for the Eye: Fiscal Salience, Perceived Return, and the Behavioral Political Economy of Systems Competition
affiliations: Duke Kunshan University

detail.title: Governing for the Eye: Fiscal Salience, Perceived Return, and the Behavioral Political Economy of Systems Competition

detail.abstract: Public debate increasingly frames infrastructure performance as evidence in a competition between political systems, contrasting, for instance, Germany's failing railways with China's high-speed network. This paper argues that such comparisons rest on a systematically biased measurement instrument: citizens' perceived fiscal return on investment (PF-ROI). Drawing on behavioral research on availability, experience sampling, and hedonic adaptation, I develop a theory in which citizens assess the state not by aggregating fiscal outcomes but by episodically sampling salient encounters with public output. Because public goods vary along a salience gradient, from highly experienceable physical infrastructure to invisible procedural and preventive goods that register only through failure, PF-ROI diverges predictably from actual fiscal efficiency. The model generates symmetric pathologies across regime types: performance-legitimacy regimes face a "salience treadmill" that rewards perpetual novel construction beyond the welfare optimum, while procedural-legitimacy regimes suffer a maintenance trap and legitimacy erosion despite comparable or superior fiscal returns. Political actors exploit the perception gap through salience arbitrage: liquidating invisible goods whose absence is unfelt until delayed, catastrophic failure. At the system level, internationally mediated salience competition drives global underprovision of invisible goods regardless of regime type. Eight falsifiable propositions link the framework to observable divergences between perceived and objective fiscal incidence, construction-to-maintenance budget ratios, and experimental salience interventions. The analysis reframes "systems competition" as a collective measurement failure rather than evidence of institutional superiority, and identifies conditions under which the bias can be corrected.

title: Two Faces of Political Violence: State Conflict, Civilian Insecurity, and Cryptocurrency Demand
affiliations: Texas State University, Texas State University and Texas State University

detail.title: Two Faces of Political Violence: State Conflict, Civilian Insecurity, and Cryptocurrency Demand
detail.abstract: We examine how political violence shapes retail cryptocurrency demand, leveragingthis setting to reconcile two competing views of cryptocurrencies: as speculative riskassets versus portable cross-border stores of value. We merge monthly country-levelcrypto exchange app downloads and active user metrics across G20 countries fromAugust 2015 to June 2022 with event-level conflict data. We distinguish between state conflict, which signals macro-political risk, and civilian insecurity, whichdirectly impacts households through localized predation. In two-way fixed-effects panelregressions, state conflict predicts reduced crypto participation, whereas civilian insecurity predicts heightened crypto adoption and participation. We further show that thenegative state-conflict effect intensifies under adverse institutional and crypto marketconditions, whereas the positive civilian-insecurity effect is strongest where householdshave access to digital financial rails. Overall, whether crypto functions as a speculativeasset or an escape hatch depends on the modality of political violence and theaccessibility of digital financial infrastructure.

title: Does News Come True? Evidence from Initial Unemployment Claims

detail.title: Does News Come True? Evidence from Initial Unemployment Claims
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates whether a news shock identified in real time carries out-ofsample forecasting content for the variable from which it is extracted. Weekly U.S. data for 1982-2026 are used to identify a Barsky-Sims maximum-forecasterror-variance-share news shock to log initial unemployment claims, re-estimated on rolling windows at each of 1,798 forecast origins. The shock delivers no usable forecasting content: it raises mean squared forecast error at every horizon from one to eight weeks under squared, absolute and Huber loss, at a cost of between 768 and 3,856 claims per week against a mean level of 331,000, and the forecast from the news-augmented VAR itself-the system in which the shock is identified-trails the univariate benchmarks at every horizon. A fluctuation test rejects stability of relative accuracy, but the variation is a level shift rather than a regime in which news worked: pre-2020 differences are an order of magnitude smaller than the deterioration that follows once a rolling identification window begins to retain the pandemic observations. Running the identical pipeline on the Barsky-Sims technology-news system yields the same forecasting verdict. In-sample identification success and out-of-sample forecasting value are distinct properties.

title: The Effects of Environmental Racism
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Effects of Environmental Racism

keywords: Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool

detail.abstract: Environmental racism refers to the disproportionate placement of pollution sources and environmental hazards near communities of color, Indigenous populations, and low-income neighborhoods, a pattern rooted in decades of discriminatory housing, zoning, and lending practices. This paper examines the historical origins of environmental racism, tracing its connection to redlining and residential segregation, and analyzes its far-reaching consequences for public health, including elevated rates of asthma, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and mental health strain among affected populations. Using Cancer Alley, Louisiana as a case study, the paper illustrates how prolonged industrial exposure devastates predominantly Black communities across generations. Beyond health outcomes, the paper explores the social and economic toll of environmental racism, including declining property values, inadequate infrastructure, and educational setbacks caused by chronic pollution exposure. Finally, it evaluates potential solutions, emphasizing the roles of government policy, corporate accountability, grassroots environmental justice movements, and technological tools such as the Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool (CEJST) in identifying and addressing environmental disparities. The paper concludes that meaningfully reducing environmental racism requires coordinated efforts across governments, businesses, nonprofits, and individuals to ensure equitable environmental protection regardless of race or income.

title: Architecting Systems for Human Flourishing – The ASPIRE® Framework: Curriculum Symbiosis and LLM-Driven Qualitative Analytics across Secondary and Tertiary Education

detail.title: Architecting Systems for Human Flourishing – The ASPIRE® Framework: Curriculum Symbiosis and LLM-Driven Qualitative Analytics across Secondary and Tertiary Education

detail.abstract:
Modern educational institutions face a structural "trilemma" in which they must continuously trade off academic rigor, stakeholder well-being, and scalable operational equity. High-stakes academic frameworks frequently hit a systemic complexity ceiling characterized by a student burnout rate of ~40%, severe faculty administrative fatigue, and an administrative "double-work tax." Furthermore, international curriculum models may suffer from “Eurocentric hegemony”, creating perceived cultural dissonance and vocational stigma.

This paper introduces the ASPIRE® Ecosystem (AI-Synthesized Portal for Integrated Readiness & Excellence), a registered operational architecture designed to resolve these systemic frictions. Grounded in signal decoupling theory, qualitative fieldwork across Latin American secondary environments, and enterprise data modeling, ASPIRE® integrates five core sub-frameworks: SafeGuard (a local-first feasibility auditing protocol), SOURCE (curriculum symbiosis, industry integration, and "rooted globalism"), The LINK Initiative (structural mental health load-balancing), PRISM (an eight-axis LLM qualitative learning analytics engine), and BEACON (longitudinal alumni outcome tracking).

The ASPIRE® Architecture reframes Large Language Models (LLMs) from passive content generators into active metacognitive mirrors and universal analytical translators, ensuring innovation is deeply rooted in local identity while frictionlessly maintaining global academic reach through national-international alignment. This framework is highly scale-invariant, translating seamlessly from upper-secondary pathways into higher-education ecosystems and lifelong learning trajectories.

title: Forecasting Foundational Learning in India: A Pre-Registered Probabilistic Assessment of NIPUN Bharat

detail.abstract: India’s NIPUN Bharat mission targets universal foundational literacy and numeracy by the end of Grade 3 in 2026-27. Existing assessments of progress report point estimates or scenario sets; none is committed to before the outcome is observable, and none quantifies how much of the answer is driven by assumptions rather than data. We construct a state-level panel of Grade 3 reading and numeracy outcomes spanning six ASER rounds (2012–2024), recovering two pre-2016 rounds from ASER’s published competency ladder and validating the reconstruction to exact agreement against later published tables. We fit a partially pooled trajectory model on the logit scale, treat COVID-19 as a level shock with an explicit recovery parameter, and calibrate forecast uncertainty from a genuine out-of-sample backtest rather than in-sample standard errors. Policy-effect priors are taken from the randomised-trial literature rather than estimated from observational panels, because programme allocation in India responds to need. 1. Three findings. First, the target will be missed by a wide margin on both indicators: the mean modelled probability of any state reaching 80% by 2026-27 is 0.001 for reading and 0.000 for numeracy, and no state is more likely than not to reach 60% on reading. This conclusion is arithmetically visible without a model—reaching 80% requires 53% of all Grade 3 children to climb one to three rungs of the competency ladder in two years, against a pre-COVID improvement rate of 0.98 percentage points annually. Second, and more consequentially for the forecasting literature, irreducible forecast error dominates everything else: a two-year-ahead forecast carries a measured out-of-sample error of 6.5 percentage points, accounting for 80% of forecast variance, against 17% for the post-COVID recovery assumption and 1% for the entire range of plausible policy effects. Neither the assumption analysts argue about nor the policies they recommend move the answer as much as the basic difficulty of forecasting two years ahead. This result is robust for reading under every recovery specification we test, but in a pre-specified extension to Grade 3 numeracy it does not replicate: there the recovery assumption is far more consequential, and which source dominates cannot be resolved with only two post-COVID observations. We report the non-replication rather than restricting the analysis to the indicator on which the finding holds. That extension also shows a divergence the reading-only analysis could not: reading was improving at 0.98 percentage points a year before the pandemic and remains below its 2018 level, whereas numeracy was nearly flat at 0.31 and has now exceeded its pre-COVID trajectory in 13 of 22 states — an apparent numeracy recovery that reflects a low counterfactual bar rather than a healthier system. Third, two national instruments measuring Grade 3 in the same season — ASER and PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024 — rank states at a Spearman correlation of only 0.41 for reading and 0.22 for numeracy. A multitrait-multimethod analysis attributes this to a method effect rather than measurement error: same-method correlations average 0.71 against 0.32 for different-method same-trait, and disattenuating for sampling error (ASER state reliability 0.986) moves the reading correlation only from 0.413 to 0.426. A threshold measure and a mean-score measure capture different features of a state’s ability distribution — and NIPUN’s own target is a threshold. We pre-register the forecast, with falsifiable calibration claims, before ASER 2026 is fielded.
