title: Language-Based Cognitive Interventions: A Scoping Review of Linguistic Cues, Task-Framing, and Self-Directed Cognitive Change
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Language-Based Cognitive Interventions: A Scoping Review of Linguistic Cues, Task-Framing, and Self-Directed Cognitive Change

declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded by the author as part of a private research initiative under the Human Optimization Framework (HOF).

publicationDetails.detailsText: Preprint version is available on Zenodo, DOI: 10.5281/ZENODO.20492756

detail.abstract:
Language is often treated as a medium for describing psychological experience, communicating instructions, or reporting internal states. Across several areas of cognitive, affective, behavioral, and applied psychological research, however, language also functions as an operative cognitive interface. Words, phrases, written prompts, verbal labels, and structured instructions may direct attention, bind cues to actions, organize affective experience, modify appraisals, support selfregulation, and compress complex procedures into repeatable task-frames.

This scoping conceptual review maps major classes of language-based cognitive interventions and related experimental literatures, including implementation intentions, self-instruction and self-talk, cognitive reappraisal and cognitive restructuring, affect labeling, expressive writing, semantic priming and verbal cueing, verbal repetition and cue phrases, and protocol-based cognitive processing as an emerging observational category.

The review does not conduct a statistical meta-analysis, does not calculate pooled effect sizes, and does not make clinical efficacy claims for unvalidated systems. The review proposes that languagebased interventions can be understood through a set of partially overlapping functional roles: attentional pointer, semantic index, task-frame, cue-action binder, affect label, narrative organizer, self-regulatory scaffold, and procedural compression unit.

This framework may help clarify how structured language can organize self-directed cognitive operations while preserving appropriate boundaries between established evidence, mechanistic plausibility, and systems requiring independent empirical evaluation

title: When Does Intraday Options Trading Predict Stock Returns?
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics, Zhejiang University - Department of Finance and

detail.title: When Does Intraday Options Trading Predict Stock Returns?
detail.abstract: We aggregate signed options trading volume from CBOE and ISE and document a persistent positive predictive power of 30-minute options order imbalance (OOI) for next-day stock returns. OOI near the market close exhibits the strongest predictability, driven primarily by open-buy positions, high-leverage options, and small orders. Consistent with informed trading, options traders appear to time the liquidity across options and stock markets, and this predictability is stronger when option liquidity is high and stock liquidity is low. The predictive power also intensifies with firm-specific and macroeconomic information events. Finally, OOI also forecasts both stock price jumps and crash risks.

title: Scalable Share Calibration for Factor Multinomial Probit Models

detail.title: Scalable Share Calibration for Factor Multinomial Probit Models

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Employed by Global Strategic Minerals Corporation
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: We give an algorithm that inverts observed shares to utilities in multinomial probit models with many alternatives, when the covariance is low-rank-plus-diagonal and supplied. Conditioning on the factors makes the alternatives independent, so one shared survival field prices all N alternatives in a single pass over Q factor nodes and L grid points, at O(QNL) cost. The same field yields resampling-free Jacobian-vector products, and share inversion at N = 1000 takes three seconds in the compiled implementation at rank two. Ten thousand alternatives stay under a minute. In convergence comparisons, the computed shares carry log-share errors of a few parts in a hundred thousand, hundred-to-one shares included. The established high-precision evaluators price one orthant at a time. The nearest factor-aware competitor computes the same share vector roughly 140× slower at matched accuracy at N = 1000, and the gap widens linearly in N .

title: Private Equity at 50: Hold Everything

detail.title: Private Equity at 50: Hold Everything
detail.abstract: Private Equity turns 50 this year. The industry was built on a simple model: buy companies, improve them, sell them, return the proceeds. For decades, that's exactly what happened. Then came the flood. PE's prolonged success transformed a specialist craft into a $10 trillion dollar industry. Scale doesn't just make complex systems bigger. It reorganizes them around new priorities. In PE, scale shifts emphasis away from performance-driven carried interest and toward AUM-driven enterprise value. Rising rates have exposed what this incentive shift already set in motion: firms are holding onto companies longer and longer. The resulting distribution drought-and a recent stretch of uninspiring performance-have PE under fire. The strain is real. But it's not universal. Just like not every 50-something buys a Porsche, not all of PE is in crisis. What you see in the headlines focuses on the behavior and circumstances of the largest firms. But their story isn't the whole story. The original model is still working. If you know where to look for it.

title: Reforms and Protests

detail.title: Reforms and Protests
detail.abstract: This paper studies how fiscal reform generates social resistance. I construct a novel highfrequency dataset linking every bill voted in the Hellenic Parliament between 2010 and 2017 to the daily incidence, duration, and composition of protests, strikes, and riots during one of the sharpest fiscal adjustments in recent history. Three findings emerge. First, protest is tightly linked to the legislative calendar: activity rises as fiscally consequential bills approach a vote and declines gradually afterward, while fiscally neutral bills generate little response. Second, resistance increases with the stakes of reform. Protest rises with both the breadth of legislation and its euro-denominated fiscal magnitude. Third, the incidence of adjustment matters. Holding fiscal magnitude fixed, protest responds strongly to spending-related reforms but not to revenue-related reforms. Union mobilization and the grievances cited in calls to riot-dominated by wage, benefit, and budget cuts-corroborate this composition effect. Roughly half of the protest activity surrounding a vote occurs after passage, when protest can no longer affect the bill's immediate legislative fate, a pattern consistent with an expressive component of collective action. The results suggest that the social resistance generated by fiscal consolidation depends not only on how much governments adjust, but also on how they do so.

title: Rethinking Time-Series Momentum in Equity Portfolios: Common Signals, Long-Only Positioning, and No Need for Volatility Timing
affiliations: University of Agder - School of Business and Law

detail.title: Rethinking Time-Series Momentum in Equity Portfolios: Common Signals, Long-Only Positioning, and No Need for Volatility Timing
detail.abstract: This paper studies how time-series momentum (TSMOM) should be implemented when the traded assets belong to the same equity market. We compare conventional portfoliospecific Momentum with a common market-level Momentum signal, Long-Short with Long-Only positioning, and strategies with and without inverse-volatility scaling across a broad set of U.S. characteristic-sorted equity portfolios. The results show that a common market Momentum signal is systematically more effective than portfolio-specific Momentum, suggesting that these portfolios are primarily exposed to a shared market state rather than distinct portfolio-specific regimes. The preferred trading rule depends on the performance objective. Market-Momentum Long-Only delivers the strongest performance when evaluated by the Sharpe ratio, whereas Market-Momentum Long-Short performs best when evaluated by six-factor alpha. Conditional-state analysis explains this difference: nonpositive Market Momentum identifies a state with lower but still positive expected returns and substantially higher risk, while its factor-adjusted expected return is negative. Finally, volatility timing mainly improves weaker Long-Short strategies and adds little to the bestperforming specifications. Overall, effective TSMOM implementation within a common equity market requires reconsidering both the source of the Momentum signal and the appropriate response to unfavorable market states.

title: Aggregate Uncertainty and Rank-Based Enforcement in Collective Action

detail.title: Aggregate Uncertainty and Rank-Based Enforcement in Collective Action
detail.abstract: I study voluntary contributions to a collective project whose provision threshold is uncertain and whose lowest contributor is sanctioned after failure. A single distributional index characterizes when symmetric full provision is supportable. Its large-group behavior is governed by the upper-tail geometry of the threshold distribution, so distributions with identical means, variances, and support can have opposite enforceability properties. Under globally weak common deterrence and convex shortfall risk, the same index yields uniqueness against asymmetric and independently mixed Nash equilibria. For a uniform threshold with 0 ≤ v < D, we derive the unique symmetric atomless mixed equilibrium when 0 < p < D-v. We then prove, without imposing symmetry, that this equilibrium maximizes provision over the entire Nash-equilibrium set. Consequently, npn → ∞ is necessary for approximate provision along any Nash-equilibrium sequence and sufficient along the symmetric selection. When 0 ≤ v < D, the full-provision support and unique-equilibrium implementation thresholds coincide. We also identify a symmetric certain-failure equilibrium in which contributions are dissipated in rank competition. A design extension shows how upper-tail incentives and the lower endpoint jointly determine the asymptotically minimal sanction needed to support full provision and exclude this characterized coordination trap.

title: Exploring the Role of Nature-Based Solutions for Climate Adaptation in the Agriculture Sector
affiliations: and Saitama University, Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences, Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences

detail.title: Exploring the Role of Nature-Based Solutions for Climate Adaptation in the Agriculture Sector

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was recived for this study.

detail.abstract: Climate change impacts are more severe and frequent in countries vulnerable to climate. Evidence indicates that Nature-based solutions (NbS) are widely used as cost-effective and sustainable adaptation strategies; however, their effectiveness varies across ecological, institutional, and socio-economic contexts. Our understanding of NbS for agricultural climate adaptation remains limited. This study systematically reviews the role of NbS in agricultural adaptation using PRISMA guidelines. Using keywords such as “NbS,” “climate adaptation,” and “agriculture,” along with their synonyms, a total of 2696 related papers in Scopus were identified. After applying relevant filters, 1740 articles were selected. During screening, 301 studies were relevant to the objectives, and after full review, 21 articles were finalized for inclusion. The methodology across these studies is diverse, including empirical methods, choice experiments, spatial modelling, policy reviews, and household surveys. The study uses VOSviewer software for network analysis, revealing several interconnected factors related to NbS for agricultural adaptation. In the word cloud analysis, key terms such as “farmer,” “agriculture,” and “practices” emerge as important. This research finds that approaches such as agroforestry, Eco-based adaptation, natural flood management, and climate-resilient crops are most frequently examined. The evidence shows that NbS are particularly effective for small farmers; therefore, they should be prioritized. However, NbS face governance and financing challenges. To address these issues, public–private partnerships involving NGOs, NPOs, and NbS should be developed and implemented in consultation with stakeholders. Finally, the review highlights several research gaps and limitations.

title: Low-Carbon Steel Before Cost Parity: Demand Heterogeneity, Carbon Pricing, and Market Formation

detail.title: Low-Carbon Steel Before Cost Parity: Demand Heterogeneity, Carbon Pricing, and Market Formation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal or financial relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study did not involve human participants or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the conditions under which a market for low-carbon steel can emerge before low-carbon production reaches conventional cost parity. The framework links technologyspecific production costs and emissions intensity to heterogeneous downstream willingness to pay for reductions in embodied emissions. Carbon pricing reduces the relative cost disadvantage of cleaner production routes, while buyer heterogeneity determines the share of demand able to absorb the remaining green premium. Producers can therefore face a commercially meaningful market even before the low-carbon technology reaches full production-cost parity. The quantitative analysis calibrates conventional BF-BOF and alternative low-carbon steelmaking routes to industry and engineering benchmarks and uses Monte Carlo simulation to incorporate uncertainty in hydrogen, electricity, raw-material, and other input costs. The results show substantial differences in the carbon prices and input-cost conditions required for alternative technologies to become competitive. Scrap-based EAF and natural-gas-based DRI-EAF become economically attractive earlier than hydrogen-based primary steelmaking, while H 2-DRI-EAF offers deeper emissions reductions but remains more sensitive to hydrogen costs and the willingness of downstream buyers to pay a green premium. A central implication is that downstream buyer-side market formation can precede producerside cost parity. Heterogeneity in willingness to pay allows an addressable market to emerge while a positive green premium remains, particularly when carbon pricing reduces the effective cost disadvantage of low-emission production. The results therefore suggest that the transition to low-carbon steel is likely to depend on the joint evolution of carbon pricing, technology costs, and downstream demand rather than on technological cost parity alone.

title:
Convergence as a Mitigation Strategy 
How Synchronized Global Adoption of Clean Technologies Reduces Systemic Risk

detail.title:
Convergence as a Mitigation Strategy 
How Synchronized Global Adoption of Clean Technologies Reduces Systemic Risk
detail.abstract:
Synchronized global adoption of clean technologies acts as a powerful stabilizer for the modern macroeconomic system, which is increasingly strained by overlapping ecological, geopolitical, and financial crises. The report argues that fragmented energy transitions—where advanced economies accelerate decarbonization while emerging markets lag—create structural imbalances that amplify systemic risk. As noted in the document, “Fragmentation in technological adoption…creates severe structural imbalances. These imbalances manifest as extreme volatility in currency markets, localized energy crises, and compounding risks across critical global supply chains.”

Using thermodynamic models of technology diffusion and dynamic factor copula frameworks for financial stability analysis, the study demonstrates that synchronized adoption compresses cost curves, reduces heavy‑tailed market dependencies, and lowers the joint probability of multi‑sector distress. As the report states, “achieving global adoption convergence effectively flattens the systemic risk curve.”

The paper concludes that convergence is not merely a climate strategy but a macro‑systemic risk mitigation imperative. Coordinated global deployment of clean technologies restructures network geometry toward decentralized resilience, prevents cascading failures, and enables a low‑entropy steady state for the global economy.

title: Teaching Against Collapse: Gendered Political Economy and the Territorialization of Education in Fragmented Yemen
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Teaching Against Collapse: Gendered Political Economy and the Territorialization of Education in Fragmented Yemen

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: This article advances a gendered political economy framework to examine how systemic educational collapse in Yemen simultaneously destroys, reproduces, and-under specific conditions-transforms structures of conflict and patriarchal authority. Drawing on 45 semistructured interviews with educators, community leaders, and local authorities across five governorates (Aden, Taiz, Hadramawt, Marib, and Sana'a), triangulated with humanitarian reports and peer-reviewed scholarship, the study argues that education in protracted conflict cannot be understood through humanitarian deficit frameworks alone. Instead, it must be analyzed as a terrain of political contestation where war economies, patriarchal bargains, and territorial governance fragment educational space. The analysis identifies three interconnected dynamics. First, the collapse of state financing has localized resource distribution through patronage and community coercion, producing new geographies of educational exclusion. Second, women's assumption of educational leadershipcelebrated in humanitarian discourse as empowerment-operates as a form of feminized survival work that extends patriarchal resilience rather than dismantling it. This concept is distinguished from feminist analyses of reproductive labor and care work by its specific focus on the public performance of crisis-time educational labor that is simultaneously hyper-visible in humanitarian narratives and structurally invisible in political economy. Third, while community-based schools and teacher-led curriculum mediation generate "everyday peacebuilding," these practices remain structurally constrained by the absence of redistributive justice and the territorialization of governance. The article concludes that sustainable educational recovery requires moving beyond humanitarian restoration toward politically-informed, gender-transformative reconstruction that addresses the political economy of teacher precarity, curriculum territoriality, and the structural devaluation of women's educational labor.

title: Information Asymmetries and Credit Constraints in SME Finance: Evidence from South Asian Developing Economies

detail.title: Information Asymmetries and Credit Constraints in SME Finance: Evidence from South Asian Developing Economies
detail.abstract: This paper examines the determinants of SME financing constraints across Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka using data from the World Bank Enterprise Survey (WBES). Employing correlation analysis, ordinary least squares (OLS), fixed-effects panel regression, and quantile regression techniques, the study investigates the influence of financing conditions, governance quality, and institutional factors on SME access to finance. The results indicate that favourable lending conditions, including lower borrowing costs, reasonable collateral requirements, and streamlined procedures, are associated with improved financial access. Conversely, corruption, political instability, weak law and order, and high tax burdens significantly constrain SME financing. The findings highlight the importance of institutional quality and financial-sector reforms in addressing persistent financing barriers. The paper contributes to the literature by providing a comparative empirical assessment of SME financing constraints across major South Asian economies and offers policy recommendations aimed at enhancing financial inclusion and economic development.

title: The Multipolar Climate Century: Climate Change, Resource Redistribution, and the Transformation of Global Power
affiliations: University of Edinburgh

detail.title: The Multipolar Climate Century: Climate Change, Resource Redistribution, and the Transformation of Global Power

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study, as it did not involve human participants, personal data, clinical research, or animal subjects. The study is based on a qualitative synthesis of publicly available academic and institutional sources.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
This article conceptualizes climate change not merely as environmental degradation or a conventional “threat multiplier,” but as a structural mechanism capable of altering the distribution of relative power in the international system. Building on Eker’s earlier concepts of Climate Multipolarity, Resource Tipping Points, and Security Ecology, it develops the “Multipolar Climate Century” as a higher-order theoretical framework. The central argument is that climate impacts revalue strategic assets through water, food, energy, critical minerals, logistical corridors, technological capacity, and institutional resilience. These shifts transform dependencies, alliance incentives, and bargaining power. 

The study adopts a qualitative theory-building design that synthesizes scholarship on climate security, energy transition, critical minerals, and multipolarity, while using the Arctic, critical-mineral supply chains, and transboundary water systems as mechanism-tracing illustrations. The article concludes that climate change does not simply generate additional risks within an otherwise stable distribution of power; it changes the material, technological, and institutional foundations through which power is produced and converted.

title: So Pedestrian: Designing AV Detection Displays Around Human Perception
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University and New York University (NYU) - New York University

detail.title: So Pedestrian: Designing AV Detection Displays Around Human Perception
detail.abstract: In-vehicle pedestrian detection displays show what a vehicle senses, but a sensor detects more than a display can usefully present. We argue that what a display surfaces should be prioritized by human monitoring: confirm the pedestrians an occupant reliably detects, and flag those they miss. In an SAE Level 4 driving simulator, participants monitored an automated drive and reported pedestrians under intermittent visual-search load. Across 488 encounters from 27 participants, moving pedestrians were detected 90-98% and a stationary, occluded pedestrian 44%, despite passing within 7 m. Detection tracked visual salience, not proximity. Projecting position into the gaze record shows the miss is split: in about half, gaze reached the pedestrian and went unreported; in the rest, gaze never arrived. Adding dashboard detail raised trust without raising workload but did not recover the missed pedestrian, implying the safety cue belongs in the environment, not on a dashboard panel.

title: Correlated Intelligence: AI Homogenization and Price Discovery
affiliations: Willamette University - Atkinson Graduate School of Management

detail.title: Correlated Intelligence: AI Homogenization and Price Discovery
detail.abstract: Financial institutions increasingly choose between shared artificial intelligence (AI) platforms and independently developed information systems. We study how this technology choice affects market price discovery. In a multi-insider Kyle model, common processing errors make private signals redundant: greater error correlation lowers price informativeness and price impact even when each trader's linear trading intensity is unchanged. Improving individual accuracy alone therefore leads to an informativeness ceiling when common errors persist. We then endogenize technology adoption. Independent technology earns a differentiation rent, but its use depends on the cost of maintaining a distinct system. For any positive cost premium, sufficiently large markets admit an equilibrium in which only finitely many traders retain independent technology, so their market share vanishes. The results imply that managers should evaluate AI systems not only by stand-alone forecast accuracy and implementation cost, but also by common-error exposure and the organizational value of preserving information diversity.

title: Amortized Tax Alpha: Simulation-based Inference for the After-Tax Value of Direct Indexing

detail.title: Amortized Tax Alpha: Simulation-based Inference for the After-Tax Value of Direct Indexing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is a principal of InnovationStrat Consulting, LLC, and of an affiliated investment advisory firm that offers tax-aware investment strategies of the kind analyzed in this paper. The paper uses only simulated data and no client information.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study uses only simulated data generated from a fixed random seed; no human participants, patient data, or personal data were involved.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received. The research was self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: Advisors sell tax-loss harvesting with a brochure number. "Direct indexing adds roughly one to two percent a year" is true on average and close to useless for a particular household, because the realized benefit depends on that household's bracket, horizon, outside gains, exit plan, and the volatility of the market it happens to live through. This paper replaces the brochure number with a calibrated distribution. We build a forward simulator of a direct-indexing harvesting account whose inputs are the client-and-market characteristics an advisor already collects, and we train one amortized posterior estimator, a mixture-density network, that maps those characteristics to a full posterior over after-tax benefit. Inference for a new client is a single forward pass of a few milliseconds rather than a fresh Monte-Carlo run. On 150 held-out configurations the amortized posterior matches a slow 1,500-path reference to a normalized 1-Wasserstein distance of 0.06 and a median error of 2.7 basis points, and after a one-parameter temperature recalibration its stated 50, 80 and 90 percent credible intervals cover at 50, 80 and 91 percent. Calibration is then audited where the aggregate test cannot see: within quintile bins of every conditioning input. The raw network fails that audit in all nine directions at once, always on the overconfident side; the single global temperature survives it with exceedances at the level chance would produce, and a log-linear conditional temperature narrows the worst client segment's 90 percent coverage from 0.875 to 0.903. We also quote the price of humility about the market itself: integrating volatility and dispersion out of the conditioning set, so the interval no longer leans on a regime forecast, widens the median client's 90 percent interval by a factor of 1.31 while recentring clients whose assumed regime was extreme. Retraining under four seeds moves posterior medians by 2.5 basis points, so the fit itself is not the fragile step. The framing, an amortized posterior over after-tax value conditioned on the client, lets a firm hand each investor an interval it can defend rather than an average it cannot.

title:
Bias-aware Signal Classification for Supply & Demand Trading Systems: 
A Comparative Study of Machine Learning Algorithms on XAUUSD
affiliations: K. N. Toosi University of Technology

detail.title:
Bias-aware Signal Classification for Supply & Demand Trading Systems: 
A Comparative Study of Machine Learning Algorithms on XAUUSD
detail.abstract: Generating trading signals is straightforward; distinguishing high-quality signals from weak ones is not. This study applies a systematic machine-learning framework-XGBoost, Random Forest, and KNN-to filter raw signals generated by a rule-based supply-and-demand strategy on XAUUSD at the M5 timeframe. Signals were backtested under realistic transaction costs and labeled by realized return, and a novel mirroring-based methodology addressed the pronounced class imbalance between profitable and unprofitable outcomes. Hyperparameters were tuned via Bayesian optimization using the Sharpe ratio as the objective. Training data was further augmented with signals from eleven additional instruments-five forex pairs, four cryptocurrencies, and two commodities-so that models could still trade gold with a broader view of market behavior. XGBoost trained on this aggregated dataset achieved the best out-of-sample performance, reaching a Sharpe ratio of 2.02 and a return of 206.4% over the test period from March 2025 to August 2026.

title: Welfare Improvements from Default Annuitization in Defined Contribution Plans
affiliations: PGIM and The American College

detail.title: Welfare Improvements from Default Annuitization in Defined Contribution Plans
detail.abstract: Most American workers save for retirement in defined contribution (DC) plans using default investments, primarily target-date funds. Adding annuities to a default investment offers two potential benefits over retail annuities: First, passive acceptance of defaults will likely increase in the percentage of workers who receive guaranteed lifetime income. Second, DC participants, and especially those participants who invest in defaults, may not live as long as retail annuity buyers, resulting in a mortality pool that allows lower fair annuity pricing. We estimate that the average DC participant has a longevity that is about two years less than the average retail annuity buyer. The more-attractive mortality pool of DC participants would result in annuity income that is 7.4 percent higher for women and 2.7 percent higher for men. Respondents who indicate a preference for investing through defaults exhibit characteristics associated with lower expected longevity than average DC participants. This suggests an additional pricing improvement to annuities that are placed in investment defaults. Welfare analyses demonstrate that a risk-averse woman with $500,000 of retirement savings who invests in a default could increase her total welfare in retirement by 18.8 percent upon annuitizing 25 percent of her wealth and by 35.0 percent upon annuitizing 50 percent of her wealth, versus not annuitizing.

title: Who Can Use an Open Law? Usable Slack as a Framework for Studying the Unequal Production of Legal Determinacy
affiliations: University of Groningen, Faculty of Law

detail.title: Who Can Use an Open Law? Usable Slack as a Framework for Studying the Unequal Production of Legal Determinacy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of Interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

detail.abstract: Legal underdeterminacy describes the range of answers that legal materials can sustain. It says less about who can keep one of those answers institutionally alive. This article develops usable slack as a middle-range concept for studying that problem. Its unit of analysis is an actor carrying a specified legal proposition through a specified institutional stage in a particular forum and historical period. Its principal observable implication is the differential attrition of historically available propositions as they pass through recognition, evidential construction, procedural preservation, endurance, settlement, review, authoritative determination, publication, and later uptake. Existing work on access to justice, legal capability, legal mobilisation, repeat players, litigation selection, and biased precedent establishes much of the surrounding terrain. Usable slack adds a propositionspecific and stage-specific framework that begins before the litigate-or-settle decision and separates actormediated use from the institutional conversion of an argument into precedent. The article does not report a new empirical test. It specifies a research programme, an evidential protocol for reconstructing legal availability, and conditions under which unequal proposition attrition should be most visible. It also preserves a claimant-centred limit: public law should not depend unnecessarily on an injured person accepting private ruin for the benefit of future strangers.

title: Stock Connect Capital Flows and Volatility Spillovers in Hang Seng Index Constituent Stocks: Evidence from a GARCH Framework
affiliations: University College Dublin

detail.title: Stock Connect Capital Flows and Volatility Spillovers in Hang Seng Index Constituent Stocks: Evidence from a GARCH Framework
detail.abstract: The Stock Connect program has substantially increased cross-border capital flows between Mainland China and Hong Kong. This paper investigates the impact of southbound capital flows on volatility spillovers among Hang Seng Index constituent stocks. Using daily data from January 2020 to March 2026, the study applies GARCH(1,1), EGARCH, and DCC-GARCH models to 50 major constituent stocks. The empirical results reveal that southbound flows significantly amplify volatility persistence and generate notable spillover effects across constituent stocks, particularly in technology and consumption sectors. Strong evidence of asymmetric volatility responses is found, with negative shocks transmitting more intensely during periods of large southbound inflows. Dynamic conditional correlations indicate strengthened market integration following increased southbound trading activity. Robustness checks using high-frequency intraday data and alternative spillover indices support the main findings. This study contributes to the literature by shifting the analytical focus from aggregate market indices to micro-level dynamics of individual Hang Seng constituent stocks. The findings offer new insights into volatility transmission under financial liberalization and carry important implications for regulators and policymakers regarding cross-border capital flow management and market stability in Hong Kong.

title:
When the Vehicle Becomes the Generator
A Framework for Mobile Distributed-energy Assets
affiliations: New York State Department of Taxation & Finance

detail.title:
When the Vehicle Becomes the Generator
A Framework for Mobile Distributed-energy Assets
detail.abstract:
Tax law is built around categories that historically mapped onto separate physical assets: vehicles
transport, photovoltaic facilities generate, batteries store, and electricity-market resources
provide grid services. Vehicle-integrated photovoltaics (VIPV), bidirectional electric vehicles, and
related energy-management systems collapse those functions into a single mobile platform. This
Article develops the Mobile Distributed-Energy Asset (MDEA) as a tax and public-finance
framework for analyzing that convergence. MDEA is not a claim that the underlying technology is
new, nor a claim that mobile photovoltaic equipment qualifies for any particular tax incentive. It is
a sequencing rule: identify the economically distinct functions inside an integrated asset before
applying statutes written for historically separate categories. The framework maps four functions -
transportation, generation, storage, and external energy services (T + G + S + X) - and favors a
component-first analysis when incremental investment can be reliably substantiated. The Article
applies that framework to the post-2025 federal incentive landscape, overlapping-basis concerns,
mobile production measurement, multistate receipt sourcing, sales and use taxation, and road
finance. New York and California demonstrate why a mobile generator creates a characterization
problem before it creates a geography problem. The Article then proposes an empirical research
design for commercial fleets and a nine-question decision rule for administrators, courts, and
lawmakers. Its central claim is modest: physical integration should not permit the noun “vehicle”
to answer tax questions that depend on function, transaction, basis, and statutory text.

title: Idea Rents and Firm Growth
affiliations: Stockholm University - Institute for International Economic Studies (IIES), Stanford University, Stanford University and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco

detail.title: Idea Rents and Firm Growth
detail.abstract:
Which firms drive aggregate productivity growth? We document that firms with high price-earnings ratios tend to see increases in their subsequent earnings relative to sales, which we interpret as rents from ideas (innovation). We construct an endogenous growth model with shocks to firm innovation step-sizes and R&D efficiency and calibrate it to match patterns in the data. The model implies that growth would be much lower, even with the same innovative effort, if firms had the same step sizes. The model can be used to infer expected growth contributions of individual firms (such as members of the Magnificent Seven). We find that the share of growth coming from smaller listed firms substantially exceeds their sales share, whereas the largest listed firms account for less than their sales share.

title: Actual Autonomy or Symbolic Sovereignty? The Qris Issues in Indonesia's Digital Payment Geopolitics
affiliations: Institut Informatika dan Bisnis Darmajaya, Darmajaya Institute Informatics and Business, Darmajaya Institute of Informatics and Business and Bina Nusantara University (BINUS)

detail.title: Actual Autonomy or Symbolic Sovereignty? The Qris Issues in Indonesia's Digital Payment Geopolitics

declarations.ethicsApproval: AI tools were used only for language editing, including grammar, spelling, and improving clarity. All research content, analysis, interpretation, and conclusions are the authors’ own work and were fully reviewed and verified by the authors.

detail.abstract: This study explored digital sovereignty in Indonesia's payment system through the case of the Quick Response Code Indonesian Standard (QRIS). Introduced in 2019 to reduce reliance on foreign networks such as Visa and Mastercard, QRIS expanded rapidly from 3.6 million users in 2020 to over 56 million by 2024. Despite its national positioning, 78% of QRIS's core infrastructure remains controlled by global firms like AWS and EMVCo. The study used a mixed-methods approach, combining big data analytics and critical discourse analysis, to investigate public perceptions and policy narratives concerning QRIS. Quantitative adoption data is integrated with a qualitative analysis of regulatory papers and public discourse. Results indicate a distinct contradiction between the symbolic interpretations of sovereignty and the technological dependencies that support QRIS. These highlights the challenges that emerging nations experience in obtaining real digital autonomy within a globalized financial framework. The study strengthens the field of economics by advancing the discussion on digital monetary policy, asymmetries in institutional authority, and the regulation of payment systems. It presents the term of "organized sovereignty" in order to explain the simultaneous existence of national control demands alongside dependence on international infrastructure. This approach improves our comprehension of the intersection between fintech advances, macroeconomic policy, and institutional development within the digital economy.

title: Fetal Pollution Exposure, Cognitive Ability, and Gender-specific Parental Investment
affiliations: Beijing Normal University (BNU) - School of Statistics, ,  and Yale School of Public Health - Department of Health Policy and Management

detail.title: Fetal Pollution Exposure, Cognitive Ability, and Gender-specific Parental Investment
detail.abstract:
We examine how prenatal exposure to air pollution interacts with gender-biased parental investments to shape long-run cognitive performance. Using nationally representative survey data from China, we show that fetal PM2.5 exposure significantly reduces cognitive ability for women, particularly among those with brothers. Our evidence suggests that the family investment channel operates primarily through education rather than health, with gender-biased educational resource allocation compounding negative outcomes for females. Specifically, conditional on the same level of fetal PM2.5 exposure, females receive less homework assistance from their families and attain lower levels of education.

title: More Frequent Than You Think: Revisiting Capital Structure Adjustment
affiliations: Stanford University, Stanford Graduate School of Business and University of Illinois Urbana Champaign

detail.title: More Frequent Than You Think: Revisiting Capital Structure Adjustment
detail.abstract:
This paper revisits the empirical evidence on capital structure adjustment and the prevalence of financing “inaction.” We show that the conclusion of infrequent leverage adjustment is sensitive to two methodological choices: high adjustment thresholds and reliance on net balance-sheet changes. Using lower thresholds and gross flows from cash-flow statements, we find adjustment is far more frequent than previously documented, and the pattern reveals pronounced size-based heterogeneity. Smaller firms exhibit considerable inertia consistent with fixed costs; the largest firms (e.g., top 1% by assets) behave as if frictions are negligible. Frictionless recapitalization models thus better describe large-firm leverage dynamics.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Dynamic Effects of Trade
affiliations: Stanford University, Princeton University and Stanford University

detail.title: Dynamic Effects of Trade
detail.abstract:
The existence of aggregate welfare gains from trade is one of the classic insights from international economics. However, these conventional welfare gains are static, in the sense that they take existing factor supplies and production technologies at a point in time as given. Recent research has highlighted dynamic effects of trade through endogenous factor accumulation and technological innovation over time, although there remains less consensus about the quantitative magnitude of these dynamic effects than about their static counterparts. Key insights from this research are that short-run and long-run responses to trade liberalization differ; capital accumulation amplifies the impact of international trade shocks; trade can facilitate technology adoption and the diffusion of ideas by changing the composition of suppliers; effects on lifetime welfare differ substantially from those on steady-state welfare, once transition dynamics are taken into account; and market failures can either magnify the overall welfare gains from trade or rationalize activist trade and industrial policies.

title: Choosing To Fail: Managerial Liability, Risk Management and Voluntary Exits of Banks
affiliations: , Columbia University - Columbia Business School and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)

detail.title: Choosing To Fail: Managerial Liability, Risk Management and Voluntary Exits of Banks
detail.abstract:
We study how extended stockholder liability shaped bank resolution during and after the Panic of 1893, comparing California state banks (unlimited liability) with national banks (double liability). Using newly assembled data linking California state bank presidents to census records and national bank stock ownership data from Examination Reports, we measure managers’ personal exposures to extended liability. For California state banks, traditional fundamentals predict involuntary liquidations but do not explain voluntary exits. Instead, voluntary exits are driven by managers’ liability exposure, local economic risk, and personal wealth, consistent with managers responding to unlimited liability by initiating preemptive, orderly resolutions. For national banks under double liability, voluntary and involuntary liquidations are more similar, and personal exposure plays a smaller role in risk management. These findings show that substantial personal liability exposure can operate for modern prudential tools like compensation clawbacks and living wills. However, such extended liability also magnifies credit contractions during downturns, highlighting a fundamental tradeoff between micro-stability and macroeconomic fragility in regulatory design.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: The Intrinsic Valuation of Biodiversity Loss
affiliations: Harvard University, Columbia University in the City of New York and Columbia University

detail.title: The Intrinsic Valuation of Biodiversity Loss
detail.abstract:
We explore the welfare costs of the loss of animal life in a consequentialist total utilitarian framework that incorporates the intrinsic value of living beings through their sentience. Moral philosophy and neuroscience define sentience as the capacity for valenced experience. Observable performance on cognitive tests represents a conservative lower bound on sentience under plausible neuroscientific assumptions. We estimate the relationship between cognition and neuron counts to cardinalize sentience. We collect population and neuron data for a wide range of animal species, and aggregate them into a single welfare measure. Across a wide range of parameters, the aggregate sentience losses of animals in the past half century outstrip the sentience gains to humans from population growth by at least 10,000-fold. Breaking even in welfare terms requires assigning a correspondingly small welfare weight to animals. Including the benefits of economic growth to humans does little to change these overall welfare losses.

title: AI in a Fragmenting World
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley, International Monetary Fund (IMF), Georgia State University, International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: AI in a Fragmenting World
detail.abstract:
We link two global trends—AI and geoeconomic fragmentation—asking how fragmentation affects the international diffusion of AI, the magnitude of gains, and their distribution across economies. We ask these questions in general but also with a focus on the MENAP economies. While the effects of AI are potentially far-reaching, the benefits are neither guaranteed nor even. Frontier AI innovation is concentrated in a small number of economies, while countries benefiting through supply-chain participation or AI adoption—with outcomes shaped by their position in global trade and production networks and their AI preparedness. Geoeconomic fragmentation slows AI diffusion and reshapes its distribution by raising trade costs, restricting technology and data flows, fragmenting digital services, and reducing cross-border investment and collaboration. Yet proactive policy choices can turn this dynamic: economies that position themselves as connectors—maintaining trade and technology links across multiple partners—can potentially capture diverted flows and outperform even the no-fragmentation benchmark. For the MENAP economies, diversified links with all major technology hubs can cushion the effects of fragmentation and provide a structural foundation to emerge as net beneficiaries of AI diffusion, but realizing that potential requires reducing AI-related trade costs, improving AI preparedness, and building local AI-related capacity.

title: The Effects of Ads on Beliefs and Implications for Consumer Search
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, Northwestern University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Northwestern - Kellogg

detail.title: The Effects of Ads on Beliefs and Implications for Consumer Search
detail.abstract:
We study how in-store display ads communicate information about a product’s price and quality, both directly through ad content and indirectly through inferences consumers draw from the presence and content of the ad. We run an incentivized experiment in a simulated online store, randomizing ad exposure, ad content, and the advertised product’s price, while also eliciting participants’ beliefs and choices. Display ads shift beliefs about price and quality, even when the ad copy does not directly reveal either attribute. We provide evidence that these belief shifts have a causal effect on searches and purchases of the advertised product. Using a stylized search model, we show that while visibility explains most of the ad effects, belief updating explains a statistically and economically significant share. Casting ad content choice as an information design problem, we show that advertisers may find it optimal to conceal product information even when it exceeds consumers’ expectations.

title: From Social Savings to Spatial Equilibrium: Evaluating Transportation Improvements in Quantitative Spatial Models
affiliations: Dartmouth College, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta and University of Oregon

detail.title: From Social Savings to Spatial Equilibrium: Evaluating Transportation Improvements in Quantitative Spatial Models
detail.abstract:
How do we evaluate the welfare gains from transport infrastructure investment? We present a quantitative spatial framework that integrates traffic and economic responses to infrastructure improvements and derives the elasticity of aggregate welfare to changes in the transportation network. The resulting formula extends the traditional ``social savings'' method to incorporate route and mode choice, agglomeration and dispersion externalities, and traffic congestion. We apply the formula to the U.S. freight network and assess the benefits of reducing costs on each segment of the U.S. Interstate Highway System. The traditional and extended measures are closely related overall, but they differ in the level of estimated gains and in the ranking of some highly valued links. Where the rankings differ, network position determines how congestion and spatial adjustment alter a link's measured benefit.

title: Reporting-Regime Transition and Bank Leverage: Evidence from Ethiopian Commercial Banks

detail.title: Reporting-Regime Transition and Bank Leverage: Evidence from Ethiopian Commercial Banks

keywords: IFRS adoption GAAP bank leverage financial reporting Ethiopian banking financial ratios reporting-regime transition panel data

detail.abstract:
I examine changes in financial ratios around IFRS adoption by Ethiopian commercial banks. Using panel data from 14 banks (2016–2023), I apply transition analysis, bank fixed effects regression, wild cluster bootstrap, sensitivity analysis, and identification diagnostics. The analysis treats CBE's September 2017 adoption separately from the 13 banks that adopted IFRS in 2018.

The results show a positive association between the post-adoption reporting regime and balance-sheet leverage. The fixed-effects estimate is +0.561 (p=0.013), remains significant under wild cluster bootstrap (p=0.018), and is similar when excluding CBE (+0.528, p=0.022). Yet the year-profile specification shows no significant leverage increase in 2018 (p=0.507). A full year-fixed-effects specification identifies the IFRS coefficient primarily through CBE's early adoption. The evidence supports a robust post-adoption association but not a causal interpretation.

Profitability evidence is weaker. ROA shows a negative and marginally significant association (p=0.089). ROE shows no significant association (p=0.441). CBE's 2016→2017 transition shows large increases in leverage (+4.55x) and ROE (+6.55 pp), but this is a single bank and illustrative only. The non-CBE 2017→2018 transition shows ROE increasing by +2.63 pp (p=0.023), but this does not survive Bonferroni correction (threshold ≈0.017).

These results should be interpreted as reporting-regime associations, not causal IFRS effects. The study contributes to the limited literature on IFRS adoption in frontier markets and highlights the identification problem in single-transition, single-sector settings.

title: Recall Fluency, Beliefs and Behavior
affiliations: University of Oxford - Said Business School, , London School of Economics and Harvard University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Recall Fluency, Beliefs and Behavior
detail.abstract:
The US Health and Retirement Study collects data on participants’ recall fluency (RF), their ability to recall words from a list, a standard measure of memory used by psychologists. Controlling for multiple demographic characteristics as well as IQ, people with a higher RF are more optimistic about stock returns, the price of their homes, and their life expectancy. We derive the predictions of a standard memory model and find that, consistent with them, the beliefs of higher RF people about each target domain are more sensitive to cues, to experiences in that domain, but also to irrelevant experiences in other domains, especially those similar to the target. These effects, in turn, carry to investment and retirement choices. RF emerges as an economically relevant personal trait.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: AI-Enhanced Multi-Objective Optimization of Cross-Border Green Logistics Networks: Balancing Cost, Delivery Efficiency, and Carbon Emissions in China-Nigeria E-Commerce Trade

detail.title: AI-Enhanced Multi-Objective Optimization of Cross-Border Green Logistics Networks: Balancing Cost, Delivery Efficiency, and Carbon Emissions in China-Nigeria E-Commerce Trade
detail.abstract:
Abstract

Cross-border e-commerce between China and Nigeria has expanded from a marginal trade channel into a structurally significant component of bilateral commerce, with total trade reaching approximately USD 22.3 billion in the first ten months of 2025 alone, a 30.2% year-on-year increase. Yet this expansion has occurred atop a logistics infrastructure that remains, by the Nigerian government's own admission, among the least efficient globally: average cargo dwell time at Nigerian ports stood at 18–21 days in 2025, roughly 475% above the global average benchmark, against 4–7 days in neighboring Benin and Ghana.

This paper develops a multi-objective optimization framework termed the Adaptive Green Corridor Model (AGCM) that combines a many-objective evolutionary algorithm (NSGA-III, extended with a machine-learning-based surrogate disruption predictor) with a discrete multimodal network representation of the China–Nigeria trade corridor, spanning maritime, air, and inland (road-fed) segments through the Lekki Deep Sea Port and Apapa/Tin Can Island gateways. Unlike prior multi-objective multimodal transport studies, which are calibrated to Eurasian rail-sea corridors or generic simulated networks, the AGCM is parameterized using verifiable 2024–2026 operational data: Nigerian Ports Authority throughput statistics, IMO/DEFRA-aligned modal carbon intensity factors, and documented demurrage cost structures.

The model is evaluated through an illustrative numerical analysis across three policy-relevant scenarios reflecting real, documented conditions on the corridor: baseline port congestion, phased customs-clearance reform under Nigeria's National Single Window initiative, and port-of-entry selection between Lagos-area terminals and the less congested Lekki Deep Sea Port. The paper's core contribution is not the optimization algorithm itself, which builds on an established and rapidly maturing literature (NSGA-III/NSGA-II hybrids, PSO-GA hybrids, robust and fuzzy-demand extensions), but the corridor-specific decision architecture: an explicit treatment of customs-clearance stochasticity and port-dwell risk as first-class, mode-dependent optimization variables rather than fixed parameters  a modeling gap that this paper argues is specific to, and materially binding in, developing-economy trade corridors such as China–Nigeria, and is largely absent from the existing multimodal green-logistics literature, which is overwhelmingly calibrated to mature-infrastructure corridors. The analysis generates a central, testable policy proposition: that Nigerian port and customs digitization reform functions as a de facto decarbonization mechanism for cross-border e-commerce logistics, by restoring the commercial competitiveness of lower-carbon sea freight relative to higher-carbon air freight for time-sensitive shipments.

title: What Access to a Mortality Pool Is Worth Funded Status and the Value of Lifetime Income in a Solved Lifecycle Model

detail.title: What Access to a Mortality Pool Is Worth Funded Status and the Value of Lifetime Income in a Solved Lifecycle Model
detail.abstract:
An idealised mortality-pool claim converts wealth into lifetime real income at actuarial value: a member who dies leaves their balance to the survivors, so no insurer's capital stands behind the payment and no permanent capital charge is passed through. We value that claim in a lifecycle model-a finite-horizon dynamic program over ages 25 to 110 with mortality, a warm-glow bequest, a subsistence consumption barrier, stochastic equity returns and a Social Security claiming decision. A companion paper establishes what it takes to build a pool that delivers such a claim. 

Access is priced by removing the instrument and resolving , then asking how much extra wealth the household would need to be as well off without it: a gain of 40% means $1M would have to become $1.4M. As a function of funded status-wealth against what the unfunded part of the floor costs to secure-the gain relative to wealth peaks at roughly a quarter to a little over a half between 0.87 and 1.69, and decays to about an eighth for a household funded six times over. In dollars it rises monotonically with wealth throughout, so the peak is a statement about the gain per dollar held, not about who receives the largest benefit. 

Below full funding the household cannot buy enough lifetime income to clear the barrier without giving up liquidity it needs sooner, so the value of access falls as funding falls: the population a pool serves best is neither the best funded nor the worst. Deep on that branch, in the baseline calibration, the household optimally buys nothing at all at 62 and values access as the option to commit later. That corner turns on what it can earn on its own balance rather than on the instrument.

title: Endogenous Reach, Technology, and Matching in Horizontal Differentiation
affiliations: University of Rome Tor Vergata - Faculty of Economics and Universitas Mercatorum

detail.title: Endogenous Reach, Technology, and Matching in Horizontal Differentiation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare they have no conflicts of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: No patients/participants
declarations.funderStatement: The paper received no funding

detail.abstract: We develop a spatial competition model in which firms choose prices and an endogenous reach: the set of consumers they can serve without horizontal mismatch. Technology operates through two channels, lowering the cost of expanding reach in geographic or product space and reducing the cost of contacting consumers while demand remains active. Within the non-overlap regime, the symmetric interior solution features positive but incomplete reach. Symmetric expansion leaves equilibrium prices and market shares unchanged, yet generates a strategic arms race in which firms incur costs to attract marginal consumers without gaining a lasting competitive advantage. Better reach technology increases reach and consumer surplus, while its welfare effect becomes negative once strategic overinvestment dominates. Relative to the social optimum, private reach can be excessive or insufficient depending on reach costs and technological efficiency. With transient demand, mobility also affects whether a seller meets a consumer before the purchase opportunity expires. The private return to mobility decomposes into socially productive match creation and pure business stealing. As demand becomes persistent, the productive component vanishes while the business-stealing incentive remains. The framework applies to customization, mobile delivery, patrol intensity, and platformenabled matching across a range of modern markets.

title: Assessing the Size of the Green Economy: Global Evidence from Harmonized Labour Force Surveys
affiliations: International Labour Organization (ILO), , Research Department (ILO) and International Labour Organization (ILO)

detail.title: Assessing the Size of the Green Economy: Global Evidence from Harmonized Labour Force Surveys

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The responsibility for opinions expressed in this article rests solely with its authors, and publication does not constitute an endorsement by the International Labour Office of the opinions expressed in it. Other usual disclaimers apply.

detail.abstract: This brief applies an ILO green taxonomy developed in Delaporte, Escudero and Adamczyk (2025) to ISCO-08 occupational task descriptions, using natural language processing. Based on these occupational categorizations, the brief subsequently measures green employment in 134 countries from the ILO’s global collection of harmonized labour force surveys (ILOSTAT). The brief proposes using ISCO standardized task descriptions and labour force survey data, on the one hand, and vacancy data, on the other hand, as complementary sources to study green employment: The former provide an internationally comparable baseline for long-term structural analysis representative of countries’ labour forces. The latter are uniquely suited to capturing emerging, more detailed and country-specific trends. Globally, an estimated 31.7 per cent of employment is in occupations that contain green tasks. In more detail, 12.1 per cent is categorized as “darker green,” relying more intensely on green tasks, while 19.6 per cent is considered “lighter green.” The analysis reveals a "green employment divide" linked to national income levels, with green employment ranging from an estimated 23.1 per cent in low-income countries to 35.7 per cent in high-income countries. Green occupations are male dominated, with men accounting for over 70 per cent of employment in these occupations, compared to a male employment share of 54.0 per cent in non-green occupations. Moreover, workers aged 15 to 24 tend to be underrepresented in green occupations.

title: The Reciprocal 1/ξ(1/2 + √s) on the Real Strip
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: The Reciprocal 1/ξ(1/2 + √s) on the Real Strip
detail.abstract: We give a working catalogue of the reciprocal completed zeta function 1/ξ(1 2 + √ s) on the real strip 0 < s < 1 2 : nine representations, from Riemann's 1859 integral through the Hadamard product, the cumulant exponential in secondary zeta values, the GGC Laplace representation equivalent to RH, the resummable Mittag-Leffler expansion, and the Euler product chart, where the Möbius-Littlewood series converges on the strip precisely when RH holds. The Thorin representation is made explicit: Lévy kernel θ Z (w) = γ>0 e-γ 2 w , Thorin measure δ γ 2 , and, by the explicit formula, an unconditional prime-side expression of the kernel, pole minus primes plus an archimedean remainder. RH is the complete monotonicity of this kernel, one rung above positivity. The bare 1/ζ admits no such representation: its pole-compensated spectrum is signed by the Riemann-Siegel phase. Ramanujan's Master Theorem applies rigorously to the reciprocal; an Esscher criterion settles when stable mixtures are Thorin; a Hankel criterion in the ladder Z(2k) linearizes RH; and RH is shown equivalent to the total positivity of the Maclaurin coefficient sequence of ξ(1 2 + √ s), whose first rung is the Turán theorem of Csordas, Norfolk and Varga and whose Toeplitz minors are rectangular Schur functions of the inverse squared ordinates. Every formula is verified numerically.

title: Optimal Early Retirement with a Partial Borrowing Constraint under Epstein-Zin Preferences
affiliations: Kyung Hee University - Department of Applied Mathematics

detail.title: Optimal Early Retirement with a Partial Borrowing Constraint under Epstein-Zin Preferences
detail.abstract: We study optimal consumption, portfolio choice, and irreversible retirement for an employed agent with Epstein-Zin stochastic differential utility and a partial borrowing constraint against human wealth. The model combines two features that have largely been analyzed separately: retirement destroys human wealth and changes the utility value of consumption, while the borrowing floor limits how much of that human wealth can be used before retirement. A human-wealth shift and scale normalization reduce the stationary stopping problem to an autonomous phase system. The unconstrained Merton solution is a hyperbolic saddle whose unstable and stable branches encode the retirement-only and borrowing-only limits. The full problem is a connector from a singular borrowing endpoint to a retirement contact set, and one scalar phase-length condition characterizes the retirement threshold. We reconstruct the value function and verify optimality over admissible systems using generalized Epstein-Zin comparison and an interior perturbation argument. Risky investment vanishes at the borrowing boundary, while consumption and the risky position jump at retirement. Recursive preferences also make intertemporal substitution affect pre-retirement risk taking despite constant investment opportunities. The retirement-only, borrowing-only, unconstrained Merton, and time-additive CRRA models arise as limiting cases.

title: From Decentralization to Institutional Integration: Blockchain Innovation in Traditional Finance
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: From Decentralization to Institutional Integration: Blockchain Innovation in Traditional Finance
detail.abstract: Decentralized finance, or DeFi, was initially framed as a challenge to traditional financial institutions. Distributed ledger technology appeared capable of enabling payments, trading, lending, and settlement without banks and other intermediaries. A more plausible outcome is now emerging: established institutions are incorporating selected blockchain capabilities while retaining regulated intermediation, custody, customer identification, and public oversight. This essay examines that convergence through digital payments and real-world asset tokenization. It argues that banks, asset managers, payment networks, and regulators are adopting programmable transactions, tokenized representations of money and assets, and more continuous transfer mechanisms without abandoning the institutional structure of centralized finance. The resulting system may deliver operational and market-access benefits, but it also raises concerns regarding liquidity mismatch, leverage, data and credit-information flows, interoperability, operational resilience, and financial stability. DeFi's lasting contribution may therefore be less the displacement of traditional finance than the demonstration of technical possibilities that traditional institutions can adapt within legal and regulatory constraints.

title: The Middle Corridor's Missing Link: Activating the Poti-Varna-Ruse Route as a Predictable EU Entry Point and Danube Distribution Hub for Bulgarian Economic Growth

detail.title: The Middle Corridor's Missing Link: Activating the Poti-Varna-Ruse Route as a Predictable EU Entry Point and Danube Distribution Hub for Bulgarian Economic Growth

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This is independent research, conducted by the author in a personal capacity as an independent researcher and UNWE graduate. It received no funding from any public, commercial or non-profit entity, and draws only on open, published sources.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study involves no human participants, patients or personal data; it is a policy-economics analysis based solely on open, published sources.
