title: Digital Weathering and Evidentiary Failure: Reconstructing Deepfake Accountability Through Platform-Aware Provenance
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Digital Weathering and Evidentiary Failure: Reconstructing Deepfake Accountability Through Platform-Aware Provenance

publicationDetails.detailsText: The manuscript was previously presented at an academic conference hosted by MNLU Nagpur and received the Best Presentation Award in the Technical Session. The manuscript has not been previously published.

detail.abstract: The rise of deepfake proliferation exposes a critical flaw in digital evidentiary standards: their reliance on pristine, static content that rarely survives outside closed systems. While current detection methods perform well on benchmark datasets like FaceForensics++ and DFDC, they assume synthetic media remains unchanged from its source. In reality, AI-generated media undergoes multi-stage transitions across platforms from TikTok to Instagram, reposted via WhatsApp or Telegram, or embedded in news articles facing systematic degradation through re-encoding, resampling, and compositing. This "Digital Weathering" erases forensic signatures and watermarks, rendering existing verification methods ineffective. This research proposes a platform-aware provenance framework shifting focus from static detection to dynamic verification resilient to real-world distribution. Based on analysis of platform processing behaviours, it maps media degradation patterns to design stabilized authentication mechanisms combining resilient neural fingerprints with blockchain-anchored attestation logs. By modelling crossplatform media journeys including EXIF stripping, format cycling, and compression stacking this study links forensic capability with legal verification, supporting deepfake accountability under emerging regulatory frameworks and real-world digital communication constraints.

title: Social Welfare Functions: A Comprehensive Survey — From Bentham to Islamic Perspectives — Properties, Principles, and Interdisciplinary Approaches

detail.title: Social Welfare Functions: A Comprehensive Survey — From Bentham to Islamic Perspectives — Properties, Principles, and Interdisciplinary Approaches

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None declared.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received.

detail.abstract: Social welfare functions constitute one of the most fundamental instruments in welfare economics, serving as the primary framework for evaluating social states, guiding public policy, and informing distributive justice. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of ten major classes of social welfare functions—from classical utilitarianism (Bentham, Harsanyi) to modern contributions (Rawls, Sen, Atkinson, Chichilnisky)—and evaluates each against fifteen fundamental principles (seven technical and eight normative). We trace the evolution of social welfare functions from cardinal utilitarian aggregation through ordinal social choice to multidimensional capability-based approaches, analyzing their respective philosophical foundations, axiomatic properties, and domains of application. Particular attention is devoted to the informational basis of each function, their sensitivity to distributional concerns, and their applicability to poverty measurement, inequality analysis, and policy evaluation. The paper further examines the Islamic perspective on social welfare, critiquing conventional approaches and proposing an integrated Islamic social welfare framework. This framework incorporates material, spiritual, social, environmental, and intergenerational dimensions. The paper concludes with a comprehensive mapping of each function against the fifteen principles, identifying Atkinson's social welfare function as the most balanced approach, and providing practical guidance for function selection based on policy objectives.

title: Sustainable Debt Securities in the Euro Area: Issuance and Holding Patterns, 2021-2025
affiliations: Central Bank of Cyprus

detail.title: Sustainable Debt Securities in the Euro Area: Issuance and Holding Patterns, 2021-2025
detail.abstract: This policy note examines the evolution of sustainable debt securities in the euro-area during the period 2021-2025. The analysis assesses their relative importance within debt markets, the distribution of holdings and issuances across sustainable debt instrument categories, and cross-country similarities in market developments. The results reveal strong growth in sustainable debt securities, although their share of total debt markets remains relatively modest. Green debt securities dominate both holdings and issuances, accounting for approximately two-thirds of the market, while social, sustainability and sustainability-linked debt securities remain less developed. Using multidimensional scaling analysis, the study identifies both common patterns and significant heterogeneity across euro-area countries. The findings highlight the growing role of sustainable debt securities in euro-area financial markets and point to scope for further diversification across sustainable debt instrument categories.

title: Conservation Is Cheap, Invariance Is Expensive: The Dimension of Responsibility Allocation Rules Immune to Corporate Restructuring

detail.title: Conservation Is Cheap, Invariance Is Expensive: The Dimension of Responsibility Allocation Rules Immune to Corporate Restructuring

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal relationships that could have influenced this work. The paper examines published methodologies of the GHG Protocol, PCAF and the responsibility measure of van den Ende, Mandel and Rusinowska (2025); the author has no affiliation with, funding from, or commercial interest in any of these organisations or their authors.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Systems that allocate responsibility for greenhouse gas emissions are asked to satisfy two properties: to allocate every tonne exactly once, and to resist manipulation through the rearrangement of legal boundaries. We show these requirements are in severe conflict. Among rules linear in emissions, conservation leaves a convex polytope of affine dimension n(n-1), one column-sum restriction per emitter, whereas invariance to the merger of trading partners collapses the admissible set from dimension n(n-1) to at most 2(n-1) on any connected production network, and to exactly n whenever the network is 2-connected, in which case the only channel through which the identity of an emitter can affect the allocation is a scalar multiple of the direct-emissions channel, and the network can inform the rule only through an emitter-blind fixed-share vector, never through emitter-specific relational weights. The exact dimension is sum_k c(G-k), the total number of components left when each agent is deleted in turn; on connected networks it is minimised by 2-connected graphs and maximised by trees. On a tree the surviving rules may depend on which branch an emitter lies in but never on its distance, which excludes any rule whose weights are strictly monotone in graph distance; the exponentially discounted responsibility measures recently characterised in the literature fail merger invariance in every configuration we compute, though an algebraic exclusion of their full parameter family remains open, and on a chain the three named accounting conventions in practical use all belong to the surviving family. We apply the results to corporate value-chain accounting and to financed emissions, and show why the remedies deployed in each (base-year recalculation, enterprise-value inflation adjustment) cannot succeed.

title: Corporate Fake News: Determinants, Market Consequences, and Corporate Responses
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, University of Technology Sydney (UTS) and

detail.title: Corporate Fake News: Determinants, Market Consequences, and Corporate Responses
detail.abstract: Using a comprehensive dataset of 12,736 fake news articles published during 2016–2020, we examine the determinants and market consequences of corporate fake news. We find that 13 percent of S&P 1500 firms are targeted by fake news. These firms have greater readership appeal, operate in uncertain and belief-sensitive information environments, and score low on Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) ratings. Following negative fake news, firms experience a statistically significant drop of 0.094 percent in abnormal returns, which is approximately a sixth of the market reaction to matched credible news, and this price impact dissipates by day two. The market reaction is driven by noise traders and firms with high arbitrage impediments, consistent with our hypothesis that boundedly rational investors lead to correlated value-irrelevant trading that sophisticated investors cannot fully arbitrage away due to transaction costs. Lastly, we find that 21 percent of target firms disclose fake news risks or directly respond to fake news during conference calls, underscoring the economic significance of fake news to public firms.

title: Searchable Menus
affiliations: Stanford University and Northwestern University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Searchable Menus
detail.abstract: Multidimensional screening is (in)famously intractable. In this paper, we study optimal screening mechanisms subject to a tractability constraint from the agent's perspective. Specifically, we require that the menu of options offered by the designer can be ordered so that, regardless of her preference type, the agent can find a utility-maximizing option via greedy search: any locally optimal choice must also be globally optimal. In one-dimensional screening with the single-crossing property, this requirement has no bite. In multidimensional environments, however, searchability restricts the set of implementable outcomes. In the multiproduct monopoly problem, the optimal searchable menu is a sparse upgrade menu: higher tiers offer higher allocation probabilities for every good, and the number of tiers is at most the number of goods. In a multidimensional screening problem with money and ordeals, the optimal searchable menu offers the agent a single way to obtain the good. In income taxation with rich multidimensional heterogeneity, a tax schedule is searchable if and only if it is progressive.

title: Quantifying the Timing of Contribution Cessation: An Analysis of Contribution Dependency Ratio Thresholds
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Quantifying the Timing of Contribution Cessation: An Analysis of Contribution Dependency Ratio Thresholds

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not required. The study is analytical and involves no human or animal subjects and no personal data.

detail.abstract: Purpose. When may a saver stop contributing toward a financial independence (FIRE) target and let compounding finish the job? Practitioners call it "Coast FIRE." We propose the contribution dependency ratio (CDR)-contribution divided by wealth-as a scale-invariant indicator. Methods. A deterministic compound-contribution model in real terms, taking the contribution rule and target as given. Results are closed-form, illustrated by three cases and tested by simulation on historical real equity returns. Results. For a given CDR stopping level, the delay does not depend on current wealth. Contributing buys earlier attainment at the CDR divided by the expected return, giving a preference-free reference point where the two are equal; a stated acceptable delay maps to a closed-form threshold. Simulation finds the benchmark conservative on most paths, though not an upper bound once returns vary. Conclusions. The framework replaces the binary, fixed-date Coast FIRE test with a continuous threshold indexed by acceptable delay.

title: Evaluating the Service Sector as a Pillar of Economic Self-Reliance in India
affiliations: University of Burdwan

detail.title: Evaluating the Service Sector as a Pillar of Economic Self-Reliance in India
detail.abstract: The concept of Atmanirbhar Bharat has traditionally emphasized manufacturing and industrial expansion as the primary pathway toward India's economic self-reliance. However, the growing contribution of the services sector to GDP, exports, digital transformation, and employment calls for a broader reassessment of its role within the self-reliance framework. This paper examines the extent to which the services sector can act as a stable and sustainable driver of Atmanirbhar Bharat through a comparative analysis of sectoral fiscal trends and macroeconomic performance indicators. Using Budget Estimates (BE), Revised Estimates (RE), and Actual Estimates (AE) data from Union Budgets 2019-20 to 2024-25, the study evaluates agriculture, manufacturing, and services sectors based on expenditure patterns and proportional deviations between planned and realised spendings. Findings indicate that the services sector exhibits lower proportional deviations between budgeted and actual expenditure, along with a steady upward trend in fiscal allocation, reflecting greater implementation stability. In contrast, the manufacturing sector, while showing higher short-term growth potential, exhibits relatively higher volatility in expenditure patterns. At the macroeconomic level, services continue to make a substantial contribution to India's GDP and export earnings, reinforcing their importance in a knowledge-and technology-driven economy. The paper argues that India's self-reliance strategy should not be viewed through a manufacturing-centric lens alone, but rather as a balanced development approach integrating industrial expansion with strong service-sector capabilities. It concludes that services should be positioned not as a substitute for manufacturing, but as a co-equal pillar of a resilient, innovation-driven, and globally competitive Atmanirbhar Bharat framework.

title: Spotify: Analyzed Through the Lenses of Platform Economics and Cultural Labor Markets
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Spotify: Analyzed Through the Lenses of Platform Economics and Cultural Labor Markets
detail.abstract:
The rise of music streaming has entirely transformed the way recorded music is produced, distributed, discovered, and monetized because digital platforms have reduced costs that come from accessing and distributing cultural goods, but simultaneously allow creators to reach vast audiences without traditional intermediaries. I believe that Spotify is a particularly interesting case to see this transformation because it is a mixed subscription and advertising platform; Spotify connects artists, rights-holders, advertisers, and listeners like you or me within one digital marketplace. Just like other digital markets, Spotify is characterized by low marginal distribution and platform-mediated access, which, for music creators, has widened the path for how their music can enter the market. 


It is key to note, however, that greater access to distribution does not necessarily imply greater equality when it comes to economic outcomes. The music industry is associated with a highly uneven cultural labor market. We will discuss Caves’ account of creative industries, where large numbers of differentiated works compete for demand in a saturated market, and artists often accept lower monetary returns because they derive value from the artistic act itself (Caves, 2000). We will also draw on Bille, who argues that strong preferences for artistic work can sustain an excess supply of artists because individuals might continue producing work despite low/uncertain earnings (Hesmondhalgh, Osborne, Sun, Barr, 2021). Digitalization also raises the notion of lower barriers to entry, as it can expand the supply of creative labor without necessarily increasing the demand or revenue available to sustain labor (Towse, 2011).


Spotify illustrates this tension because streaming was initially associated with the expectation that digital distribution would create a “long tail” where niche artists could more easily reach audiences. While this may be true to some extent, we will discuss evidence that remains strongly skewed towards a relatively small group of successful creators. This leads to broader discussion of classic winner-take-all and superstar markets, which are significant in the music industry because creators often work on a freelance or project-by-project basis, meaning their financial position is closely tied to the success of individual works (Hesmondhalgh, Osborne, Sun, Barr, 2021).


In this essay, I examine Spotify through the interconnected topics of digitalization and platforms and cultural labor markets. I argue that while Spotify has lowered barriers to producing and distributing recorded music, this democratization of access has not been matched by an equivalent democratization of economic reward. In fact, more creative supply has intensified competition for scarce visibility, while pro-rata remuneration and platform curation translate unequal attention into unequal earnings. Spotify ought to be seen as a platform that reorganizes and reinforces winner-take-all dynamics that are all too common in cultural labor markets. In this essay, I first examine how digitalization lowers barriers to entry and expands creative supply before considering the implications of too much labor supply, platform-mediated visibility, superstar dynamics, and streaming remuneration for the sustainability of creative careers.

title: Mapping Strategic Decision Space: A Comparative Diagnostic Model of Sovereign Strategic Capacity

detail.title: Mapping Strategic Decision Space: A Comparative Diagnostic Model of Sovereign Strategic Capacity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial, professional, or personal interests that could have influenced the research presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study, as it does not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Strategic Decision Space (SDS) was introduced as an integrative framework for understanding the practical capacity of states to formulate, implement and sustain sovereign strategic decisions across five interdependent dimensions: political capacity, institutional capacity, economic capacity, security capacity and the external strategic environment. The conceptual framework, however, raises a subsequent analytical question: how can differences in strategic decision space be represented and compared across states without prematurely reducing a multidimensional strategic phenomenon to a single numerical index? This paper addresses that question by developing the Strategic Decision Space Radar Model, a researcherdeveloped visual-diagnostic application of the SDS framework. Rather than producing a composite score or international ranking, the model represents the relative breadth, internal balance and configuration of strategic decision space across its five dimensions. It therefore shifts attention from how much strategic capacity a state possesses in aggregate to how that capacity is configured and where significant constraints or asymmetries occur. The paper develops a structured diagnostic methodology and applies it comparatively to selected states representing different institutional, economic, security and geopolitical configurations. The comparative analysis demonstrates that states may possess broadly similar overall strategic capacity while exhibiting substantially different internal profiles. This distinction gives rise to what the paper terms the geometry of strategic decision space: the proposition that the configuration and balance of strategic capacity may be as consequential as its overall breadth. The paper contributes to the operational development of SDS by providing a transparent framework for comparative diagnosis while deliberately distinguishing analytical mapping from cardinal measurement. It concludes that the SDS Radar Model can support comparative research, strategic diagnosis and policy analysis while providing a foundation for subsequent empirical testing and, if justified by future evidence, more formal measurement.

title: Prospects of Triveni Custom
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Prospects of Triveni Custom
detail.abstract: This study attempts to explore the strategical weighty and opportunity of Triveni Custom Office of Gandaki Province of Nepal, a major transit point across Nepal-India. The preliminary objectivity is to access is to functioning encounters and printout possibilities to optimized Triveni Customs' role in regional integration in socio-cultural exchange, tourism promotion, and bilateral economic benefits. The research integrates qualitative and scrutiny of government reports, performance of custom data, and observation of infrastructure assessment of location and social contextualization is possible via mixed-method approach. Verdicts expose critical constraints including underprivileged structure, inadequate cargo handling capacity, poor road connectivity along Korala-Pokhara-Triveni passages and imperfect administrative digitalization. In distinction sizable opportunities occur for unified trip and venture tourism development, leveraging Gandaki sacred Hindu and Buddhist sites and closeness to large pilgrimage population in Indian states. Continuing infrastructure investment on aiming to improve transportation connectivity, predicted to boost trade and connectivity within few years. Improving modernization of customs operation, infrastructure upgrading, bilateral cooperation, and transparent governments is recommended to unlocked sustainable economic growth. This exploration also contributes to realize customs enablement as a catalyst for transboundary development of socioeconomic and regional alignment in South Asia.

title: Who Absorbs Climate Risk? Institutional Transmission and Risk Sharing in Chinese and U.S. Bond Markets

detail.title: Who Absorbs Climate Risk? Institutional Transmission and Risk Sharing in Chinese and U.S. Bond Markets
detail.abstract: Bond-market climate research usually asks whether exposure changes yields. That is incomplete because a yield is only one point in a chain through which losses may be recognized, delayed, insured, guaranteed, refinanced or transferred to public balance sheets. This structured review compares Chinese corporate bonds and U.S. municipal bonds through five layers: information, pricing, contracts, liquidity and public support. U.S. municipal studies more directly identify the roles of maturity, insurance, pledged revenues, mitigation and federal assistance. Chinese studies more often document environmental or climate-related financing effects where ratings, state ownership and guarantees alter risk visibility and loss allocation. The evidence does not rank either market as more resilient; it shows that similar hazards reach investors through different obligors, information systems and loss-sharing arrangements. Companion diagnostics illustrate measurement boundaries and are not pooled crosscountry estimates. An absorber is the private or public balance sheet that contractually, institutionally or de facto bears part of a climate-related loss. The review proposes an auditable architecture linking legal-entity exposure, disclosure, pricing, credit enhancement, liquidity surveillance and contingent fiscal support, plus a feasible comparative design using common standardized hazards and outcome families estimated separately within each market.

title: From Moscow to Hormuz: The Self-Concealing Windfall of Financial Sanctions

detail.title: From Moscow to Hormuz: The Self-Concealing Windfall of Financial Sanctions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declared no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship, or publication of this article.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study uses only published macroeconomic series and involves no human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no financial support for the research, authorship, or publication of this article.

detail.abstract: Financial sanctions are usually viewed as a confrontation between the imposing and the targeted states. This analysis examines the costs incurred by the third party. Capital flows from Russia after 2022 and from Iran after 2025 have flowed steadily to small neutral economies. The analysis includes four transit economies along the Russian corridor, as well as Jordan and the smaller intermediary states of the Gulf after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in February 2026. Their central banks have absorbed these inflows by buying reserves and issuing domestic debt in return, which has come at a cost. According to IMF data for Armenia, Georgia, and Kazakhstan, sterilisation capacity fell by 7.2 to 8.7 percent of GDP, or $31.3 billion. The cost is measured from the IMF International Reserves and Foreign Currency Liquidity and World Economic Outlook databases. These quasi-fiscal expenditures accumulate on the central bank's balance sheet, not in the state budget. Meanwhile, growth, fiscal balances, and public debt improved together in three of the four corridor economies, compared with a base rate of 17 percent for 66 comparable economies outside it. Compared with the 25 non-aligned economies outside the corridor and the 41 sanctioning countries, corridor growth is higher by 3.38 and 4.80 percentage points, respectively. Sanctions imposed on the same economy of origin in 2014 serve as a test case and provide the opposite picture, so the impact is contingent and not structural. States that do not participate in the making of binding decisions pay for their consequences. Moreover, this payment is recorded as an improvement in the national accounts. We call this a self-concealing windfall. This is the price of weaponised interdependence, paid by a third party.

title: Human-Capital Beta, Career Options, and the Compensation of Former Regulators
affiliations: University of Leicester

detail.title: Human-Capital Beta, Career Options, and the Compensation of Former Regulators

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothin to declare
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: This paper develops a structural career-option model of regulator human-capital beta, defined as the firm-level exposure of value and compensation to regulatory expertise. The framework is motivated by evidence that financial firms hiring former regulators experience positive announcement returns, pay compensation premia, and obtain performance effects that are specific to regulatory rather than generic government experience. Regulatory expertise, rule interpretation, and policy-signal quality enter as primitives that shift project cash flows, regulatory costs, financing conditions, and market beliefs. Human-capital beta summarizes the firm-level exposure to those primitives. A regulator's private-sector opportunity is represented as a convex career claim on firm equity value, with the public-sector continuation value serving as the strike-like outside option. The model generates three main implications. First, announcement returns are increasing in regulatory exposure and agency-firm match quality. Second, compensation premia arise because the same expertise that raises firm value also raises the value of the regulator's career option. Third, when equity-linked compensation, leverage, and weak debt penalties interact, value-enhancing regulatory human capital can also move a firm toward a leverage-vega default-risk boundary. The paper does not assume that all revolving-door moves are opportunistic; instead, it identifies the subset of career paths in which regulatory human capital is capitalized into firm value and private compensation is equity-linked.

title: Beyond Climate Risk: Measuring Climate Uncertainty and Its Macroeconomic and Financial Effects
affiliations: Università di Milano Bicocca and Goethe University Frankfurt

detail.title: Beyond Climate Risk: Measuring Climate Uncertainty and Its Macroeconomic and Financial Effects
detail.abstract: We study the distributional dynamics of extreme weather in Europe and its macroeconomic and …nancial consequences, distinguishing climate risk from climate uncertainty. Using a balanced panel of forty European countries over 1981-2024 and the E3CI composite index and its seven hazard components, we condition the distribution of extreme weather on anthropogenic radiative forcing and natural climate oscillators, measuring climate risk by the conditional median and climate uncertainty by the conditional interquartile range. Both moments respond nonlinearly to greenhouse gas concentrations. Still, the contribution of natural forcing is asymmetric: climate risk re ‡ects anthropogenic and natural drivers, whereas climate uncertainty is predominantly anthropogenic, with wild…res as the main exception. The post-2010 acceleration in warming is re ‡ected in both moments, although with distinct spatial patterns. Both risk and uncertainty depress economic activity through a common productivity channel: real wages absorb most of the e¢ ciency loss, consumption contracts by more than output, and labor utilization remains largely unchanged. Uncertainty e¤ects are roughly twice as large as risk effects for a typical annual change, and their incidence is governed more by countries' absorptive capacity than by physical exposure, making climate change a source of economic divergence within Europe. In …nancial markets, climate exposures are concentrated in the uncertainty measures, with the value factor loading negatively on maximum-temperature and wild…re uncertainty and risk. Overall, the evidence is consistent with irreversibility and precautionary behavior as important mechanisms through which climate uncertainty a¤ects macroeconomic activity and asset prices.

Sharpe 0.55. [Half-Title: Sectoral Intramonth Momentum Cycle -A Quantpedia Preprint.] Calendar Anomaly

detail.abstract: We document a persistent intramonth momentum cycle in U.S. sector ETFs that yields meaningful risk-adjusted returns when properly sequenced. Using the nine original Select Sector SPDR ETFs and SPY as the market benchmark from December 1998 through June 2026, we show that trailing 252-day sector momentum generates a positive spread on the first trading day of the month— and then sharply reverses on days two and three. A third, independent leg of the cycle emerges in the window from ten to five trading days before monthend, consistent with the intramonth momentum cycle recently documented at the single-stock level by Nathan et al. (2026). Stitching the three legs together into a single composite strategy delivers 5.99% annualized return at a 0.55 Sharpe ratio for the long-short variant, and 3.77% at 0.54 for the market-neutral variant—all while being invested fewer than half the trading days each month. Our contribution is twofold: we extend the calendar-anomaly literature from individual equities to sector-level portfolios, and we provide practitioners with a transparent, low-turnover framework that translates these academic patterns into actionable trade schedules.

title: The Cost Floor of a Low-Tax Jurisdiction: Decomposing the Effective Burden on Owner-Managed Companies in Bulgaria, 2026

detail.title: The Cost Floor of a Low-Tax Jurisdiction: Decomposing the Effective Burden on Owner-Managed Companies in Bulgaria, 2026

declarations.ethicsApproval: No human participants, patients, or identifiable personal data were involved. The paper analyses publicly available statutory parameters and aggregate official statistics only; ethics approval and consent were not required.

detail.abstract: Bulgaria is routinely described by its headline rates: a flat 10% corporate income tax and a 5% withholding tax on dividends, the joint-lowest combination in the European Union. This paper argues that for the population that actually relocates-owner-managed companies with a single resident owner-manager and no employees-the headline pair explains only part of the burden, and the smaller part at low profit. Using published 2026 statutory parameters, the paper derives a closed-form decomposition in which the effective burden equals a constant 14.5% plus 85.5% of the fixed cost base expressed as a share of profit. Because mandatory social insurance contributions are levied on a chosen base bounded below by a statutory minimum, that fixed component does not scale down with profit. The result is a strongly regressive effective rate: 31.0% at €10,000 of annual profit, 22.8% at €20,000, 17.8% at €50,000 and 15.2% at €250,000, before any professional fees. The paper then compares the arrangement with Romania's micro-enterprise regime after the 2026 reversal, shows that the Romanian regime is margin-sensitive rather than profit-sensitive, and identifies the profit range in which neither jurisdiction repays the cost of the structure. Three pressures on the Bulgarian position are documented: a 12.6% minimum wage increase in a single year, a VAT registration threshold now measured on a calendar-year basis, and a general government deficit of 5.7% of GDP. The paper is a practitioner analysis of published parameters and reports no new empirical data.

title: Regional Inequality and the Agricultural Labor Market in Spain: a Structural Analysis of the Andalusian Case

detail.title: Regional Inequality and the Agricultural Labor Market in Spain: a Structural Analysis of the Andalusian Case
detail.abstract:
Spain is strongly characterized by regional inequalities, an analysis of which reveals a pattern of marked polarization, persistent despite decades of overall economic growth and European integration processes.
The aim of this paper is to critically examine the structural gap between the southern regions, particularly Andalusia and Extremadura, and the more advanced areas of central and northern Spain, such as Madrid, Catalonia and the Basque Country. My focus is on the role of the agricultural labor market, characterized by high seasonality, informality and precarious employment. From a historical and institutional perspective, I attempt to reconstruct the cause-effect dynamics that have crystallized these disparities, from the autarchic policies of the Franco regime to the current framework of rural cohesion and welfare policies.

title: Governance Under Institutional Stress: Structural and Behavioural Board Mechanisms and Firm Performance
affiliations: Indian Institute of Management Mumbai, Indian Institute of Management Mumbai and Indian Institute of Management Mumbai

detail.title: Governance Under Institutional Stress: Structural and Behavioural Board Mechanisms and Firm Performance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests, personal relationships, or affiliations that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, human data, or animal subjects. Therefore, ethics committee approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Research Question/Issue

This paper investigates whether an exogenous institutional shock and subsequent regulatory reforms reshape the relationship between board composition, executive compensation, shareholder mechanisms, and firm performance in a concentrated-ownership emerging market, using the 2018 collapse of a major Indian financial conglomerate as a natural experiment.

Research Findings/Insights

Using a Bayesian dynamic panel model on 95 of India’s largest listed firms (2015-2022), we find separating the board chair and chief executive roles is associated with a robust post-shock performance premium. Board diversity shows a stable positive association across both regimes, while board independence displays a regime-dependent compliance ceiling; executive pay alignment and shareholder policies remain statistically insignificant. Channel estimates show the shock increased board independence but not board role separation or executive pay alignment.

Theoretical/Academic Implications

The findings recast the governance-performance relationship as conditional on the distance between formal and informal institutions: mechanisms that operate structurally translate into improved performance, while those requiring behavioural compliance from controlling owners are neutralised in substance even when formally complied with. This reframes mixed emerging-market evidence as a predictable consequence of the formal-informal gap rather than as conflicting findings.

Practitioner/Policy Implications

Enforcement should target the quality of board oversight rather than formal structure, because mandates that raise compliance floors compress the variation that distinguishes firms. Investors should read composite governance scores as measures of disclosure rather than governance quality in promoter-controlled firms; boards benefit most from structural mechanisms that deliver returns independent of regulatory pressure.

title: Screening for Mean Reversion in Statistical Arbitrage: Size, Power, and the Limits of Per-Name Identification

detail.title: Screening for Mean Reversion in Statistical Arbitrage: Size, Power, and the Limits of Per-Name Identification
detail.abstract: Statistical arbitrage strategies built on factor residuals routinely screen candidate positions by fitting an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process to the cumulative residual over a short window and retaining names whose estimated mean-reversion speed exceeds a cutoff. We show that this screen is an unlabelled Dickey-Fuller test, and that it fails in both directions. Its null hypothesis is false by construction: because the residuals come from an in-sample regression with an intercept, the cumulative residual ends at zero and begins within O p (L-1/2) of it relative to the path's typical excursion, so it converges to a Brownian bridge (Ploberger and Krämer, 1992), which reverts to its own mean mechanically. In simulation the conventional screen retains 98.65% of series containing no mean reversion whatsoever. Replacing it with a correctly sized test does not solve the problem, because at the conventional sixty-day window a 5% test has almost no power: it rejects 6.1% of the time against a fifteen-day half-life, against a size of 5.0%. Attaining 80% power requires between five hundred and seven hundred fifty observations, a span over which the constant-parameter assumption the method rests on is untenable. Using 11.0 million stock-days of US equity data from 1999 to 2026, with delisted names retained, we find the conventional screen retains 98.85% of stock-days against a null of 98.65%, stays within a percentage point of that null in every year of the sample, and does so under every residualisation we try. Pooling across the cross-section, residual mean reversion is nonetheless real and strongly significant, and a simulated method of moments estimator recovers a representative half-life of 22 business days, a speed the same sixty-day window has no power to detect in an individual name. Reversion is real. It is simply not identified name by name at the horizon the method requires. Consistent with this, not screening at all is the best rule we examine at every positive trading cost, though its margin over the conventional screen is not statistically distinguishable from zero.

title: When Waiting Is Risky: A Closed-Form Model of Home-Purchase Timing

detail.title: When Waiting Is Risky: A Closed-Form Model of Home-Purchase Timing
detail.abstract: Recent evidence that buyers who lose a previously inspected property transact sooner motivates an ex ante question: how much is waiting worth when the current dwelling may be sold to someone else? Housing-search and auction models value future opportunities; this paper instead isolates the option to wait on a match already identified. For an eligible household, losing that match means continuing to rent rather than reverting to a wealth-only position. Willingness to pay therefore has a finite ceiling: the household’s own value of ownership plus the certainty equivalent of the rent that purchase avoids. Paying above the ownership value can be rational, but it remains bounded. A higher risk of losing the match raises the reservation price and erodes the value of waiting. Once matches are short-lived, that erosion has a rate: what is left is approximately the price uncertainty the buyer can expect to resolve before the match is gone, decaying with an elasticity approaching one half. Because equivalent replacements are not genuine losses, buyer-side liquidity is availability net of close substitutes, not listing turnover. The result is a closed-form decision rule for an eligible buyer facing a perishable match, and a price on the time she has left.

title: Public Guarantees, Private Discretion: Evidence from Small Business Lending

detail.title: Public Guarantees, Private Discretion: Evidence from Small Business Lending
detail.abstract: Government loan guarantees can expand credit, but they may also create moral hazard by insulating private lenders from the losses associated with their lending decisions. I study this trade-off in the SBA’s Preferred Lender Program (PLP), which delegates loan approval to selected lenders without removing the federal guarantee. Using the universe of SBA 7(a) loans, I study lender portfolios around entry into the PLP and compare delegated versus non-delegated loans within the same lender. Delegation is not associated with deterioration in loan performance. Yet this portfolio-level stability masks systematic sorting within lender portfolios: relative to reviewed loans from the same lender, delegated long-maturity loans charge off more, while delegated short-maturity loans charge off less. These patterns suggest that lenders use delegated authority selectively rather than simply shifting risk onto the government guarantee.

title: The Rule Ecology of Corruption: Compliance Decisions, Social Feedback, and Institutional Equilibria
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Rule Ecology of Corruption: Compliance Decisions, Social Feedback, and Institutional Equilibria
detail.abstract: We model a society's corruption level as an equilibrium property of its entire rule system rather than as the product of corrupt individuals or weak punishment. Individuals face a portfolio of heterogeneous rules whose internalized normative force varies with the congruence between law and norm; each encounter is a discrete compliance choice coupled to others through conformity, shared enforcement capacity, and two tiers of institutional legitimacy, one rule-specific and one system-wide. The framework, in the discrete-choice-with-social-interactions tradition of Brock and Durlauf (2001), delivers four contributions. First, a rule-portfolio microfoundation: corruption proper, the violation of entrusted-role rules, is generated inside a wider ecology of rule compliance and coupled to it through the model's dynamics. Second, a theory of equilibrium regimes: threshold dispersion governs whether a society has a unique compliance equilibrium or clean and corrupt equilibria between which it can tip, and both extremes of the corrupt equilibrium can be strictly Pareto-dominated yet self-enforcing. Third, endogenous institutional legitimacy: observed violation degrades enforcement capacity, rule-level legitimacy, and system-level legitimacy, producing hysteresis and gradual-then-sudden transitions. Fourth, instrument matching: which anti-corruption instrument works depends on the regime, with simplification dominating punishment under cognitive overload and moderately selective enforcement capable of raising corruption through procedural-legitimacy erosion. Two boundary results follow as corollaries: in a large diverse rule portfolio, every equilibrium features strictly positive violation with probability approaching one, and a planner facing a bounded enforcement technology optimally tolerates a strictly positive level, even when zero corruption is finitely attainable.

title: The EU AI Act and Kenya's National AI Strategy: A Comparative Assessment of Risk Allocation, Capability Building, and the Training-Data Gap
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The EU AI Act and Kenya's National AI Strategy: A Comparative Assessment of Risk Allocation, Capability Building, and the Training-Data Gap

keywords: African Union Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy

detail.abstract:
The European Union (EU) and Kenya are converging on the same artificial intelligence (AI) governance failure from opposite directions: rules without a supervisor capable of enforcing them. The EU could not deliver its own regime on schedule, and Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 deferred the core high-risk obligations of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act by sixteen months, six days before they were due to apply. Kenya has fragmented into three partly inconsistent governance tracks that disagree about the identity of the regulator. In both cases, the binding constraint is institutional capacity rather than drafting. A second finding is that intellectual property in AI training data is now the fastest-widening gap in the Kenyan framework: it is load-bearing for the flagship ambition of locally grounded language models, and it is the gap least amenable to a purely national solution.

The paper reaches those findings by comparing Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the Artificial Intelligence Act) with the Kenya Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025–2030 across scope, achievement, shortfall, deterioration over time, and reform. It argues that the two instruments are routinely compared as though they were commensurable, and that this framing distorts assessment of both. The European instrument is a binding risk allocator built on existing product-safety architecture; the Kenyan instrument is a non-binding capability builder addressed at the preconditions for an AI ecosystem that does not yet exist. Each is strongest where the other is silent.

The paper offers eight reform proposals for Kenya and six for the EU. It concludes that the transferable lesson from Brussels to Nairobi is not the substance of the risk taxonomy but the discipline of naming, funding and empowering an enforcer, and that the training-data question requires regional coordination through the African Regional Intellectual Property Organization and the African Union rather than national legislation alone.

title: Two-Thirds of Whom? Section 108 of the Constitution of Sierra Leone, the Majority Required to Amend It, and the Question of Construction for the Supreme Court
affiliations: Kanu & Associates

detail.title: Two-Thirds of Whom? Section 108 of the Constitution of Sierra Leone, the Majority Required to Amend It, and the Question of Construction for the Supreme Court
detail.abstract: The Constitution of Sierra Leone (Amendment) Bill 2025, the fruit of a review process reaching back to the 1999 Lomé Peace Agreement and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, carries significant reforms, among them a strengthened and renamed National Electoral Commission with higher qualifications for commissioners, and a constitutional quota for the nomination of women as well as greater political participation by dual citizens. Its passage on 10 August 2026 was overshadowed by a contestation, which may soon be before the Supreme Court, over the majority that section 108(2)(b) requires for constitutional alteration: whether two-thirds of the entire membership of Parliament, or two-thirds of the Members present and voting; the voting method used; and whether the special majority governs the committee stage or only the second and third readings. This article states both constructions as fairly as it can, addresses the quorum question each raises, identifies the points on which they truly join issue, and commends the matter to the Supreme Court, whose authoritative clarity would place the gains of the reform on secure constitutional footing.

title: Do Richer Personas Improve LLM Survey Simulation? A Fidelity Paradox
affiliations: , Prolific Inc., Prolific Inc., Prolific Inc. and Prolific Inc.

detail.title: Do Richer Personas Improve LLM Survey Simulation? A Fidelity Paradox

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors are employees of Prolific Ltd., which is the platform used to collect the participant data for this study.
declarations.funderStatement: All funding for this research was provided by Prolific Ltd.

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as substitutes for human survey respondents, despite documented failures in their accuracy and realism. We field a 21-item survey on political opinion and consumer insights to a politically representative online US sample (N = 996), supplement it with AI-moderated qualitative interviews, and attempt to reproduce the human data with LLM-simulated respondents at increasing levels of persona fidelity, from no information at all, through demographic personas, to demographics plus verbatim idiographic interview transcripts. We find a fidelity paradox in that richer persona context does not straightforwardly improve accuracy. Individual-level simulation with demographic personas, a dominant "silicon sampling" design, roughly triples distributional error relative to simply asking the model for an aggregate distribution, due to severe variance collapse. We show this collapse is largely a reporting artefact rather than a knowledge deficit. Eliciting a per-persona probability distribution instead of a single forced answer improves distributional accuracy by 35 to 48 percent while preserving the individual-level data subgroup analysis requires. Post-stratifying the best synthetic datasets through the same MRP model used for the human data leaves distributional error unchanged, marking the residual as model error that survey correction cannot reach, and even the best pipeline never approaches the sampling-noise floor two real polls of this size would share. Throughout, distributional fidelity and point accuracy systematically dissociate, so no single statistic certifies synthetic data as accurate, only accurate for a specified target. These conclusions replicate across two frontier models, and support using LLM simulation for directional, exploratory work rather than as a substitute for measurement.

title: Rights Without Reasons? Public Disclosure Of Human Review In Automate Credit Decision

detail.title: Rights Without Reasons? Public Disclosure Of Human Review In Automate Credit Decision
detail.abstract: A right to challenge an automated credit decision is difficult to use without reasons, while an explanation is weak if no one will reconsider the decision. I audit this explanation-contestability link for 88 ECB-supervised banking groups. In a frozen July 2026 human-coded evidence set, 13 groups provide meaningful logic, 23 provide a substantive review or challenge route, and 6 provide both. A later current-source re-retrieval, followed by targeted human verification, finds 36 groups with both and identifies retrieval sensitivity as a first-order measurement problem. The paper therefore contributes both a consumer-facing accountability construct and a warning: coding reliability does not establish retrieval completeness.

title: Admissibility, Reachability, and Retention: A Structural Analysis of Persistent Occupation

detail.title: Admissibility, Reachability, and Retention: A Structural Analysis of Persistent Occupation
detail.abstract: Persistent occupation is a common feature of dynamical systems, yet the observation of sustained occupancy does not by itself identify the mechanisms responsible for producing it. Existing analyses typically approach this problem through concepts such as stability, attraction, recurrence, invariance, or confinement. This paper examines the problem from a structural perspective. We introduce retention as a category intended to capture persistence following access, formalized as the expected duration of the first sojourn within a region conditional on that region having been reached. This definition generalizes, in continuous graded form, the classical distinction between absorbing and transient states in Markov chain theory, and connects naturally to first-passage and metastability theory. The proposed framework distinguishes three layers of analysis: admissibility, reachability, and retention. Admissibility specifies which states belong to a domain. Reachability characterizes which admissible states can be accessed under the governing operators. Retention concerns the expected duration for which accessible regions sustain occupation following access. To investigate this distinction, we construct a synthetic dynamical laboratory in which admissibility remains fixed while local dynamical mechanisms vary across regions of the domain. The resulting experiments show that regions exhibiting comparable accessibility may display substantially different occupation patterns, 1 with retention estimates for strongly contractive regions found to be fully right-censored at the simulation horizon. A subsequent isolated experiment, sweeping the local contraction rate λ under fixed noise, shows that retention grows approximately exponentially with λ (R 2 = 0.998) while reachability remains essentially constant, providing direct quantitative evidence (consistent with Kramers-type escape scaling) that reachability and retention are governed by different aspects of an operator's local geometry. The analysis suggests that retention is an operator-dependent property, represented as Ret F (R), rather than an intrinsic property of states or regions.

title: Competitive Insurance Pricing in a Multi-period Stochastic Duopoly: Open-Loop and Markov-perfect Equilibria
affiliations: University of Hong Kong and The University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Competitive Insurance Pricing in a Multi-period Stochastic Duopoly: Open-Loop and Markov-perfect Equilibria
detail.abstract: We study a multi-period stochastic insurance duopoly in which two risk-averse insurers set premiums that drive the stochastic evolution of their portfolios. The number of in-force policies follows a conditional Poisson transition model whose intensity depends on the previous portfolio size and on current relative pricing. Insurers evaluate terminal wealth under exponential utility. Under compactness and a finite moment-generating function condition, we establish the existence of a selected Markov-perfect equilibrium. Under a boundary convention and with strictly positive initial portfolios, we show that the set of open-loop Nash equilibrium paths coincides with the set of deterministic premium paths induced by the selected Markov-perfect-equilibrium construction. Under an additional contraction condition, this common equilibrium path is unique. This equivalence is driven by three structural features: the absence of wealth effects under exponential utility, the multiplicative structure of the portfolio dynamics, and a boundary selection rule for extinct portfolios. Under contraction, interiority, and time-invariance assumptions, the model predicts a terminal-period premium increase, and the numerical examples display a backward-propagating sawtooth pattern. We prove a local terminal oscillation under symmetric parameters and show that strategic complementarity induces synchronization of competitors' premiums when continuation-value shifts move in the same direction. The numerical sensitivity analysis further illustrates how risk aversion, price sensitivity, and expense rate reshape both premium levels and intertemporal oscillations.

title: Can EMIR 3 Be Evaluated from Public CCP Disclosures?

detail.title: Can EMIR 3 Be Evaluated from Public CCP Disclosures?
detail.abstract: A regulation can be public while its effectiveness remains impossible to evaluate from public data. EMIR 3 provides a clean example. I match quarterly Eurex OTC interest-rate-swap and LCH SwapClear public quantitative disclosures from 2022 Q1 to 2026 Q1 and track Eurex's share of combined required initial margin. The share rises only modestly after the Active Account Requirement deadline, with a larger movement in house accounts and no unique quarterly break. ESMA's restricted-data assessment shows a clearer shift for the legally relevant EU population. The central result is therefore about evaluability: standardized public CCP totals lose the assignment dimensions needed to assess a counterparty-specific rule.

title: Sentiment and Return Predictability in Global Value Chains
affiliations: University of Duisburg-Essen - House of Energy Markets and Finance

detail.title: Sentiment and Return Predictability in Global Value Chains
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether textual information disclosed by economically linked firms is reflected in asset prices. I combine a global sample of earnings-call transcripts with multi-regional input-output tables to construct firm-level measures of customer and supplier sentiment. Customer sentiment positively predicts focal-firm returns, whereas supplier sentiment often predicts lower returns, consistent with a demand channel on the customer side and an input-cost or bargaining-power channel on the supplier side. Double-sort portfolios show that network sentiment contains information beyond the focal firm's own tone. Spillover effects are strongest among low-attention firms, consistent with gradual information diffusion. Mechanism tests further show that customer effects strengthen under favorable demand and profitability conditions, whereas supplier effects increase with input-cost pressure and global supply-chain stress.

title: Outside Options under Tariff Pressure: Export Networks and Third-Market Adjustment

detail.title: Outside Options under Tariff Pressure: Export Networks and Third-Market Adjustment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses publicly available, aggregate secondary data and does not involve human participants, personal data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper studies whether export networks established before a partner-specific tariff increase condition subsequent adjustment in third markets. A sequential game formalizes the exporter's latent outside option, while the empirical analysis measures the pre-event breadth of non-targeted export relationships. The data combine the Base pour l'Analyse du Commerce International (BACI), produced by the Centre d' Études Prospectives et d'Informations Internationales (CEPII), for 2015-2024 with the Global Tariff Database (GTD) for 2015-2021, yielding 1,356 exporter-year observations and 131 events. In the event sample, a one-standard-deviation increase in pre-event third-market diversification is associated with 0.146 log points higher thirdmarket export growth from t-1 to t + 1 (exporter-clustered standard error 0.057; p = 0.013), equivalent to approximately 15.7 percent under the log interpretation. Breadth-based measures are positive, whereas concentration-based measures are negative. Mean third-market growth increases monotonically across diversification quartiles. The secondary interaction between a tariff event and lagged global diversification is positive but imprecisely estimated and sensitive to the inclusion of 2021. The paper's most robust empirical fact therefore concerns third-market reallocation rather than aggregate export protection; the annual country-level design does not identify causal product-level trade diversion.

title: Measuring Civic Belonging: Towards an Evidence-based Framework for European Union Policymaking
affiliations: International Institute for Diplomacy and Social Affairs (IIDSA)

detail.title: Measuring Civic Belonging: Towards an Evidence-based Framework for European Union Policymaking
detail.abstract: European democracies routinely measure electoral participation, institutional trust, social cohesion, discrimination and identification with political communities. Yet these indicators do not fully capture whether individuals experience themselves as recognised, consequential and legitimate members of the democratic communities in which they live. This working paper proposes civic belonging as an integrative policy concept centred on substantive democratic membership and develops a European application, the European Civic Belonging Framework (ECBF-EU). The framework distinguishes five core dimensions-Recognition, Institutional Trust, Civic Voice, Equal Access and Social Connection-complemented in the European Union context by a sixth contextual dimension, European Political Attachment. Rather than introducing new democratic phenomena, the ECBF-EU reorganises established dimensions of democratic experience around a distinct policy question: whether individuals experience themselves as recognised and consequential members of the political community. The paper proposes that the framework should initially operate as a multidimensional diagnostic dashboard rather than a composite index. Existing European datasets could populate a substantial part of the framework before additional survey instruments are developed. Potential applications include European Citizens' Panels, the European Citizens' Initiative, EU participation programmes and local and regional democratic initiatives. The paper concludes with a staged research agenda for conceptual validation, measurement development, European piloting and policy evaluation.

title: From Mandate to Regulated Voluntarism:: IFRS S1/S2 Regulatory Reversal, Concurrent Events, and Capital-Market Identification in Brazil
affiliations: Fundação Getulio Vargas

detail.title: From Mandate to Regulated Voluntarism:: IFRS S1/S2 Regulatory Reversal, Concurrent Events, and Capital-Market Identification in Brazil

However, the views and analyses presented in this paper are solely those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions, strategies, or opinions of the author's employer. The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced this research.
