title: Reflexive Market Structure: Leveraged ETFs, Liquidity Congestion, and the Amplification of Financial Shocks The 2026 Korean Semiconductor Market as a Focal Case

detail.title: Reflexive Market Structure: Leveraged ETFs, Liquidity Congestion, and the Amplification of Financial Shocks The 2026 Korean Semiconductor Market as a Focal Case
detail.abstract: This paper develops a conditional framework of reflexive market structure: modern financial markets are intentionally linked, but those linkages can become amplifying when a price change in one market mechanically induces position changes in another and the resulting flows feed back into the same underlying securities. The paper uses leverage density as a stress concept—the amount of mechanically responsive exposure relative to the market capacity available to absorb its adjustment—rather than as an estimated causal coefficient. South Korea’s 2026 equity market provides a focal case. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix became dominant KOSPI constituents while domestic and cross-border single-stock leveraged products expanded rapidly. Nine KOSPI market-wide circuit-breaker events occurred through July 29, two before the May 27 domestic product launch and seven afterward. Because the post-launch observations are selected by the occurrence of a Korean circuit breaker, crossmarket comparisons are descriptive severity benchmarks rather than treatment-effect estimates. On those seven event-defined dates, the KOSPI declined by an average 7.82% versus 3.01% for the Nikkei 225, producing a mean KOSPI-minus-Nikkei return differential of −4.82 percentage points. The strongest ETF-specific mechanism evidence occurred on June 23, when Bloomberg Intelligence estimated approximately $6 billion of mechanically required leveraged-ETF selling in Samsung and SK Hynix, equivalent to roughly 14% of their combined turnover. July 29 provides separate evidence of broader leveraged-position liquidation but does not isolate single-stock ETF flows. The evidence does not establish that leveraged products initiated or caused the Korean selloffs. It is consistent instead with a conditional amplification mechanism in which cross-market coupling, issuer concentration, mechanically responsive leverage, investor positioning, and constrained liquidity interact after an initiating shock. The broader concern is not any one product in isolation, but the difficulty of anticipating second- and higher-order effects when multiple linked markets respond mechanically to the same price movement.

title: Mixed Markets, Mixed Enforcement? An Empirical Study of EU Competition Law Enforcement against State-owned Enterprises
affiliations: Utrecht University School of Law

detail.title: Mixed Markets, Mixed Enforcement? An Empirical Study of EU Competition Law Enforcement against State-owned Enterprises

keywords: Mixed Enforcement? An Empirical Study of EU Competition Law Enforcement Against State-owned Enterprises

detail.abstract:
State ownership has been rediscovered across the EU for industrial policy purposes, proving effective in the pursuit of strategic autonomy and sustainability transitions. State-owned enterprises (SOEs) are historically prominent in critical markets such as energy, extraction, utilities, finance and transportation, while allowing for more government influence than in private firms.

The above developments have led to a resurgence of state ownership through nationalization, active shareholding and subsidization in the EU, creating new risks for so-called mixed markets, where SOEs and private firms compete. This, in turn, raises questions about competition law enforcement of such markets. SOEs may be inclined to behave anticompetitively and create obstacles for private enterprises. However, there is little understanding of how competition law is enforced against SOEs in practice. This PhD research seeks to establish the first empirical insights into the practice and constraints of competition law enforcement against SOEs. 

• As PhD researcher, you will undertake a 4-year research project aimed at answering to what extent, and on what grounds, the enforcement of EU competition law differs between State-owned enterprises and private undertakings. 
• This PhD project envisions a mixed methods approach, combining data-driven, experimental and qualitative methodologies.
• The envisioned output of this PhD is 4 academic articles suitable for publication in peer-reviewed academic journals in competition law or policy.
• Throughout this project you will work in close collaboration with two dedicated PhD supervisors, who will coach you towards becoming an independent academic researcher.

title: Inflation thresholds and infant mortality in Sub‐Saharan Africa: Moderating roles of public spending and telecommunication infrastructures by degree of economic diversification
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Douala and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Inflation thresholds and infant mortality in Sub‐Saharan Africa: Moderating roles of public spending and telecommunication infrastructures by degree of economic diversification
detail.abstract: This study examines the presence of nonlinear threshold effects in the relationship between inflation and infant mortality in Sub‐Saharan Africa, while analysing the moderating roles of public health spending, military expenditure and telecommunication infrastructures. Using a dynamic panel threshold model (Kremer et al., 2013) followed by the Driscoll‐Kraay (1998) estimator on a panel of 45 countries over the period 2000‐2024, we find an inflation threshold of 6.49% for the full sample. The marginal effect is about ten times larger below the threshold (0.40) than above it (0.035). This effect varies considerably with the degree of economic diversification. In highly diversified economies, inflation has no detectable impact, indicating a protective role of diversification. In moderately diversified countries, low inflation has a very strong effect (0.51‐0.55), while high inflation has a weak but significant effect (0.035). Conversely, inflation is beneficial in weakly diversified countries. Telecommunication infrastructure robustly mitigates the adverse effect of high inflation, particularly in moderately and weakly diversified countries, whereas military spending amplifies it in moderately diversified economies. Public health spending does not play a robust moderating role. These results underscore the importance of keeping inflation below 7%, investing in telecommunications, and promoting economic diversification to protect child health in Sub‐Saharan Africa.

title: Interest Rates and Stock Returns of Nigerian Quoted Insurance Firms
affiliations: University of Ilorin, Ilorin, Nigeria, Bayero University, Bayero University and Bayero University

detail.title: Interest Rates and Stock Returns of Nigerian Quoted Insurance Firms
detail.abstract: The study used the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) estimation model to establish the short-run and long-run relationship between interest rates and the return on the stock of insurance firms listed in Nigeria. The study adopted ex-post facto research design because it used secondary sources to extract data regarding the exchange rate of the Nigerian naira to the United States dollar, inflation rate and interest rate. The population of interest comprised all Nigerian insurance businesses, publicly traded on the stock exchange between January 2019 and December 2020. As of December 2020, there were 25 insurance firms listed on the Nigerian Stock Exchange, representing the target population for the research. After applying a filter, twelve (12) specified insurance firms were included in the sample size. For data testing, the research used parametric techniques. Using Eviews version 9 software, the model is estimated using Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) methods. The findings of the longrun and short-run coefficients showed that interest rates affect the return on the stock of insurance firms listed in Nigeria. The exchange rate positively and significantly impacted stock returns over the long and short run. Conversely, inflation and interest rates negatively and significantly long-short-run affect the insurance industry's portfolio returns. As such, Investors should diversify their investment in developing and emerging markets domestically and abroad to reduce the risk associated with the interplay of interest rates.

title: Roadblocks of University Students to Start a New Business

detail.title: Roadblocks of University Students to Start a New Business
detail.abstract: Entrepreneurship has become an important driver of economic growth, innovation, and employment generation. Despite having entrepreneurial potential, many university students in Bangladesh are discouraged from starting new businesses due to various challenges. This study aims to identify the major roadblocks influencing students' entrepreneurial intentions and examine the support mechanisms that can encourage business creation. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire from 50 university students using the convenience sampling technique. Descriptive statistical analysis was employed to evaluate students' perceptions regarding entrepreneurship and the barriers they encounter. The findings reveal that financial constraints, fear of failure, academic workload, family influence, and limited institutional support are the primary factors affecting students' decisions to start a business. The study further highlights that entrepreneurship education, mentoring, networking opportunities, and financial assistance can play a significant role in fostering entrepreneurial intentions among university students in Bangladesh.

title: Blockchain-Based Identity and Access Management in IoT Networks
affiliations: , Service Accoutn Specialist BOSCH, Otis elevator company, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Bangladesh University

detail.title: Blockchain-Based Identity and Access Management in IoT Networks
detail.abstract: The accelerated growth of Internet of Things (IoT) devices in the smart city, healthcare, industrial automation, and critical infrastructures present a major challenge in managing identities and access control because of the heterogeneity of the devices, the need to scale, and because device identities are usually centralized on a single trusting authority. Commonly, traditional identity and access management (IAM) systems are not sufficient to combat the security vulnerabilities of single points of failure, unauthorized access, and identity spoofing in large-scale IoT systems. In order to address these constraints, in this paper, a blockchain-based identity and access management system has been developed that will offer decentralized, secure, and tamper-resistant authentication and authorization to IoT networks. The proposed solution uses the distributed ledger technology and smart contracts to make self-sovereign device identities, finegrained access control policies and transparent auditability all without resorting to centralized authorities. There is the inclusion of lightweight cryptographic primitives to fit the resource limits of the IoT devices and off-chain storage mechanisms are employed to increase system scalability and performance. Security analysis proves that the proposed framework works well in preventing the typical attacks such as identity forgery, replay attacks and unauthorized privilege escalation. The results of experimental evaluation show the better access latency, the increased system reliability, and the decreased administrative overhead of experimental IAM solutions in comparison with traditional centralized IAM solutions. The identified blockchain-based IAM architecture will provide a scalable and reliable platform of the secure IoT implementations in the next-generation cyber-physical systems.

title: Error-Correction Local Projections: Impulse Response Estimation in Cointegrated Systems
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Error-Correction Local Projections: Impulse Response Estimation in Cointegrated Systems
detail.abstract: This paper develops the asymptotic theory for local projection estimation of impulse responses in cointegrated systems. We study what we call the error-correction local projection, implied by the Granger representation, that regresses the $h$-period change in levels on error-correction terms and lagged differences. Our main finding is that the asymptotic behavior of the estimator is determined first by the response direction and then by the horizon. Along transitory directions, the estimator is $\sqrt{n}$-consistent at every horizon. Along permanent directions, it is $\sqrt{n}$-consistent at fixed horizons, converges at rate $\sqrt{n/h}$ at intermediate horizons, and becomes inconsistent when the horizon is proportional to the sample size, converging instead to a random limit. Because the Granger representation decomposes the response along the same permanent and transitory directions, this diagnosis also suggests a remedy: a hybrid estimator that combines a reduced-rank estimator of the long-run responses with a local projection estimator of the short-run responses is $\sqrt{n}$-consistent and asymptotically normal over horizons up to a fixed fraction of the sample. We further propose a self-normalization inference procedure for the hybrid estimator, which is tuning-free and asymptotically pivotal over that entire range. Simulations and an empirical application show that the hybrid combines the long-run discipline of reduced-rank estimation with the robustness and flexibility of local projection.

title: When Qualifications Travel but Capabilities Don't: A Capability Approach to Cross-Border Skill Recognition

detail.title: When Qualifications Travel but Capabilities Don't: A Capability Approach to Cross-Border Skill Recognition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal relationships that could have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper based on synthesis of existing literature.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

keywords: and Skills Change Provide your feedback on BizChat

detail.abstract: Migration and mobility scholarship has long treated formal qualifications as portable assets that travel with the individual across borders. Yet a growing body of labour-market evidence suggests otherwise: credentials that signal competence in one institutional context frequently fail to convert into equivalent employment outcomes in another. Drawing on Amartya Sen's Capability Approach-and informed by the author's own applied research and professional experience in workforce development across emerging markets-this paper reframes qualification recognition not as a bureaucratic hurdle but as a structural constraint on the conversion of human capital into genuine employability-what Sen terms the gap between "resources" (credentials, skills) and "capabilities" (real opportunities to function). Building on prior mixed-methods research into vocational training and workforce development strategy in emerging markets, this paper extends that framework to internationally qualified professionals navigating crossborder labour markets. It argues that three conversion factors-institutional recognition regimes, employer-level credential legibility, and destination-market social capital and professional embeddedness-jointly determine whether a qualification becomes an employability asset or a "stranded" credential. The paper further situates this argument within the context of accelerating skill change, of which AI-driven disruption is one visible driver, which is compressing the shelf-life of formal qualifications and placing renewed pressure on recognition systems designed for a slower-moving labour market. The paper concludes with implications for recognition-system design, employer practice, and future comparative empirical research.

reference: NHH Dept. of Economics Discussion Paper No. 10/2026
title: The Major Divide: Student Sorting, Meritocratic Admissions & Upward Mobility
affiliations: NHH Norwegian School of Economics - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Major Divide: Student Sorting, Meritocratic Admissions & Upward Mobility

publicationDetails.detailsText: NHH Dept. of Economics Discussion Paper No. 10/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Norwegian School of Economics, Department of Economics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Large earnings gaps by socioeconomic status (SES) persist among college applicants even where tuition is free. Using the universe of Danish applications linked to administrative earnings, I ask whether these gaps reflect low returns to selective majors, admission rules, or students' own choices. Leveraging GPA admission cutoffs from a centralized matching algorithm, I apply a regression discontinuity design (RDD) to examine whether low-SES students benefit from selective college majors. Scoring just above the cutoff for admission to a more selective major raises low-SES students' income by 9% at age 30, partially closing the class gap in earnings. For high-SES students I find no detectable gain. To disentangle the contribution of major-specific returns from that of students' choices as sources of inequality, I then estimate a joint model of college major choice and earnings in which returns depend on peer composition, using students' rank-ordered application lists to correct for selection on unobservables. Low-SES returns exceed high-SES returns, relative to their outside options, across most of the major selectivity distribution. Current GPA-based meritocratic admissions are inefficient in terms of maximizing earnings: implementing need-affirmative admissions, holding capacity fixed, would reduce the class gap by 15% through upward mobility of disadvantaged students. Notably, the class gap in earnings could largely be eliminated if students selected college majors based on returns, though this requires expanding capacity. Thus, disparities persist not because disadvantaged students experience low returns from selective majors, but because of how seats are allocated and which majors students choose.

title: The Economic Value of Body Size: A Systematic Review of Gender and Contextual Variation in Labour Market Outcomes
affiliations: Griffith University and Griffith University

detail.title: The Economic Value of Body Size: A Systematic Review of Gender and Contextual Variation in Labour Market Outcomes
detail.abstract: The economic consequences of body size are not uniform, they depend on gender and on the institutional and cultural context in which body size is evaluated. This systematic review synthesises evidence published between 2010 and 2025, drawing predominantly on longitudinal studies, on when, for whom, and through which mechanisms body size becomes an economic penalty, null association, or premium in labour market outcomes. Following PRISMA guidelines, searches of Web of Science, EconLit, and PsycINFO identified 38 eligible studies, most from high-income economies and a smaller number from East and Southeast Asia. The evidence shows a consistent penalty for women, who experienced lower wages, reduced employment, and longer unemployment across most settings. Findings for men were far more heterogeneous: modest penalties or null effects in Western economies, but positive associations between body size and earnings among men in China and Indonesia, with Sweden a further exception in which no female penalty was observed. Of the mechanisms proposed, discrimination is most consistently supported for the female penalty, while cultural and institutional factors better explain the variation among men. The labour market consequences of obesity are therefore gendered and context-dependent rather than uniform.

title: SPATIOTEMPORAL VARIATION IN FUELWOOD CONSUMPTION AND ASSOCIATED EMISSIONS IN LIMPOPO PROVINCE, SOUTH AFRICA
affiliations: University of Venda and University of Venda

detail.title: SPATIOTEMPORAL VARIATION IN FUELWOOD CONSUMPTION AND ASSOCIATED EMISSIONS IN LIMPOPO PROVINCE, SOUTH AFRICA
detail.abstract: Approximately 2 billion people worldwide continue to rely primarily on solid fuels to meet their household energy needs. The rural communities in Limpopo Province continue to experience increasing air quality challenges associated with residential fuelwood burning, highlighting the need for reliable baseline emission inventories to support effective air quality management. This study therefore aimed to assess household fuelwood consumption patterns and estimate emissions associated with residential fuelwood combustion in rural Limpopo Province. A total of 25 households per village participated in the study. The household fuelwood consumption was measured over two seasons (summer (2022) and winter (2022)) using the weight-survey method following standard protocols. The findings revealed that households consumed an average of 5,337.58 ± 1,654.36 kg hh⁻¹ yr⁻¹ of fuelwood, equivalent to 1,135.15 ± 286.02 kg capita⁻¹ yr⁻¹. This consumption corresponded to estimated annual household emissions of 16,820.94 ± 11,935.98 kg CO₂ hh⁻¹ yr⁻¹, 519,986.76 ± 161,154.35 kg CO hh⁻¹ yr⁻¹, 2,359.45 ± 731.24 kg NO hh⁻¹ yr⁻¹, 816.73 ± 253.12 kg SO₂ hh⁻¹ yr⁻¹, and 71,237.28 ± 22,077.86 kg PM₁₀ hh⁻¹ yr⁻¹. Average daily household fuelwood consumption was 14.62 ± 4.50 kg hh⁻¹ day⁻¹, equivalent to 3.11 ± 0.78 kg capita⁻¹ day⁻¹. Seasonal variations in fuelwood consumption and associated emissions were also observed, with significantly greater fuelwood consumption and correspondingly higher emissions during winter than during summer. The findings demonstrate the continued importance of residential fuelwood combustion as a source of household air pollutant emissions in rural communities and highlight the need for targeted mitigation measures, improved access to cleaner household energy alternatives, and sustainable energy interventions to reduce emissions and associated air-quality and public-health risks.

title: ABiGRU-Attention：A Hybrid Prediction Model for Air Quality
affiliations: Wuhan Institute of Technology, Wuhan Institute of Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Central China Normal University, Wuhan Institute of Technology and Trinity College Dublin

detail.title: ABiGRU-Attention：A Hybrid Prediction Model for Air Quality
detail.abstract: The persistent decline in air quality in industrialized countries has posed a significant threat to sustainable economic growth and public health, drawing broad concern across society. As PM2.5 is one of the primary pollutants, accurately predicting its concentration is of great importance. In this paper, ABiGRU-Attention is proposed to predict PM2.5 concentrations based on real-world mass concentration data collected from Jinan and Tai’an in Shandong, China.The ARIMA model utilizes historical data to conduct preliminary predictions of future trends, and its forecasting results help enhance the predictive capability of the BiGRU model. BiGRU serves as the primary time series modeling tool, capable of learning complex temporal dependencies from input features, thereby providing strong support for the final predictions. The attention mechanism helps the model automatically focus on the time steps that are most important for prediction, enabling more accurate forecasting. The proposed ABiGRU-Attention model can fully leverage the statistical characteristics of historical data, capture both long-term and short-term dependencies in sequential data, and selectively attend to features at critical time points.It can reduce the risk of overfitting and improve the stability of the training process.Performance metrics included RMSE values of 8.04 for Jinan and 6.92 for Tai’an, MAE values of 5.09 and 4.62，respectively. Furthermore, comparative experiments with seven other statistical and machine learning methods confirmed the robustness of the proposed model across different geographical contexts and underscored its capability to capture temporal pollution patterns. These findings highlight the practical utility of ABiGRU-Attention in supporting environmental decision-making and safeguarding public health.

title: Asymmetric Effects of Oil Price Shocks and Climate Policy Uncertainty on Renewable Energy Consumption in the United States: Evidence from a Nonlinear ARDL Model
affiliations: Kansas State University

detail.title: Asymmetric Effects of Oil Price Shocks and Climate Policy Uncertainty on Renewable Energy Consumption in the United States: Evidence from a Nonlinear ARDL Model
detail.abstract: Renewable energy investment depends on both fossil fuel prices and the credibility of climate policy, yet whether these drivers act asymmetrically, with rises and falls exerting unequal effects, remains unresolved. Using monthly U.S. data from April 1987 to September 2025 and a nonlinear ARDL model that decomposes oil prices and climate policy uncertainty into positive and negative shocks, this study shows that both drivers operate asymmetrically and primarily through long-run channels. Oil price declines significantly reduce renewable energy consumption, while price increases have no significant effect; reductions in climate policy uncertainty significantly increase consumption, while increases do not reduce it. Neither driver exhibits short-run asymmetry, and both long-run effects are absent before 2001, emerging only during the period of increasing commercialization and policy relevance of the U.S. renewable sector. The long-run response to climate policy uncertainty is more sharply asymmetric than the response to oil prices, though comparable in magnitude. These findings suggest that renewable energy consumption in the United States is shaped by two distinct long-run mechanisms: a market channel operating through fossil fuel price dynamics and a policy channel operating through the credibility of climate policy. The stronger and more persistent asymmetry observed in the policy channel highlights the importance of reducing policy uncertainty as a key priority for supporting the energy transition.

title: No Compliance, No Enforcement: What a State Attorney General Can Do About Ambient Biometric Devices While the Commission Will Not

detail.title: No Compliance, No Enforcement: What a State Attorney General Can Do About Ambient Biometric Devices While the Commission Will Not
detail.abstract: On February 25, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission announced that it will not bring enforcement actions under the Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule against operators who collect personal information for the sole purpose of determining a user's age. The announcement has been read as a general retreat from children's privacy enforcement in the age of biometric sensing. That reading is wrong, and the error matters. The policy statement is narrow by its own terms. It reaches general audience and mixed audience services, it requires that the collection serve age determination and nothing else, it conditions relief on prompt deletion, and it withholds relief from any operator not otherwise in compliance. An ambient biometric device satisfies none of these conditions. It collects because collection is the product, it retains because retention is the product, and it collects from bystanders who are not its users at all. The Commission did not license ambient biometric collection. It built a lane that ambient devices cannot enter, and then declined to walk down the other one. This paper argues that the resulting gap is an enforcement gap rather than a legal one, and that it is a gap State attorneys general are already authorized to close. Section 6504 conditions State enforcement on a single obstacle, the pendency of a Commission action against the same defendant for the same regulation. Where the Commission has announced it will not act, that obstacle is absent by the Commission's own representation. Section 6502(d) preempts only inconsistent State law, and the Ninth Circuit, with the Commission's own agreement as amicus, has held that State causes of action which proscribe the same conduct COPPA proscribes are not inconsistent. The paper closes by taking the Commission's premise seriously: if the measuring instrument cannot separate a child of twelve from a child of fourteen, a rule that turns on that boundary cannot be administered, and the boundary should be moved to where measurement is not required, as the European, United Kingdom, and South African regimes already illustrate in different ways.

title: Split-Construction Sensitivity in RGB–Thermal Segmentation: A Null-Calibrated Protocol Audit
affiliations: University of Haifa

detail.title: Split-Construction Sensitivity in RGB–Thermal Segmentation: A Null-Calibrated Protocol Audit
detail.abstract: We audit how split construction changes the score reported by a fixed frozen-probe segmentation pipeline.With background included in both the objective and metric, the probe on PST900 thermal scores 32.42 fiveclassmIoU under the released official protocol and 51.44 after random-frame repartitioning of the samerelease: a 19.02 ± 1.52-point paired mean ± sample SD across five seeds. Across five separately generatedrepartitions the difference is 20.26 ±1.69 points (mean ± sample SD across draws). This E1 result is aprotocol contrast: its training and evaluation memberships both change, so it is not an isolated causalleakage effect.An E2 scene-overlap stress test holds training-set size and the evaluation probe fixed. Across threeoutcome-blind probe selections, its maximal-overlap endpoint differs by 20.74 ±3.36 points (mean ± sampleSD across probes), and on the original probe one-quarter overlap produces a 13.99-point change, or 59.8% ofthe full observed endpoint difference. E2 retains scene-identity and scene-diversity confounding; it thereforeestablishes a controlled overlap association, not a purified causal dose–response.A fixed DeepLabV3–ResNet50 replication corroborates E1 at 41.67 ±1.96 points and E2 at 23.90 ±3.61points across three seeds under the same standard convention.The mechanism is sampling policy, not shared files: no train/test pair is SHA-256 identical in any auditedrelease or modality. Establishing this requires more than one similarity instrument and a within-trainingredundancy reference. Calibrating each official split against that reference disqualifies dHash on PST900thermal, where the baseline is itself already 56.62% at Hamming-≤ 8: the instrument collides on morethan half of arbitrary within-training pairs, leaving the 77.78% cross-boundary rate uninterpretable. Frozenfeatures resolve the same boundary decisively. Similarity shifts are reported within each of 4 releases; theirmagnitudes are not ranked across datasets because the KAIST control differs. The primary load-bearingresults use the background-inclusive five-class convention used by the cited literature. Supporting analyseslabelled foreground-restricted exclude ground-truth class-0 pixels from the confusion matrix; their absolutevalues are not leaderboard-comparable. The downstream claim is restricted to PST900 thermal, where afrozen probe and one full-network architecture agree; it is not system-wide.

title: Bootstrap Wasserstein Alignment for Stable Feature Attribution in Low-Data Regimes
affiliations: Tokyo International University and Tokyo International University

detail.title: Bootstrap Wasserstein Alignment for Stable Feature Attribution in Low-Data Regimes
detail.abstract: Feature attribution methods become unreliable in low-data regimes (𝑁 ≪ 𝑑), producing inconsistent explanations across bootstrap replicates. We propose BWA (Bootstrap Wasserstein Alignment), a geometric framework that projects each bootstrap-replicate attribution to a probability measure on the feature simplex and aggregates the replicates via a Wasserstein-barycenter consensus paired with a per-feature sign-abstention mechanism. We present two versions: BWA-v1 with a hard binomial sign test, and BWA-v2 with a magnitude-weighted Bayesian soft sign and a per-feature median absolute-value scale that preserves natural attribution magnitudes. BWA-v2 closes a documented sign-accuracy deficit of BWA-v1 by 5–15 percentage points across eight experiments spanning synthetic data (𝑁=20, 𝑑=100, 𝐵=50, 100 trials), MNIST saliency (𝑁=100, 𝑑=784, 5 seeds × 50 images), Golub leukemia gene expression (𝑁=72, 𝑑∈{500,2000}), and four UCI tabular datasets (𝑁∈{20,50}, 𝑑∈{13,30,34,60}). On sparse-signal domains BWA-v2 produces significantly sparser attribution maps than every Euclidean baseline: MNIST Gini 0.645 vs. 0.613 Vanilla Mean and 0.584budget-matched SmoothGrad; gene-expression Gini 0.417 at 𝑑=500 and 0.427 at 𝑑=2000 vs. Vanilla Mean 0.397/0.405 (all 𝑝bonf ≪ 0.001). On dense tabular UCI data, BWA-v2 ties Vanilla Mean on every metric – a scope limitation we disclose explicitly. We pair the method with a bootstrap-level uncertainty 𝜎UQ (model-retraining variance, an order of magnitude larger than SmoothGrad’s input noise variance) and a continuous per-feature soft-sign confidence signal, supporting explicit reliability estimation of attributions under data scarcity. Theoretically, Lemma 1 formalises the worst-case norm collapse failure of Euclidean averaging under sign-flip symmetry, motivating the geometric approach.

title: Audit-Grade Pre-Validation of Trading Strategies: Five Contributions to the López de Prado Stack

detail.title: Audit-Grade Pre-Validation of Trading Strategies: Five Contributions to the López de Prado Stack

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and sole owner of Travidence, LLC (Wilmington, Delaware, USA), which operates the commercial strategy-validation service implementing the methodology described in this paper. This relationship is disclosed in the paper itself. The author declares no other competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was funded internally by Travidence, LLC.

detail.abstract:
Pre-validation ahead of the prop firm challenge is a structural blind spot of contemporary retail trading. FPFX Tech data on 300,000+ accounts document that 86% of challengers fail to clear the evaluation and only 7% ever receive a payout — systematic evidence of overfitting that existing tools do not resolve at audit grade. Implementation libraries implementing the López de Prado stack (mlfinlab, RiskLabAI) operate as technical infrastructure without issuing certification; the aggregation-only retail consumer offering delivers an aggregate score without gates or procedural signing. Prop trading firms, simultaneously, sit on a structural conflict of interest that prevents them from offering honest pre-validation. This institutional vacuum motivates an independent third-party methodology with audit-grade discipline.

This paper presents five novel contributions to the López de Prado stack: (i) dual n_trials reporting in the Deflated Sharpe Ratio to taxonomize selection bias; (ii) Capital-normalized Calmar that strips margin-leverage inflation; (iii) sub-period schema with monotonic decay detection; (iv) component isolation test for multi-component strategies; (v) vol-on / vol-off MUST-PASS regime taxonomy. The five integrate into the Robustness Score — a hybrid continuous-gate score on [0, 100], inspired by the procedural discipline of the professional auditing industry.

The methodology is applied to three textbook strategies on public data: Golden Cross on CL crude oil futures (2000–2025), RSI-14 on BTC perpetual (2020–2025), and Asian Range Breakout on EUR/USD (2015–2025). None reaches a Robust band — consistent with the documented 86% failure rate. Under the production audit engine (trade-level returns, self-derived p50 regime cut, admissibility floors), CL and BTC close with a Disclaimer of Opinion for insufficient sample (18 and 31 trades), while EUR/USD emits the framework's public end-to-end score: 56 / 100, Limited Robustness, with no gate binding. The gate-vs-continuous behavior against pure aggregation that defines the defensible methodological differentiator of audit-grade pre-validation is exhibited by the repository's NQ Opening Range Breakout case — admitted with 2,424 trades and capped by the regime and subperiod gates; across the five repository case studies the portfolio covers the three public outcomes of the framework: score emitted, gated, and insufficient sample.

title: Partial Unemployment Insurance During the Pandemic
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Partial Unemployment Insurance During the Pandemic
detail.abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of Unemployment Insurance (UI) recipients rose dramatically and the share collecting partial UI (benefits earned while working part-time) doubled from 8% pre-pandemic to 16% in 2021. This rise coincided with temporary changes to the UI program, including the $600 Federal Pandemic Unemployment Compensation (FPUC), which induced a steep income cliff for part-time workers. I construct a job search model with moral hazard in which workers can choose to work part-time on UI, and I use this model to show how FPUC induces low-earning workers to reduce their work hours without causing them to reject employment offers. A counterfactual higher replacement rate replaces a larger share of lost earnings without the same incentive to reduce work hours.

title: Assessment of Room Clutter via Image-Derived Cue Fusion
affiliations: Boston University, Boston University and Boston University

detail.title: Assessment of Room Clutter via Image-Derived Cue Fusion
detail.abstract: The presence of clinically significant clutter is a core diagnostic indicator of hoarding disorder. Ideally, the assessment of clutter in a dwelling requires direct visual inspection or reliance on photographs to provide ratings using a validated measure, which is labor-intensive, subjective, and only approximately repeatable. A Clutter Image Rating (CIR) scale was proposed to improve clutter-assessment consistency, but still requires ”manual” comparison of a living space to a set of reference images. Automatic clutter classification from images would be a useful decision-support proxy, yet the task is difficult because labeled data are limited, labels are ordinal, and neighboring CIR levels can differ only by subtle changes in object density, obstruction, and stacking. The most successful clutter-assessment method to date is based on the Vision Transformer (ViT). In this work, we improve on the RGB-only ViT baseline through partial transformer updating, tuned optimization, and geometry-preserving augmentation, while keeping the benchmark’s loss function and evaluation protocol unchanged. On the HINDER-2025 clutter-image dataset, this tuning improves performance by 6.28 percentage points in classification accuracy, while an additional DINOv2 initialization further boosts the accuracy by 1.01 percentage points. We also investigate whether clutter prediction can be improved by fusing auxiliary cues derived from the same RGB image, without requiring new manual annotations to enlarge the dataset. We evaluate the impact of structural cues from object detection, semantic cues from clutter-focused image masking, and volumetric cues from relative depth estimation. The structural and semantic cues provide modest gains over the tuned RGB baseline, while the volumetric cue provides the largest improvement. With DINOv2 initialization, the model using RGB+Depth reaches 63.42% accuracy, improving over the RGB-only ViT baseline by 9.96 percentage points. Impressively, this model achieves 96.27% accuracy within ±1 from the ground truth, which is important in practice since professionals acknowledge challenges in assigning exact CIR values. Effectively, this level of accuracy suggests that an automated algorithm can serve as a reliable proxy for assessment by professionals, thus potentially leading to reduced labor costs, elimination of subjectivity and precise repeatability.

title: Treatment-seeking behavior for acute and chronic illnesses: do people in slums choose differently? Evidence from a survey in Delhi ​
affiliations: University Enclave - Institute of Economic Growth, University Enclave - Institute of Economic Growth and University Enclave - Institute of Economic Growth

detail.title: Treatment-seeking behavior for acute and chronic illnesses: do people in slums choose differently? Evidence from a survey in Delhi ​
detail.abstract: Slum populations face a rising burden of non-communicable diseases alongside traditional acute illnesses, yet little is known about how their healthcare-seeking behavior differs between these conditions. This study addresses the critical challenge of healthcare access in Delhi’s informal settlements by analyzing the choices of 5,377 individuals across 1,084 households. It specifically examines whether the type of illness, acute versus chronic, alters the utilization of public and private services. The paper adds to the literature by demonstrating a significant dichotomy in provider preference: while 64.4% of residents seek private providers for acute illnesses, 65% prefer public facilities for chronic conditions. This shift is driven by the economic necessity of managing long-term ailments, as medicine availability in public clinics is notably higher for chronic care (56%) than for acute needs (19%). However, the study highlights a critical paradox: while public care reduces medical costs, it imposes a high geographic burden. For chronic care in the public sector, transportation costs comprise 46% of total out-of-pocket expenditure (OOPE), reflecting the inconvenient locations of facilities. The implications for public health practice are significant, suggesting that the "cost" of public healthcare for the urban poor is often measured in time and travel rather than fees. To improve health equity, policy must move beyond just providing free services to ensuring localized, decentralized primary care, such as expanded Mohalla Clinics that reduces the transport burden. Addressing overcrowding and perceived medicine quality in the public sector is essential for shifting demand away from expensive, unregulated private providers.

title: Aggregation of Class Activation Maps for Explaining Deep Learning at a Population Level
affiliations: Leiden University - Leiden University Medical Center (LUMC), Medis Medical Imaging Systems BV, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Leiden University - Leiden University Medical Center (LUMC), Medis Medical Imaging Systems BV, Leiden University - Leiden University Medical Center (LUMC), Leiden University - Leiden University Medical Center (LUMC), Medis Medical Imaging Systems BV and Leiden University - Leiden University Medical Center (LUMC)

detail.title: Aggregation of Class Activation Maps for Explaining Deep Learning at a Population Level
detail.abstract: Background and Objective. Class activation maps (CAMs) are frequently used to help understand the inference by deep learning (DL) models, especially in medical imaging that requires high reliability and explainability. Because a single CAM only provides qualitative insight from one case, population-level validation requires aggregation of CAMs. Currently, this aggregation is performed manually in observer studies, which are time-consuming and potentially biased.Methods. We propose an automatic CAM aggregation workflow, based on image segmentation. Objective validation of the aggregation method requires ground truth regarding the importance of specific image patterns for classification. We define this importance as the posterior probability of a class given the presence of specific pathological regions. A series of simulated classification tasks was designed with predefined posterior probabilities for virtual image patterns. We evaluated whether mean CAM activation within pathological regions consistently reflected these probabilities.Results. A high reliability and sensitivity was demonstrated, showing a strong correlation (r = 0.98) between known posterior probabilities and regional mean activations. The results also demonstrate that the CAM aggregation can generate hypotheses about the causality between these regions and the clinical outcomes. The validated aggregation method was then applied to a rheumatoid arthritis-related dataset, to prove its potential applications in clinical practice.Conclusions. We expect that the proposed CAM aggregation can help validate DL models at a population level and reveal possible correlations between regions containing specific image patterns and clinical outcomes.

title: Default, Fraud Classification, and Lender Heterogeneity in  Guaranteed Lending: Evidence from One Million Loans
affiliations: University of Leeds - Credit Management Research Centre (CMRC)

detail.title: Default, Fraud Classification, and Lender Heterogeneity in  Guaranteed Lending: Evidence from One Million Loans
detail.abstract: This paper examines default and fraud classification in UK COVID‑19 government‑guaranteed lending using loan‑level data on 1.1 million BBLS and CBILS facilities. Applying survival and logit models with matching and validation against Companies House records, it analyses both default timing and lender fraud classification. Three findings emerge. First, measured fraud reflects lender practices as well as borrower behaviour: conditional on default, challenger and fintech lenders classify fraud far less often than major banks, implying substantial under‑classification confirmed by external validation. Second, scheme design is crucial: BBLS loans default more frequently, default faster and attract higher fraud‑classification rates than CBILS loans. Third, standard credit‑risk indicators remain predictive despite the crisis context. Overall, fraud statistics in delegated guarantee schemes are not directly comparable across lenders, and crisis‑lending design shapes both outcomes and their measurement.

title: Dynamic Optimization Algorithm for Personalized Physical Training Programs Based on Reinforcement Learning and Response Surface Methodology
affiliations: Shandong Sport University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Dynamic Optimization Algorithm for Personalized Physical Training Programs Based on Reinforcement Learning and Response Surface Methodology
detail.abstract: Aiming at the problem of inadequate individual adaptability caused by the static and empirical nature of traditional physical training programs, a two-layer dynamic optimization framework integrating the Response Surface Methodology (RSM) and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) is established. A response surface model of training parameters-physical fitness gain is constructed via the Central Composite Design (CCD) to quantify the interaction effects of training intensity, training frequency and recovery cycle. An intelligent decision-maker based on the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) architecture is designed, which can perceive athletes’ physiological states in real time and adjust the training load adaptively. Dynamic constraints for fatigue accumulation and supercompensation are built, and multi-objective optimization is adopted to balance short-term athletic performance and long-term physical health. Experimental verification results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is significantly superior to traditional methods in terms of training efficiency improvement, injury risk control and personalized precision, and it provides an intelligent solution for scientific training in competitive sports.

title: A Duality Framework for Convexity in Movable-Boundary Structural Optimization
affiliations: China Railway Eryuan Engineering Group Co Ltd

detail.title: A Duality Framework for Convexity in Movable-Boundary Structural Optimization

keywords: Movable-boundary variational problem \sep Convexity analysis \sep Duality \sep Energy balance \sep Structural optimization

detail.abstract:
This paper presents a duality-based framework for analyzing convexity in a class of movable-boundary structural optimization problems. The key difficulty is that design parameters enter through boundary conditions, making the admissible space parameter-dependent and preventing direct convexity analysis. The framework overcomes this via a Legendre transformation that shifts parameter dependence from primal constraints to dual coefficients, while the dual admissible space remains fixed. Partial minimization then establishes convexity of the value function. A unified configurational energy balance condition emerges: at the optimal movable boundary, the sensitivity of strain energy equals that of external work, $dU/dp = dW/dp$. This condition manifests as $w'(x_k)=0$ for beam supports, the stationarity of bending moment for arch shapes, and $\phi'(x_k)=0$ for dynamic systems, connecting optimality conditions to configurational forces. The framework is demonstrated on static beam support positioning, optimal arch shape, and dynamic beam support positioning. The force method reduces each problem to a finite-dimensional convex quadratic program. Numerical implementation uses cubic B-spline parameterization of the arch geometry and an inner-outer iteration scheme. For a 432\,m span railway bridge arch, the strain energy is reduced by up to 98.98\,\% and the maximum bending moment by 90.1\,\%. Results are validated against OpenSeesPy to numerical round-off, confirming consistency within linear elasticity.

Background Chronic low-grade systemic inflammation has been increasingly implicated in metabolic disorders, but its long-term role in metabolic syndrome (MetS) remains incompletely understood.Methods We evaluate 26 circulating inflammatory biomarkers using routine health check-up data from the West-China Hospital Alliance Longitudinal Epidemiology Wellness (WHALE) database through a three-layer analytical framework. At the population level, a cohort study of 288,929 MetS-free individuals assessed associations between baseline markers and subsequent MetS, and a nested case-control study characterized longitudinal changes in mean biomarkers levels preceding MetS onset (n=157,014). At the individual level, trajectory modeling among participants with ≥3 biomarker measurements (n=186,695) identified distinct biomarker trajectories associated with subsequent MetS. Finally, we conducted trans-ethnic mendelian randomization (TEMR) analyses to assess causality.Findings In the cohort analyses, higher-than-median levels of 21 of 26 biomarkers were significantly associated with incident MetS. Nested case-control analyses revealed that MetS cases had sustained elevations in leukocytes, neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, complement C3/C4, T lymphocyte subsets, and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio for up to 13 years before diagnosis, whereas the platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio was inverse. In trajectory analyses, increasing or persistently high levels trajectories of leukocytes (relative risks [RRs]: 1.19-1.38), neutrophils (RR [95% CI]: 1.26 [1.13-1.39]), lymphocytes (RRs: 1.12-1.50), monocytes (RRs: 1.19-1.26), and complement C4 (RR [95% CI]: 2.31 [1.09-4.92]), were strongly associated with future MetS. Moreover, TEMR suggested possible causal links between these markers and MetS.Interpretation Leukocytes, neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, and complement C4 demonstrated strong and consistent associations with subsequent MetS, highlightin

title: Flow-Field Guided Reinforcement Learning for Sequential Multi-Cable Routing
affiliations: Zhejiang University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Zhejiang University

detail.title: Flow-Field Guided Reinforcement Learning for Sequential Multi-Cable Routing
detail.abstract: In aircraft Electrical Wiring Interconnection System (EWIS) routing design, cable routes exhibit strong sequential dependencies, where subsequent routes are influenced by previously generated routing structures. Conventional route-by-route planning methods cannot explicitly model such sequential dependencies, resulting in limited route coordination in complex constrained environments. To address this issue, this paper proposes a Flow-field Guided Reinforcement Learning (FGRL) framework for sequential cable routing. First, a Cylindrical Projection-based Reparameterization (CPR) method transforms complex 3D fuselage environments into a continuous 2.5D semantic map, reducing environment-interaction cost while preserving routing geometry. Second, a direction-aware dynamic flow field encodes historical routing structures as continuous spatial priors by integrating routing density and dominant directions, thereby guiding subsequent routes toward shared routing corridors and reducing route crossings. Built upon these representations, a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based framework is developed for sequential cable routing under complex geometric constraints.Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed CPR representation improves reinforcement learning efficiency and training stability, enabling the RL planner to achieve a routing success rate of 99.70\% while increasing environment-interaction throughput by 6.5$\times$ compared with direct 3D modeling. Flow-field ablation studies further show that routing density effectively promotes route sharing, while directional information reduces average route crossings from 0.90 to 0.25 and improves bundling intensity from 7.29 to 9.37 in the 30-bundle routing task. Comparative experiments against search-based methods and reinforcement-learning baselines without flow-field guidance demonstrate that FGRL provides a learning-based paradigm for coordinated sequential cable routing, balancing routing quality, bundle formation, crossing suppression, and online efficiency.

title: The Role of Technology in Sustainable Fashion: An Empirical Study on Digital Apps Usage and Purchase Intention for Organic Clothes
affiliations: Dwaraka Doss Goverdhan Doss Vaishnav College (Autonomous)

detail.title: The Role of Technology in Sustainable Fashion: An Empirical Study on Digital Apps Usage and Purchase Intention for Organic Clothes
detail.abstract: The fashion industry is among the largest contributors to global environmental degradation, and the diffusion of digital technology has begun to reshape how consumers discover, evaluate, and purchase sustainable apparel. This study examines how digital and social media usage, together with health, ecological, normative, and price-related determinants, shape consumer attitude and purchase intention toward organic clothing among consumers in Chennai city, India. A descriptive, cross-sectional research design was adopted. Primary data were collected from 133 organic clothing consumers in Chennai using a structured, five-point Likert-scale questionnaire administered through online and offline modes. Six latent constructs Customer Attitude (CA), Social Media Usage and Influence (SUI), Premium Health Concerns (HC), Eco-Literacy Knowledge (LK), Willingness to Pay (WP), and Environmental Subjective Norms (ESN) were used to predict Purchase Intention (PI). Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis (Cronbach's alpha), tests of normality (Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Shapiro-Wilk), weighted mean ranking, Pearson correlation, and stepwise multiple regression in SPSS. All six constructs demonstrated acceptable internal consistency (α = 0.781 to 0.834). Price, comfort, and quality emerged as the top-ranked reasons for purchasing organic clothing, ahead of environmental impact and brand. Pearson correlation revealed significant positive associations among all study variables (p < 0.01), with Environmental Subjective Norms and Eco-Literacy Knowledge showing the strongest correlation with Purchase Intention. Stepwise regression indicated that Social Media Usage and Influence (β = 0.495, p < 0.001) and Willingness to Pay (β = 0.281, p = 0.001) were the only statistically significant predictors of Customer Attitude, jointly explaining 51.1 per cent of its variance (R² = 0.511, Adjusted R² = 0.503, F = 67.801, p < 0.001), while Premium Health Concerns, Eco-Literacy Knowledge, and Environmental Subjective Norms did not add significant unique explanatory power once social media influence and willingness to pay were accounted for. The study contributes to the sparse empirical literature on technology-enabled sustainable consumption in emerging-market, tiermetro contexts by empirically demonstrating that digital and social media exposure rather than ecological knowledge alone is the dominant lever shaping consumer attitude toward organic clothing, with direct implications for digital marketing strategy in the sustainable fashion sector.

title: From Dancing at Weddings to Digging Wells: The Talmudic Vision of the Spiritual Leader
affiliations: City University of New York (CUNY) - Koppelman School of Business

detail.title: From Dancing at Weddings to Digging Wells: The Talmudic Vision of the Spiritual Leader
detail.abstract: This paper argues that classical rabbinic literature offers an enduring model of leadership that both anticipates and extends contemporary theories of servant and purpose-driven leadership. Through close analysis of aggadic narratives from the Babylonian Talmud, the Jerusalem Talmud, and Midrash, this study shows that the sages understood leadership not as authority detached from communal life, but as active, morally grounded service directed toward a higher purpose. Key figures such as Hillel, Rabban Gamliel II, Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, Rabbi Huna, and Nechunya are depicted engaging in concrete acts of stewardship and public responsibility. These include directly assisting those in need, hosting guests, distributing resources during famine, clearing public hazards, and providing water for pilgrims. While not strictly historical reports, these narratives articulate a coherent leadership ideal marked by humility, compassion, accessibility, and a deep commitment to the vulnerable. Viewed through modern leadership frameworks, the Talmudic model demonstrates how genuine authority fuses service to others with devotion to transcendent moral ends. Ultimately, this article shows how rabbinic texts enrich contemporary leadership theory by grounding it in a legacy of ethical responsibility, communal care, and sacred purpose.

title: Inflation Memory, Money-Holding Behaviour, and the Velocity of Money: A Behavioural-Macroeconomic Framework and Conceptual Analysis with Reference to Turkey
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Inflation Memory, Money-Holding Behaviour, and the Velocity of Money: A Behavioural-Macroeconomic Framework and Conceptual Analysis with Reference to Turkey
detail.abstract: This study presents an integrative framework that examines, at a theoretical and conceptual level, the behavioural effects of inflation memory on the velocity of money (V). The central argument is as follows: past experiences of high inflation may permanently alter the money-holding behaviour of economic agents even after disinflation has been achieved. This mechanism requires that the V component of Fisher's equation be positioned not as a purely monetary magnitude but as the output of a behavioural-cognitive process. The study synthesises five distinct strands of literature-velocity of money and money demand, inflation expectations and information stickiness, inflation persistence, behavioural macroeconomics and experience effects, and dollarisation and currency substitutionwithin a single conceptual backbone. Spanning from Friedman's (1956) portfolio theory of money demand and Cagan's (1956) hyperinflation models to Malmendier and Nagel's (2016) experience-weighted learning findings and Turkey-specific evidence on currency substitution and expectation stickiness, this synthesis constructs, on strong theoretical grounds, the chain of 'inflation memory → expectation inertia → weakening of money demand → persistently high velocity.' It is established that this chain has not been addressed as a unified framework in the existing literature. In the Turkish context, decades of high inflation history, deep dollarisation, and chronic expectation distortion provide strong structural evidence supporting the plausibility of the proposed mechanism. The study does not offer an empirical test; instead, it provides conceptual contributions that lay the groundwork for future empirical inquiry.

title: Where Organizational Change Actually Lives When Institutions will not hold Still: Treating Change Capacity as an Embedded Structure Instead of an Ordered Process

detail.title: Where Organizational Change Actually Lives When Institutions will not hold Still: Treating Change Capacity as an Embedded Structure Instead of an Ordered Process
detail.abstract: The staged models that dominate change management were written for a world of stable rules, reliable chains of command, and staff who stay put from the first step to the last. Transitional economies satisfy none of those conditions, yet the sequenced templates are still transplanted into them almost verbatim. This article asks a diagnostic question rather than offering a recipe: once the ordered sequence can no longer be kept whole, which organizational property must shoulder the work that ordering used to perform? I argue that the answer lies in the organization's administrative infrastructure. From that starting point I set out an Administrative Change Leadership Framework built on four interlocking capacities-the management of overlapping operating states, coordination that moves fluently across formal and informal channels, the externalisation of knowledge for the sake of continuity, and communication aimed at building legitimacy. None of these is presented as a general badge of administrative competence; each is instead matched to one specific institutional weakness identified in the literature on post-socialist transition. Digitalisation enters not as a separate topic but as a force that magnifies each of those weaknesses, above all by generating co-existing analogue and digital states that regulatory delay forbids the organization from merging. The framework's core logic is decoupling: every capacity moves change capacity off a brittle, person-dependent sequence and onto durable structures and records that survive both institutional shocks and staff losses. The paper is expressly conceptual. It advances five falsifiable propositions, sets out the study designs that could test them, and translates the framework into practical tools for hiring and for the design of administrative authority.

title:
Human-Centered Cybersecurity in the Enterprise

A Governance and Risk Management Framework for Security Culture, Usability, and Resilience

detail.title:
Human-Centered Cybersecurity in the Enterprise

A Governance and Risk Management Framework for Security Culture, Usability, and Resilience
detail.abstract: The analysis draws on academic literature, government frameworks, and professional research while extending those discussions toward the practical implementation of HCC within enterprise environments. The Enterprise Human-Centered Cybersecurity Framework (E-HCCF) developed in this paper represents my proposed synthesis of organizational maturity, human-centered measurement, and continuous improvement within a governance and risk-management structure. It is offered as a conceptual framework for further consideration and evaluation and should not be interpreted as an official NIST framework, recommendation, or position. Marymount University is listed as my current academic affiliation. The views and conclusions expressed in this paper are my own and do not imply institutional endorsement. All AI-assisted output was critically reviewed, revised, and verified by me, and I take full responsibility for the content of this paper.

title: Breadth or Behavior? Multistate Operations and the Regulatory Enforcement Record

detail.title: Breadth or Behavior? Multistate Operations and the Regulatory Enforcement Record
detail.abstract: How much of a firm's enforcement record reflects what it does, and how much reflects how much of it there is to regulate? Using the number of U.S. states a firm names in its annual report, penalty actions compiled from about fifty federal and state agencies, establishment-level workplace inspections, permitted-facility evaluation files, and audit disclosures from 2005 through 2024, we document a steep footprint gradient: one more state is associated with roughly three percent more penalty actions, and a standard deviation in footprint with close to thirty percent. Wider parents do not draw more visits. Inspection frequency is flat in parent footprint, and two-thirds of permitted facilities are never evaluated. But their visits produce more findings per visit, and their filings carry more restatements and adverse control opinions, a margin where examination is universal. Breadth of regulated activity, not site-level scrutiny, drives the record.

title: Agentic Schema Convergence: An AI-Driven Pipeline for Combined Schema Design and Data Migration in Technology M&A

detail.title: Agentic Schema Convergence: An AI-Driven Pipeline for Combined Schema Design and Data Migration in Technology M&A
detail.abstract: Schema convergence and data mapping are consistently the slowest, most manual stages of technology M&A integration-typically weeks of analyst effort, tribal knowledge, and spreadsheet-based mapping documents that go stale before implementation finishes. Recent work applying large language models to schema matching and entity resolution suggests these tasks are structurally well suited to AI assistance, but most published work treats schema matching as an isolated benchmark task rather than as one stage in an end-to-end migration pipeline with real compliance and reliability constraints. This paper proposes Agent-Assisted Schema Convergence (AASC), a five-agent architecture-Schema Intelligence, Data Profiling, Canonical Design, Mapping, and Pipeline Design agents-that carries the work from raw source/destination schema review through to a deployable migration pipeline, with a defined human-in-the-loop checkpoint at every stage and no agent output auto-applied to production schema or data without reviewer sign-off. The Mapping Agent's confidence-scoring and review-queue design receives the most detailed treatment, since it is where automation and regulatory risk intersect most directly. Two case illustrations are worked through: a ticket/interaction data migration (chosen specifically because it is comparatively PII-light yet still carries distinct compliance obligations that argue for separating it from the main customer data migration) and a customer/account data migration, where the same fiveagent pipeline runs with materially different review posture. The result is a practical, implementable blueprint for where agentic AI can accelerate M&A data integration work, and an equally explicit account of where it cannot yet be trusted to run unsupervised.

title: Sectoral Stock Market Responses to the U.S.-China Trade War in Türkiye: An Event Study Analysis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Sectoral Stock Market Responses to the U.S.-China Trade War in Türkiye: An Event Study Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of the July 6, 2018 U.S.-China trade war tariff announcement that heightened market volatility on the Turkish stock market. Existing studies usually investigate the effects of the trade war on the whole market; whereas this paper focuses on sectoral heterogeneity by analyzing three specific indices on Borsa Istanbul (BIST): Industrial (XUSIN), Electricity (XELKT), and Technology (XUTEK). Using an Event Study methodology, this study first estimates a Market Model regression over a 60-day pre-event estimation window [-90,-31] to derive sector-specific market risk parameters (α and β). Abnormal Returns (AR) and Cumulative Abnormal Returns (CAR) are then calculated around the July 6, 2018 event date across multiple event windows, with statistical significance shown via t-tests. The findings indicate a strong sectoral divergence: on the event date, the Industrial and Electricity sectors exhibited negative abnormal returns while the Technology sector showed a positive abnormal return. This divergence persisted in CARs, where Technology demonstrated statistically significant positive performance. The findings are consistent with the possibility that Turkish technology firms were perceived as more resilient to global trade tensions, while manufacturing and energy sectors were affected negatively.

title: Teaching Against Collapse: Gendered Political Economy and the Territorialization of Education in Fragmented Yemen
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Teaching Against Collapse: Gendered Political Economy and the Territorialization of Education in Fragmented Yemen

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: This article advances a gendered political economy framework to examine how systemic educational collapse in Yemen simultaneously destroys, reproduces, and-under specific conditions-transforms structures of conflict and patriarchal authority. Drawing on 45 semistructured interviews with educators, community leaders, and local authorities across five governorates (Aden, Taiz, Hadramawt, Marib, and Sana'a), triangulated with humanitarian reports and peer-reviewed scholarship, the study argues that education in protracted conflict cannot be understood through humanitarian deficit frameworks alone. Instead, it must be analyzed as a terrain of political contestation where war economies, patriarchal bargains, and territorial governance fragment educational space. The analysis identifies three interconnected dynamics. First, the collapse of state financing has localized resource distribution through patronage and community coercion, producing new geographies of educational exclusion. Second, women's assumption of educational leadershipcelebrated in humanitarian discourse as empowerment-operates as a form of feminized survival work that extends patriarchal resilience rather than dismantling it. This concept is distinguished from feminist analyses of reproductive labor and care work by its specific focus on the public performance of crisis-time educational labor that is simultaneously hyper-visible in humanitarian narratives and structurally invisible in political economy. Third, while community-based schools and teacher-led curriculum mediation generate "everyday peacebuilding," these practices remain structurally constrained by the absence of redistributive justice and the territorialization of governance. The article concludes that sustainable educational recovery requires moving beyond humanitarian restoration toward politically-informed, gender-transformative reconstruction that addresses the political economy of teacher precarity, curriculum territoriality, and the structural devaluation of women's educational labor.

title: The Two-echelon Load-dependent Electric Vehicle Routing Problem
affiliations: Beijing Union University, , Beijing Union University and China Academy of Transportation Sciences, Beijin

detail.title: The Two-echelon Load-dependent Electric Vehicle Routing Problem
detail.abstract: The two-echelon distribution system comprises line-haul trunk transportation and last-mile urban delivery, and is widely used for its high efficiency. Meanwhile, electric vehicles are increasingly utilized in urban delivery due to their environmental benefits. However, their energy consumption is highly sensitive to loads. In this study, we investigate a novel two-echelon load-dependent electric vehicle routing problem, where internal combustion engine vehicles handle long-haul transportation and electric vehicles perform last-mile delivery with load-sensitive energy use. To solve this problem, a hybrid heuristic algorithm that combines the commercial solver CPLEX and adaptive large neighborhood search with tailored operators is developed. We conduct numerical experiments to evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm and the impact of load-dependent energy consumption on routing strategies. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach can obtain high-quality solutions within reasonable computation times. This paper further highlights the effect of loads on the optimized distribution strategies.

title: Guarded Guests: Immigration and Crime in Taiwan
affiliations: National Chung Cheng University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Guarded Guests: Immigration and Crime in Taiwan
detail.abstract: This paper documents the gap in crime rates between the foreign-and native-born populations in Taiwan, whose large guest-worker population lives under a tightly regulated regime. Using administrative records, I construct monthly crime rates, measured by the number of suspects per 100,000, for both populations, and examine the relationship between the foreign-born population share and local crime rates. The foreign-born rate averages 24 per 100,000 per month, compared with 56 for the native-born, and the gap persists across crime types and after adjusting for age-gender differences. County-panel regressions find no positive association between the foreign-born share and local crime rates, and within the guest-worker population, crime rates decline with the size of local co-national community. I attribute the gap to institutional selection and deterrence, and the co-national community may lower crime rates and explain the variation within migrant workers.

title: The Legal Realism of W.E.B. Du Bois

detail.title: The Legal Realism of W.E.B. Du Bois
detail.abstract:
The great writer, activist, and scholar W.E.B. Du Bois saw his career unfold alongside the development of Legal Realism, an intellectual movement whose rapid rise to prominence in American legal thought was concentrated in the 1920s and 1930s. Though more often remembered as a sociologist or historian, Du Bois's work contained considerable theorizing about law that tracked key Realist insights. 

But this Article shows that Du Bois wasn't simply another legal theorist. He was an outstanding one, whose own theorizing emerged not through colorblind critiques of classical legal thought (what the Realists did), but through thinking, organizing, and propagandizing against race hierarchy. The slave trade, sharecropping, Lynch Law, race riots, and cases like Bailey v. Alabama comprised his distinct objects of study. And Du Bois's embeddedness in domestic and transnational social movements for civil rights, decolonization, and global peace inescapably shaped his constant thinking toward emancipation. All this fueled an extraordinary range of legal theorizing, from experimental notions of "legal violence," to more mature concepts like the "dictatorship of property," to intertwined critiques of rights, capitalism, and the U.S. Constitution. Such theorizing is not only visible in classic texts, like Du Bois's famous Black Reconstruction, but also in underexamined ones, like his 1896 dissertation on the transatlantic slave trade, and his and the NAACP's remarkable 1947 petition to the new United Nations. 

In charting the development of Du Bois's legal thought, this Article advances two main claims. First, that radical commitments to overcoming racial subordination provide critical pathways to understanding American law. Partisans for racial justice, like Du Bois, have produced profound legal-theoretical insights not in spite of, but because of, their normative commitments. 

Second, that Du Bois belongs in the canon of American legal thought. Who and what comprise the canon is a matter of perennial importance. As someone who thought deeply about law's relation to the project of multiracial democracy in the United States, and that project's inextricable connection to the problem of the global color line, now is as good a time as any to confirm Du Bois's place.

title: Intentional Alliance and Rivalry Networks and Conflict Diffusion: Simulating the Effect of Network Structure
affiliations: and Waseda University

detail.title: Intentional Alliance and Rivalry Networks and Conflict Diffusion: Simulating the Effect of Network Structure
detail.abstract: Why does a major war happen? Under what conditions is a local bilateral war likely to escalate to a "world war"? We aim to identify the conditions that make the diffusion of war likely, focusing on the role of alliance and international rivalry. To explore the conditions under which a war tends to diffuse to other states, we develop a computational model of war diffusion on international networks in which states are connected by alliances and rivalries. Simulated experiments show that the structure of alliances and rivalries exerts complex effects on the war diffusion dynamics. This study proposes a theoretical model that links local war joining processes to macro-level regional/global outcomes.

title: A Bayesian and Monte Carlo Framework for Equity Valuation in Frontier Markets
affiliations: Duke University - Fuqua School of Business

detail.title: A Bayesian and Monte Carlo Framework for Equity Valuation in Frontier Markets
detail.abstract: Discounted cash-flow (DCF) valuation is designed for developed economies which have mature capital markets. DCF falls apart in frontier markets, where it has to rely on unwarranted assumptions about distribution, stability of means and variances, roughly normal distributions, and independence of shocks. Frontier market currencies exhibit highly sporadic patterns like occasional jumps, fat tails, and simultaneous movements in depreciation rate, inflation, and risk-premium. Forecasting cash-flows denominated in such currencies inevitably transfers the same issues with the currencies to the DCF analysis, rendering it less useful. The current paper embraces the peculiarities of currencies in frontier markets and proposes an alternative approach to valuation that works better than regular DCF. The approach employs Bayesian analysis to update growth priors, jump-diffusion model of depreciation. It is careful to capture dependence between inflation, depreciation, and risk-premium shocks by using student-t copula and then a probabilistic risk assessment is conducted via monte-carlo simulations to generate a distribution of values of the asset. The approach is specifically designed to be nimble and allow more flexibility as additional information becomes available. To counter one of the main issues DCF faces in frontier markets, the methodology is designed to rely on a shorter history of data than is typical in modern macroeconomics. Overall, the proposed framework weaponizes the uncertainties related to the value of an asset in frontier markets into a competitive advantage.

reference: NHH Dept. of Business and Management Science Discussion Paper No. 2026/9
title: Regulatory Models and Pricing Mechanisms for District Heating in the Nordic Countries: Implications for Norway
