This two-sided sorting confounds observational estimates of consumer preferences and may lead standard restaurant entry models to systematically mispredict which areas are best for potential new entrants. We estimate a joint model of restaurant entry and household location choice in the Baltimore metropolitan area, exploiting the 2024 Francis Scott Key bridge collapse and Baltimore County's four-year zoning cycle as quasi-experiments to identify consumer demand and household sorting preferences. The bridge collapse reveals that consumers are meaningfully sensitive to travel time, with demand decreasing by 3.9% for every 10% increase in travel time, while the zoning event study identifies a nonmonotonic preference for living near restaurants, with households valuing restaurant access at moderate distance but disliking living too close. We then embed these quasi-experimental estimates into a dynamic entry model and show that an endogenousmarket specification, which anticipates household sorting in response to area amenities, significantly reduces out-of-sample prediction error relative to a standard exogenousdynamics baseline. Counterfactual analysis of transit improvements further shows that the two specifications rank candidate road improvements differently, and project different long-run profitability effects for nearby business locations. Taken together, our results show that "crowded" markets are often not as saturated as they appear, as higher competitive density can make neighborhoods more attractive places to live and expand local demand in the long-term.

title: AI for Climate Stabilization: Forecasting, Optimization, and Autonomous Mitigation Systems

detail.title: AI for Climate Stabilization: Forecasting, Optimization, and Autonomous Mitigation Systems
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is becoming the core operating system for planetary climate stabilization, replacing the latency‑bound, parameterization‑heavy workflows of classical Earth System Models with real‑time, physics‑informed emulation and cyber‑physical control. Modern neural operators and foundation climate models—such as Fourier Neural Operators, GraphCast, ClimaX, and NeuralGCM—deliver 10,000× faster global forecasts while resolving sub‑grid turbulence and convective cloud microphysics with physically constrained stability.

Across infrastructure systems, deep reinforcement learning and model predictive control enable dynamic grid balancing, synthetic inertia injection, virtual power plant coordination, and industrial thermodynamic optimization, achieving up to 87% renewable curtailment mitigation and 15–30% energy reductions in hard‑to‑abate sectors.

In carbon removal, generative materials models (Crystal Diffusion VAEs) discover high‑performance MOFs that cut DAC regeneration energy from 1,200 to 650 kWh/tCO₂, while multimodal satellite‑IoT MRV systems provide cryptographically verifiable carbon accounting with sub‑50 m leak localization and 95% credible interval bounds across oceanic and geological sinks.

The report further establishes multi‑objective AI guardrails for Solar Radiation Management, reducing hydrological distortion by 65% and constraining termination shock risk through autonomous radiative forcing caps.

Collectively, mature climate AI systems can abate 4.8–6.2 Gt CO₂e annually by 2030, scaling to 12.8 Gt CO₂e by 2040, with an Enablement Ratio exceeding 45:1, demonstrating that optimized AI‑driven mitigation overwhelmingly outweighs its computational footprint.

title: Risk-Aware Third-Party Labor Procurement and Staffing Flexibility in Large-Scale Logistics Operations
affiliations: Wright State University

detail.title: Risk-Aware Third-Party Labor Procurement and Staffing Flexibility in Large-Scale Logistics Operations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests, personal relationships, or organizational affiliations that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, the research presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because the research does not involve human participants, patients, personally identifiable information, clinical data, or animal subjects. The study is based on conceptual framework development, engineering optimization methods, lifecycle assessment principles, and, where applicable, publicly available secondary datasets.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any public, commercial, or not-for-profit funding agency. The study was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Large logistics organizations increasingly combine internal employees, temporary workers, and third-party labor contracts to absorb demand variation, cover specialized tasks, and protect service continuity. Yet repeated reliance on ad hoc third-party labor can create cost leakage, duplicate staffing, inconsistent procurement decisions, and exposure to availability or compliance risk. This study proposes a risk-aware decision framework that classifies site-level labor needs into four actions: retain ad hoc third-party labor, transition to structured procurement, expand internal staffing, or discontinue external coverage. The framework combines an interpretable procurement-readiness score with scenario-based cost modeling and conditional value-at-risk optimization. Decision variables incorporate utilization frequency, requested hours, demand stability, operational criticality, internal headcount gaps, relative labor cost, supplier availability, duplication risk, and compliance exposure. A synthetic network of 120 logistics sites is evaluated across 5,000 Monte Carlo scenarios under demand shocks, forecast error, and supply-side fill uncertainty. The proposed policy is compared with ad hoc-only staffing, a fixed 30-hour procurement threshold, and a risk-neutral optimizer. Results show that risk-aware classification can substantially reduce expected service shortfall relative to ad hoc-only and risk-neutral policies while avoiding the excess reserved capacity produced by a simple threshold rule. Sensitivity analysis demonstrates a transparent cost-service trade-off as the risk-aversion parameter changes. Because the experiments use reproducible synthetic data and normalized cost units, the framework does not depend on confidential employer information. The study contributes a transferable analytical architecture for logistics workforce governance, procurement-readiness screening, cost-leakage detection, and staffing-flexibility decisions under uncertainty. It also produces manager-readable reason codes for each recommendation.

title: The Architecture of Want: Incentivisation, Reward Psychology, and the Systematic Engineering of Human Cognition — From Vedic Wisdom to the Age of Artificial Intelligence.

detail.title: The Architecture of Want: Incentivisation, Reward Psychology, and the Systematic Engineering of Human Cognition — From Vedic Wisdom to the Age of Artificial Intelligence.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. The author's professional affiliations — Co-Founder, Bharat Responsible AI Forum; Partner, Jananiti; Advisor, TESG Center for Health and Wellness Research — are disclosed above for transparency; none of these organisations funded, commissioned, or had editorial input into this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a conceptual and theoretical framework paper drawing exclusively on published secondary sources — academic literature, classical texts, and existing empirical studies cited in the References. It does not involve human participants, animal subjects, primary data collection, or identifiable personal data, and therefore did not require review or approval by a research ethics committee.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. It was conducted independently of, and without financial support from, the author's affiliated organisations.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes and defends a novel framework grounded in the claim that behavioural economics, platform design, political communication, cognitive-warfare doctrine, and classical Indic philosophy have been independently describing the same underlying object: a systematic architecture for engineering human want. Existing literatures treat these as separate domains — a psychology of reward, a design discipline for attention, a security concern about influence operations, a strand of comparative philosophy — and in doing so understate how tightly coupled they are as a single, layered system operating on human cognition from biology to metaphysics. This paper introduces five original constructs to close that gap.

The Want Architecture models desire engineering as six simultaneous, interacting layers — biological, psychological, social, narrative, epistemic, and existential — and argues that single-layer analyses (dopamine-only accounts of addiction, politics-only accounts of polarisation, or AI-only accounts of algorithmic harm) are structurally inadequate to the phenomenon.

The Reward Weaponisation Spectrum (RWS) offers a six-stage, consent-and-awareness-based taxonomy running from legitimate Incentivisation through Influence, Manipulation, Conditioning, and Weaponisation to Subjugation, distinguishing it from mechanism-based frameworks such as nudge theory and the dark-patterns literature.

Incentive Adharma names the ethical failure mode at the centre of the paper: the deployment of reward engineering absent any obligation toward the cognitive sovereignty of the person being engineered.

Cognitive Flattening names the population-level erosion of attentional and deliberative capacity that this paper argues, with appropriate methodological caution, is consistent with the observable output of sustained, unaccountable reward engineering.

The Dumbing Down Dividend names the strategic and commercial benefit that accrues to actors — state and corporate — whose position improves as populations' capacity for independent judgement declines, without requiring coordination among them.

This is offered as a foundation paper: a shared frame, complete with an explicit statement of scope, methodology, and falsification conditions, for researchers working on reward psychology, platform accountability, disinformation, and AI alignment to build upon, contest, and extend.

title: A Public Inquiry Without a Predetermined Verdict: Evidentiary Scope, Media Accountability and the Jason Arday Controversy
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title: A Public Inquiry Without a Predetermined Verdict: Evidentiary Scope, Media Accountability and the Jason Arday Controversy
detail.abstract: The death of Professor Jason Arday on 14 August 2026, following weeks of intense scrutiny concerning plagiarism, academic work, biographical claims and institutional appointment processes, has generated calls for a public inquiry into alleged media harassment. A Good Law Project open letter addressed to the Prime Minister and Culture Secretary calls for an immediate inquiry and states, in categorical terms, that press harassment directly caused Arday's death, that racism lay at the heart of the coverage and that press self-regulation failed [1]. Those propositions are politically and ethically consequential, but they are not presently equivalent to coronial, judicial or independently established findings. Police described Arday's death as unexpected and not suspicious, and no public cause of death had been announced when this article was completed [2]. This commentary argues that the strongest case for an inquiry is therefore not that the petition has already proved its conclusions, but that a sufficiently serious public controversy exists to justify independent examination of how allegations were generated, verified, framed, repeated, moderated, transmitted to institutions and corrected. Drawing on the Inquiries Act 2005, parliamentary guidance, the Leveson model, current press standards, research-integrity procedure and suicide-reporting guidance, the article develops an Inquiry-Trigger/Inquiry-Verdict distinction and a Functional Accountability Principle. It proposes that scope should follow function rather than labels: conventional newsrooms, specialist research-integrity journalism, blogs, newsletters, comment hosts, universities, journals and campaign organisations should be examined where documentary evidence shows that they originated, verified, amplified, moderated, referred or operationalised claims. The analysis separates coronial causation from systemic accountability, proposes a source-lineage audit capable of distinguishing republication from independent corroboration, and sets out neutral terms of reference for a statutory inquiry. The central proposition is that public concern may justify investigation without deciding the investigation. A credible inquiry should be capable of identifying serious failures if the evidence establishes them, but equally capable of rejecting claims of harassment, racism, causation, coordination or institutional misconduct where the evidence does not.

title: Chasing One Rabbit or Many: Pandemic Driven Shifts in Attentional Dominance Among IT and Financial Services Organizations
affiliations: Oakland University, Oakland University - School of Business Administration and Oakland University

detail.title: Chasing One Rabbit or Many: Pandemic Driven Shifts in Attentional Dominance Among IT and Financial Services Organizations
detail.abstract: We introduce attentional dominance—operationalized as the degree to which a single issue or a narrow set of issues monopolizes collective organizational attention, thereby displacing competing topics from the strategic agenda—as a novel construct within attention-based view (ABV) scholarship. Integrating ABV’s structural distribution principle and industry velocity, we evaluate pandemic-driven strategic shifts by analyzing 80 S&P 500 shareholder letters (2020–2023). Our findings reveal that dominance patterns diverge by industry velocity: high-velocity IT firms exhibited low dominance during the pandemic—framing the crisis as a distributed opportunity landscape—but transitioned to elevated dominance post-pandemic around innovation and generative AI. Conversely, low-velocity financial firms displayed crisis-induced high dominance, followed by post-pandemic diversification driven by institutional normalization. Our work extends ABV theory by conceptualizing attentional dominance as a distributional, portfolio-level construct.

title: Analysis spatial network development and driving factors for energy carbon emission efficiency in China's Yangtze River Economic Belt and Yellow River Basin​
affiliations: Qinghai Normal University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Analysis spatial network development and driving factors for energy carbon emission efficiency in China's Yangtze River Economic Belt and Yellow River Basin​

keywords: Yangtze River and Yellow River Basins

detail.abstract: The findings are as follows: (1) From a temporal perspective, the average carbon emission efficiency increased from 0.88 in 2007 to 0.91 in 2022. Spatially, significant regional differences exist,Significant regional differences exist spatially, with the overall pattern showing a high proportion in the east and west and a low proportion in the west.(2) Over time, network connectivity has improved, exhibiting a clear "core-periphery" structure. Jiangsu, Zhejiang, and Shanghai Municipality in the Yangtze River Basin are the provinces in the center of the network. However, the COVID-19 pandemic in 2022 caused Shanghai's centrality to decline while Shandong Province and Henan Province in the Yellow River Basin became more central, indicating spatial spillover effects. (3) The four sectors are geographically distinct. The broker sector mainly consists of surrounding provinces of the net beneficiary sector, namely Anhui, Hubei, and Jiangxi. The net spillover sector is characterized by resource-based provinces, mainly located in the upper reaches of the Yangtze and Yellow River basins. The net beneficiary sector consists of Jiangsu and Zhejiang provinces. The two-way spillover sector is characterized by the geographical features of Shandong, Henan, and Sichuan. (4) According to the QAP regression results, the main influencing factors that are significant at the 1% level are geographic proximity, economic development level, and innovation level.

title: Weight-Lifting and the Character of Our Leaders
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Weight-Lifting and the Character of Our Leaders
detail.abstract: Physical fitness displays by American politicians are nothing new. Presidents George Washington and Ulysses S. Grant, among others, were depicted riding warhorses as symbols of leadership and executive ability. Theodore Roosevelt was renowned for his love of fisticuffs, and Bill Clinton was often photographed jogging around Washington, D.C. Recently U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Defense Secretary, Pete Hegseth, garnered attention for weight-lifting videos. Some of these actions reflect a sincere love of sport, others a desire for good health, and others evidence of martial preparedness. Some displays of fitness are merely performative, meant to convey something about the character of the leader. This article examines what we can reasonably glean about a leader’s moral character based on their physical fitness.

title: When Forecast Accuracy Misleads Public Planning: Persistence Benchmarks and Structural Heterogeneity in Thai Provincial Healthcare Demand
affiliations: and Thammasat University, Faculty of Economics

detail.title: When Forecast Accuracy Misleads Public Planning: Persistence Benchmarks and Structural Heterogeneity in Thai Provincial Healthcare Demand
detail.abstract: Public healthcare planners increasingly use predictive models to anticipate service demand, but high aggregate accuracy may provide limited planning value when administrative panels are dominated by persistence and structural heterogeneity. This paper develops a diagnostic protocol for this problem and applies it to Thai provincial healthcare utilisation forecasting. We construct a longitudinal panel of 924 province-year observations covering 77 provinces from 2012 to 2024, extracted and audited from Ministry of Public Health annual reports. Annual DEA efficiency scores, structural Tobit regressions, deep learning architectures, tree-based comparators, and classical benchmarks are used to test whether an efficiency-style administrative indicator adds planning value once persistence and province heterogeneity are accounted for. A trivial persistence forecast dominates every model tested on inpatient admissions, with R² = 0.992 compared with R² = 0.841 for the best forecasting architecture. Bangkok, Thailand's dominant referral hub, accounts for much of the panel's variance and most models' apparent accuracy; removing Bangkok's test observations causes seven of eight architectures to fall below a naive baseline. Only the province-aware architecture retains positive predictive value for the remaining provinces. The DEA score alters performance conditionally but functions as a target-adjacent proxy rather than an independent planning covariate. The paper contributes a low-cost diagnostic protocol, persistence benchmarking, variance decomposition, dominant-unit exclusion testing, and classical benchmarking, for evaluating predictive models before using aggregate accuracy to guide public healthcare resource allocation.

title: The First Draft Problem: Productivity, Quality, and Physiological Strain in LLM-Assisted Writing
affiliations: , University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School and University of Pennsylvania - Operations & Information Management Department

detail.title: The First Draft Problem: Productivity, Quality, and Physiological Strain in LLM-Assisted Writing

keywords: and Terwiesch: The First Draft Problem

detail.abstract: The use of large language models (LLMs) has grown rapidly over the past few years, especially in health care, where documentation burden remains a persistent problem for practicing clinicians. However, despite the deployment of many ambient scribes for documentation, it is still unclear how LLMs impact those who work with them. Across two preregistered studies, we examine how this shift-from writing documentation to editing an LLM-generated draft-impacts workers. We study this "first draft problem": eliminating the blank page does not remove the work of documentation but relocates it into revising and editing. In Study 1, an online experiment with 16 clinicians producing documentation following a teletherapy patient encounter, we establish the puzzle: counter to our hypotheses, editing an LLM-generated draft of the documentation as opposed to writing it from scratch does not result in time savings or quality improvements on average. Instead, while some clinicians experience no time savings but large improvements in quality after making substantial revisions, others experience meaningful time savings and no change in quality after making limited revisions. In other words, we observe significant heterogeneity in how clinicians engage with the same draft, which leads to variation in productivity and quality. In Study 2, a lab experiment with 100 university students summarizing video interviews, we unpack the mechanisms underlying this heterogeneity using granular keystroke logs, validated self-reports of workload, and micro-level physiological and eye-tracking measurements. In this setting, we find the expected productivity improvements: editing reduces task completion time by roughly 70%, raises quality, and lowers self-reported workload. Yet the physiological evidence tells a more nuanced story. Physiological markers indicate that fatigue accumulates faster when editing an LLM-generated draft than when writing from scratch. Thus, we find that (a) time savings can be real, but are setting dependent; (b) quality improvements are possible, but the relationship between how heavily a draft is revised and the quality of the result differs sharply across our two settings; and (c) while editing an LLM draft lowers reported cognitive load, the body still tires faster over time.

title: Toward a Validated Evaluation Framework for Hyper-Automation Anxiety in AI-Augmented Software Engineering

detail.title: Toward a Validated Evaluation Framework for Hyper-Automation Anxiety in AI-Augmented Software Engineering
detail.abstract: Hyper-Automation Anxiety has recently been proposed as a construct describing the job insecurity, identity loss, and career-progression paralysis reported by software engineers navigating autonomous, prompt-driven AI agents, operationalized across four psychological dimensionsjob security risk, loss of craft fulfillment, career progression ambiguity, and hyper-velocity learning fatigue-together with a candidate measurement index. That construct has not yet been situated within established organizational-psychology theory, nor has a validation path for the index been specified. This paper addresses both gaps. We position each of the four proposed dimensions against existing frameworks-technostress creators (Ragu-Nathan et al. 2008), occupational burnout (Maslach and Jackson 1981), and self-determination theory (Deci and Ryan 2000)-to clarify what the construct adds beyond established measures rather than duplicating them. We then set out a concrete validation roadmap for the Hyper-Automation Anxiety Index, covering sampling, reliability, and convergent and discriminant validity testing against these established scales, together with longitudinal tracking suited to a technology that itself changes on a near-weekly cycle. Finally, we read prospective index scores against the three organizational responses previously proposed for the construct, arguing that this mapping exposes the limits of managerial intervention as much as it guides it. The result is not a validated instrument-that empirical work remains for future research-but a theoretically grounded and methodologically specified path toward one.

title: Vehicle Routing Problem in Sustainable Pharmaceutical Cold Supply Chain: Optimizing Vaccine Distribution for Equity Enhancement
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Tehran

detail.title: Vehicle Routing Problem in Sustainable Pharmaceutical Cold Supply Chain: Optimizing Vaccine Distribution for Equity Enhancement
detail.abstract: Efficient and equitable distribution of vaccines through cold supply chains is essential for public health, particularly when products have strict temperature and shelf-life requirements. Real-world challenges such as variable demand, environmental sustainability goals, waste minimization requirements, and high distribution costs make planning and management complex. This study develops a multi-echelon bi-objective optimization model that integrates facility location, inventory control, routing decisions, and dynamic shelf-life constraints to address these challenges. The model aims to minimize total system cost and carbon emissions while ensuring fair allocation across demand points. An LP-metric method is applied to balance objectives, and the model's performance was evaluated using an actual case study, where it was solved with a metaheuristic method. Sensitivity analyses examine the effects of changes in key model parameters, such as shelf-life of the vaccine and cost of disposing expired vaccines, on the objective functions. The findings confirm that the proposed model improves cost efficiency (12–18% cost reduction), reduces environmental impact (11% emission savings), and enhances distribution fairness (≥94% demand fulfillment across all centers). These quantitative results offer practical insights for organizing vaccine cold supply chains.

title: Editorial: Information Literacy: A Discipline for the Future
affiliations: University of Sheffield, University of Missouri, , University of South Florida and

detail.title: Editorial: Information Literacy: A Discipline for the Future
detail.abstract: This special issue of Information Matters explores how the discipline of Information Literacy (IL) can develop: in the future, and for the future. The argument that IL is a subject of research and practice in its own right has been gaining ground, in particular with the formation in 2021 of the international collaboration, ILIAD (Information Literacy is a Discipline).
